r1.riskReason: Adobe offers COPPA/FERPA-compliant K-12 education terms when schools deploy Enterprise/Federated IDs, but standard individual Adobe IDs allow content analysis, marketing, and broader data sharing without the same K-12 protections.
r1.parentSummary: Adobe Acrobat Pro collects account information, usage data, device details, and document metadata to provide PDF services. For K-12 schools, Adobe offers special student data terms that comply with COPPA and FERPA when schools use Enterprise or Federated IDs, ensuring student data is not sold or used for advertising. However, if students use individual Adobe IDs instead of school-managed accounts, they do not receive these K-12 protections and Adobe may analyze content, share data with third parties, and use information for marketing purposes.

r2.minAge: 13 for individual Adobe ID; Under 13 with school consent via Enterprise/Federated ID
r2.riskReason: Adobe has separate K-12 education terms with COPPA/FERPA compliance when schools deploy Enterprise or Federated IDs, but the general consumer product collects extensive data including for advertising and shares with third parties, requiring careful K-12 implementation.
r2.parentSummary: Adobe Creative Cloud collects student login information, usage data, and content stored on Adobe servers. For K-12 schools, Adobe offers COPPA and FERPA-compliant deployment using Enterprise or Federated IDs where Adobe acts as a school official and does not use student data for advertising or sell it. However, if students use individual Adobe IDs (age 13+), their data may be used for advertising and shared with third parties, so schools must properly configure education accounts to protect student privacy.

r3.minAge: 13 for individual Adobe ID, Under 13 with school-managed Enterprise/Federated ID
r3.riskReason: While Adobe has strong K-12 compliance commitments (COPPA/FERPA) for school-managed accounts, the general consumer version collects extensive data, sells personal information for profit, and uses data for targeted advertising and profiling.
r3.parentSummary: Adobe Express collects names, email addresses, usage data, location, and content created by students. For K-12 school-managed accounts (Enterprise/Federated IDs), Adobe acts as a 'school official' under FERPA and commits not to sell student data or use it for advertising. However, individual Adobe IDs (age 13+) are subject to different terms that allow data sharing with advertisers and third parties. Schools should use the education-specific version with managed accounts to ensure maximum privacy protections.

r4.minAge: 13, Under 13 with school consent via K-12 education terms
r4.riskReason: Adobe has K-12 specific terms with FERPA/COPPA compliance for school-managed accounts, but individual Adobe IDs (age 13+) may involve broader data collection and marketing uses, and free users grant Adobe extensive licenses to inputs/outputs for any purpose.
r4.parentSummary: Adobe Firefly collects account information, usage data, and content created by users. For K-12 education accounts managed by schools, Adobe acts as a school official under FERPA and does not use student data for marketing or AI training. However, individual Adobe IDs allow broader data use, and free tier users grant Adobe perpetual licenses to their prompts and generated content. Schools must use Enterprise or Federated IDs to maintain student privacy protections.

r5.minAge: 13, Under 13 with school consent for Enterprise/Federated ID
r5.riskReason: Adobe Fresco requires an Adobe account and syncs artwork to Creative Cloud; for K-12 use, schools must deploy Enterprise or Federated IDs and obtain parental consent for students under 13, as individual Adobe IDs involve broader data sharing with advertising partners.
r5.parentSummary: Adobe Fresco collects account information, device data, usage analytics, and automatically syncs student artwork to Adobe's cloud servers. For K-12 students, schools should use Enterprise IDs (not personal Adobe IDs) to ensure student data is managed by the school with FERPA/COPPA protections and limited third-party sharing. Individual Adobe IDs are intended for adults and may involve advertising and tracking that is inappropriate for children.

r6.riskReason: Adobe Illustrator is a professional design tool not specifically built for K-12 education; when used via school-managed enterprise accounts with K-12 terms, Adobe acts as school official and complies with COPPA/FERPA, but individual consumer accounts collect extensive data including usage analytics and content analysis for product improvement.
r6.parentSummary: Adobe Illustrator collects personal information including name, email, payment details, usage data, and content created or stored. For K-12 schools using enterprise education licenses, Adobe agrees to act as a school official under FERPA and complies with COPPA, with schools managing student accounts and data rights. However, individual consumer accounts (not managed by schools) involve broader data collection, sharing with advertising partners, and machine learning analysis of content for product improvement, making school-managed deployment essential for K-12 privacy protection.

dataSharedWith: Business customers using Adobe Experience Cloud
r7.riskReason: Adobe collects extensive usage data and shares information with advertising partners; while COPPA/FERPA compliant for K-12 institutional accounts, individual Adobe IDs require age 13+ and default content analysis settings may raise privacy concerns.
r7.parentSummary: Adobe Lightroom collects account information (name, email), usage data, photo metadata, and device information to provide photo editing services. For K-12 use, schools must set up institutional accounts with appropriate consent; individual Adobe IDs require users to be 13+. Adobe has specific student data protections and acts as a 'school official' under FERPA, though the platform shares data with advertising partners and analyzes cloud-stored content by default unless users opt out in privacy settings.

r8.minAge: 13, Under 13 with school consent via Enterprise/Federated ID
r8.riskReason: Adobe's standard consumer version collects extensive data and shares with advertising partners, but offers K-12 education-specific terms with COPPA/FERPA compliance when schools use Enterprise/Federated IDs and proper configuration.
r8.parentSummary: Adobe Photoshop collects personal information including name, email, usage patterns, and content created or stored in the cloud, which may be analyzed using machine learning and shared with advertising partners. For K-12 schools, Adobe offers education-specific accounts with enhanced privacy protections, acts as a 'school official' under FERPA, and does not sell student data or use it for advertising when properly configured with Enterprise or Federated IDs, though schools must obtain parental consent for children under 13.

dataSharedWith: Business partners for advertising and sales
r9.riskReason: Adobe Podcast requires parental consent for students under 13 and Adobe acts as a school official under FERPA when deployed through K-12 institutional accounts, but individual Adobe ID accounts used outside school-managed deployments may expose students to advertising, profiling, and broader data sharing practices.
r9.parentSummary: Adobe Podcast collects audio recordings, transcripts, email addresses, and usage data to provide podcast recording and editing services. When used through a school's managed account, Adobe does not sell student data and acts as a school official under FERPA and COPPA. However, if students create individual Adobe IDs outside of school management, Adobe may use data for marketing and share it with advertising partners, making school-managed deployment critical for K-12 privacy protection.

r10.minAge: 13, Under 13 with school consent via Enterprise/Federated ID
dataCollected: Biometric data (for certain features like face grouping)
r10.riskReason: While Adobe has specific K-12 Student Data Terms committing to COPPA and FERPA compliance when schools use Enterprise/Federated IDs, Premiere Pro is a professional tool with broad data access provisions, cloud processing features, and content licensing terms that may concern schools without proper institutional deployment.
r10.parentSummary: Adobe Premiere Pro collects account information, usage data, device details, and content uploaded to Adobe's cloud services. For K-12 use, schools must deploy the software through Enterprise or Federated IDs to ensure COPPA and FERPA compliance, giving the school (not Adobe) control over student data. Adobe states it does not sell student data and acts as a 'school official' under FERPA, but the general privacy policy allows Adobe to access user content for service improvement and moderation, and grants Adobe a license to use uploaded content for operating services.

r11.riskReason: Amira operates as a school official under FERPA with strong privacy protections including no sale of student data, no targeted advertising, encryption, de-identified voice recordings, and districts retain full control over data.
r11.parentSummary: Amira collects student names, voice recordings as children read aloud, and reading progress data to provide personalized tutoring and assessment. The platform never sells student data or uses it for advertising, stores voice recordings in de-identified format, and does not share data with public AI platforms. Schools control all data collection and families can request access, corrections, or opt-out through their district.

dataSharedWith: Operational third parties for service delivery
Third-party analytics providers (Adobe, Google, Microsoft, Snapchat, Yahoo)
Colleges and universities (via Student Search Service with opt-in)
r12.riskReason: College Board shares extensive student data with multiple third parties including analytics vendors, has faced enforcement actions for data privacy violations, and uses tracking technologies that may enable behavioral profiling despite claims of no targeted advertising.
r12.parentSummary: AP Classroom collects detailed student information including name, demographics, assessment responses, and usage activity. Data is shared with teachers, school/district administrators, and the hosting platform Academic Merit LLC. College Board states it complies with FERPA and prohibits data sales, but has faced controversy over sharing student information with analytics companies like Adobe, Google, and Facebook for advertising purposes. Parents should be aware that student data may be used for internal research and shared with educational institutions.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: Privacy policy states it may be updated with notification required up to one week prior to exam date, but general notification process for policy changes is not clearly documented across all services.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: Privacy policy provides comprehensive list of data collected including personal identifiers, demographics, academic information, usage data, assessment submissions, and device information.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: Policy clearly states data is collected directly from students during registration, automatically through platform use, from schools/districts, and via cookies and tracking technologies.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: Student information belongs to the student, though College Board receives a perpetual license to use it; students retain independent rights to their test scores.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Students can request data deletion through a webform or email, but deletion may result in loss of access to account and scores; policy states deletion within 30 days unless legal obligation to retain.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: Policy states data is retained as needed for legitimate educational purposes and legal obligations, but does not specify exact retention periods for different data types.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: College Board describes ISO 27001 and SOC-2 certifications, industry-recognized security practices and standards, and administrative, technical, and physical safeguards to protect data.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: While security certifications suggest encryption, the privacy policy does not explicitly state that all data is encrypted in transit and at rest; credit card data uses tokenization.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: No mention of strong password enforcement requirements in the publicly available policies; students create accounts with passwords but strength requirements are not specified.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No mention of multi-factor authentication availability for student or educator accounts; accounts use username and password only.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: Cookie policy comprehensively lists cookie types (strictly necessary, performance, functional, marketing) with purposes and provides opt-out mechanisms including Global Privacy Control support.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: Policy names some third parties (Academic Merit LLC, ETS, analytics providers like Adobe and Google) but uses broad generalizations like 'operational third parties' and 'trusted vendors' without exhaustive listing.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: Policy states data is shared with specific entities but does not detail exactly what data each third party receives; uses grouped descriptions like 'usage data' or 'enrollment information.'
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Students can opt out of Student Search Service and marketing cookies, but cannot opt out of operational third-party sharing necessary for service delivery; limited opt-out for educational data sharing.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: Policy explicitly states that operational third parties have contractual requirements to protect data, cannot relicense or sell information, and are prohibited from using data except for College Board services.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: Privacy statement indicates it may be updated and users should review periodically, but does not explicitly commit to notifying users of changes to third-party relationships or data sharing practices.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: College Board explicitly states it does not display any third-party advertising on its site, meeting the requirement for no ads or platform-only ads.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: While College Board claims no targeted advertising, investigations found tracking cookies from ad vendors (Adobe, Google, Facebook, Snapchat) that could enable cross-site tracking and profiling.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Third-party tracking technologies from advertising vendors are present; College Board honors Global Privacy Control for opt-out but tracking cookies remain active for analytics purposes with limited transparency.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Policy acknowledges use of web beacons/pixels, cookies, and tracking technologies from third parties including Google, Adobe, and social media platforms for analytics and campaign measurement.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Cookie management tools allow opt-out of marketing cookies and GPC support exists, but opt-out for all third-party analytics and tracking is unclear; some tracking continues for 'functional' purposes.

The platform tracks learning progress to help students improve their ASL skills. The company explicitly states it never sells or shares student data with third parties and complies with both COPPA and FERPA regulations, making it a privacy-conscious choice for K-12 schools.

Children cannot create accounts themselves—only authorized adults (teachers, parents, or organizers) can grant access. The platform states it complies with COPPA and FERPA, does not sell student data, and allows parents to request data deletion.

The platform states it does not sell student data and mentions FERPA compliance for schools. However, the privacy policy does not explicitly address COPPA requirements for children under 13, though schools can provide consent on behalf of parents in educational contexts. Data is stored on AWS servers in the United States and shared with third-party service providers.

Student work is not stored after tasks are completed, and data is never sold or used to train AI models. The platform is FERPA and COPPA compliant with strong privacy protections, though student names may be stored if teachers include them in prompts.

r18.parentSummary: BusinessU collects student learning data (like assignment scores, time on task, and submitted work) to help teachers track progress, but does not collect student names unless the teacher chooses to add them. The platform is COPPA and FERPA compliant, does not sell student information to outside companies, and only shares data with teachers and district administrators. Parents can request to view or delete their child's information by contacting the teacher or school.

For Canva Education users, the platform is COPPA and FERPA compliant with iKeepSafe certification, does not show ads to students, does not sell student data, and does not use student work to train AI. Schools must obtain parental consent for children under 13 and supervise student use through teacher accounts.

CareerSafe is certified by iKeepSafe for K-12 privacy compliance and explicitly commits to COPPA, FERPA, and SOPIPA standards, with schools providing consent on behalf of parents for students under 13.

complianceNotes.SECQ2: Third-party source mentions Common App uses encryption and the platform is described as secure, but the privacy policy itself does not explicitly state encryption practices in available excerpts.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: Terms of use mention username and password requirements and user responsibility for account security, but no mention of enforced password strength requirements.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No mention of multi-factor authentication availability or requirement in the policy or terms of use.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: Cookie notice is referenced and appears to exist as a separate document with categories of cookies (necessary, functional) described on support pages.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: Policy specifically names third parties including service providers for address verification, payment card processors, member colleges and universities, and third-party organizations for aggregate data.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: Policy groups third parties by general category and describes general purposes (e.g., address verification, payment processing) but does not specify exact data shared with each named party.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: No opt-out mechanism for third-party sharing is mentioned in available policy sections, though data sharing with colleges is inherent to the application service.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: Policy states service providers are required to maintain confidentiality and security of children's information, providing some vendor responsibility, but full contractual requirements are not detailed.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: Policy states it may be modified at any time with changes posted, which could include third-party changes, but no specific notification process for third-party changes is described.

complianceNotes.ADVQ2: No targeted advertising is mentioned or evident; platform operates as a college application service without commercial advertising model.

complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Cookies are used for functional and security purposes based on cookie notice references, not for advertising tracking.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Not applicable as the platform does not appear to engage in advertising or share data with advertisers.

r93.minAge: 13 (Under 13 cannot create FSA ID per COPPA; paper application required)
r93.riskReason: StudentAid.gov is a federal government website operated by the U.S. Department of Education with strong privacy protections under FERPA and the Privacy Act of 1974, explicitly states data is not sold for marketing, and is not designed for K-12 use.
r93.parentSummary: StudentAid.gov is not a K-12 platform—it's a federal website for college financial aid. The site collects extensive personal and financial information including Social Security numbers, tax data, and loan history to administer federal student aid programs. Data is protected under federal law (FERPA and Privacy Act of 1974), is not sold to marketers, but is shared with colleges, loan servicers, and government agencies for educational and loan administration purposes.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: Privacy policy updates are posted with 30-day advance notice for material changes per servicer sites, but main StudentAid.gov privacy policy page was not fully accessible to verify comprehensive notification process.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: Comprehensive list of data collected is provided including name, SSN, address, financial information, tax data, employment, loan history, and educational information.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: Data collection methods are clearly specified including from FAFSA applications, IRS data transfers with consent, educational institutions, loan servicers, and consumer reporting agencies.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: Data ownership resides with the student/borrower under FERPA protections; government acts as custodian for federal student aid administration purposes.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Students can request updates, modifications, or deletion of personal information through online accounts or by contacting servicers; FERPA provides amendment rights.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: Personal information for loan servicing is retained for at least 7 years after full loan payment per federal requirements, with longer retention when legally required.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: Security measures are explicitly stated including physical access controls, monitoring by security personnel, firewalls, and Security Information Event Management systems.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: As a .gov federal website, HTTPS encryption is enforced throughout; multiple references to secure connections and encrypted transmission of sensitive data.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: Password requirements for FSA ID accounts are not specified in accessible documentation; no mention of enforced password complexity standards.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: Multi-factor authentication availability for FSA ID accounts is not clearly documented in accessible privacy policy materials.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: Cookie usage and tracking mechanisms are mentioned generally but comprehensive cookie policy listing all cookies with specific purposes was not accessible.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: Specific third parties are named including loan servicers (Edfinancial, MOHELA, Aidvantage), service provider Fiserv, IRS, Department of Defense, consumer reporting agencies, educational institutions, and state agencies.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: Specific types of data shared with each third party category are detailed including loan information to servicers, tax data to IRS, educational records to schools, and credit history to reporting agencies.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: No opt-out mechanism is available for mandatory data sharing required for federal student aid program administration and compliance with federal law.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: Third-party servicers and contractors are bound by Privacy Act of 1974 and FERPA requirements; federal government maintains responsibility for vendor compliance.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: General statement that privacy policy may be updated is present, but specific notification process for changes in third-party sharing relationships is not clearly documented.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: No advertisements are displayed on StudentAid.gov as a federal government website.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: No targeted advertising occurs; federal website does not engage in behavioral advertising or user profiling for marketing purposes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: No third-party tracking for advertising purposes; website is a federal .gov domain operated solely for student aid administration.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Only functional tracking for website operation and security; no web beacons or tracking pixels for advertising purposes on federal government site.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Not applicable as no data is shared with advertisers; federal law explicitly prohibits selling information to third parties for marketing purposes.

r91.riskReason: The platform explicitly prohibits users under 18, making it inappropriate for K-12 students, uses a generic WordPress privacy policy with no COPPA or FERPA compliance statements, collects extensive student data including demographics and phone numbers, shares data with third parties including Gravatar without clear consent mechanisms, and provides no specific educational data protections.
r91.parentSummary: HOSA collects student names, emails, phone numbers, demographic information, and activity data through its online affiliation and tracking systems. The platform's Terms of Service explicitly state users must be over 18, which conflicts with its K-12 student membership base. Data is shared with third-party services like Gravatar and embedded content providers, with minimal privacy protections and no COPPA or FERPA compliance mentioned.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: No advance notification process or revision history for policy changes is mentioned in either the Privacy Policy or Terms of Service.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: Some data types are listed (comments, cookies, email, images) but the extensive student affiliation data collected through the CMS system (demographics, phone numbers, charter information) is not addressed in the privacy policy.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: General statements about data collection through comments, cookies, and account creation exist, but specific collection methods for student affiliation data are not explained in the privacy policy.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: Data ownership is not addressed; the policy does not clarify whether users own their data or if the organization claims any ownership rights.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users can request data deletion but with significant limitations - data required for administrative, legal, or security purposes is retained indefinitely without specific timeframes.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: No specific data retention periods are stated; comments and metadata are retained indefinitely, and other data retention timeframes are not disclosed.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: No specific security measures are described in the privacy policy beyond standard WordPress cookie functionality; no mention of encryption, secure storage, or data protection protocols.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: No encryption practices are mentioned in either the Privacy Policy or Terms of Service.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: No password strength requirements or enforcement policies are mentioned; instructional documents reference passwords but do not specify security requirements.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No multi-factor authentication options are mentioned, and standard account creation appears to only require email and password.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: Cookies are mentioned with some purposes (saving comment details, login information, screen display choices) and durations (1 year for comment cookies, 2 days to 2 weeks for login cookies), but a comprehensive list of all cookies is not provided.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: Specific third parties are partially named (Gravatar/Automattic for profile pictures, spam detection services mentioned generically) but embedded content providers and other third-party services are described in broad terms without specific identification.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The privacy policy does not specify what data is shared with each third party; it only mentions that Gravatar receives an anonymized email hash and embedded content providers may collect data, use cookies, and track users.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: No opt-out mechanisms for third-party data sharing are provided; users cannot easily opt out of Gravatar integration or embedded content tracking.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: No mention of requiring third parties to follow vendor agreements or data protection standards; the policy explicitly disclaims responsibility for third-party practices.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: No notification process for changes to third-party relationships or additions of new third-party services is mentioned.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: No advertising is mentioned in the privacy policy or terms of service; the platform appears to operate as a non-profit student organization without ads.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: No targeted advertising is present or mentioned; the platform does not appear to use user data for advertising purposes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: No third-party advertising tracking is mentioned, consistent with the absence of advertising on the platform.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Web beacons for advertising are not mentioned, though embedded content from other websites may use tracking methods; Gravatar integration may enable some cross-site tracking of user profiles.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Not applicable as no advertising data sharing is present, though users cannot opt out of third-party services like Gravatar that may track profiles across sites.

complianceNotes.DCQ3: Privacy Policy does not clearly state that users own their data and grants Modern States extensive rights to user content.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Privacy Policy states users can cancel accounts and request deletion but indicates Modern States may retain data for legal compliance, security, and fraud detection without clear timeframes.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: Privacy Policy states data is retained while account is active and may be retained after cancellation for various purposes but does not specify retention periods.

complianceNotes.SHRQ2: Privacy Policy does not specify what data is shared with each category of third party or provide granular disclosure.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Privacy Policy does not provide clear opt-out mechanisms for third-party data sharing except for email marketing and social media connections.

complianceNotes.SHRQ5: Privacy Policy does not indicate Modern States will notify users of changes to third-party sharing arrangements.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The privacy policy does not provide information about policy change notification processes or version history availability.

complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy mentions data is collected through registration forms and email communications but lacks detailed explanation of all collection methods.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The privacy policy does not specify who owns the data collected from participants.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: The privacy policy does not mention user rights to delete their data or account information.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The privacy policy does not specify how long participant data is retained or when it is deleted.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The privacy policy does not describe specific security measures used to protect participant data.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The privacy policy does not mention encryption of data in transit or at rest for participant information.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The privacy policy and registration documents do not mention password strength requirements or enforcement.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: The privacy policy and registration documents do not mention multi-factor authentication availability.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The privacy policy mentions that cookies may be placed on users' computers but does not list specific cookies or their purposes.

complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Participants can opt out of email communications and mailing lists by contacting the CyberPatriot Program Office or clicking unsubscribe links in emails.

complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The privacy policy does not state whether users will be notified of changes to third-party sharing arrangements.

r371.riskReason: GroupMe lacks end-to-end encryption, has no parental controls, lacks FERPA compliance documentation, and shares data with Microsoft affiliates and third parties for various purposes including personalized advertising.
r371.parentSummary: GroupMe collects personal information including names, phone numbers, contacts, messages, photos, and location data. The app lacks end-to-end encryption meaning Microsoft can read messages, and has no parental controls to limit content or contacts. Data is shared with Microsoft affiliates, vendors, and used for personalized advertising and service improvements.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: Microsoft provides advance notice of policy changes and maintains a summary of changes with effective dates on their Services Agreement Updates page.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: Microsoft Privacy Statement lists specific data types collected including names, contact information, device data, usage data, location, messages, and media content.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The privacy statement explains data is collected directly from users during account creation, through service usage, and via interactions with products.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: Microsoft claims rights to process user data for various purposes including personalized advertising and service improvements, with unclear ownership boundaries.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users can access and delete data through Microsoft privacy dashboard, but deletion may be limited by operational and legal requirements with unclear timeframes.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy mentions data retention for operational purposes and legal compliance but does not specify exact retention periods for most data types.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The privacy statement mentions security measures generally but does not provide specific technical security controls or encryption details.

complianceNotes.SECQ5: The privacy statement mentions cookies are used for preferences, sign-ins, and personalized ads but does not provide a comprehensive list of all cookies used.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The policy mentions data sharing with Microsoft affiliates, vendors, and service providers but does not name specific third-party partners.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy groups third parties into broad categories without specifying what data is shared with each individual third party.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can opt out of personalized advertising through Microsoft privacy dashboard settings, but cannot opt out of data sharing with vendors and service providers.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: Microsoft states that vendors and agents working on their behalf must abide by data privacy and security requirements and cannot use personal data for other purposes.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: Microsoft provides notice of policy changes on their Updates page but does not explicitly state that users will be notified specifically about changes to third-party sharing.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: GroupMe does not display ads within the core app experience, but data is used for personalized advertising across Microsoft products and services.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Microsoft uses data to personalize user experiences and send promotional communications, which may include targeted content based on user interactions.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Microsoft uses cookies and tracking technologies for personalized advertising purposes with no clear opt-out specifically for GroupMe users beyond general Microsoft settings.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Microsoft uses web beacons, cookies, and similar tracking technologies including advertising IDs to deliver personalized ads and gather usage data.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Users can opt out of personalized advertising through Microsoft privacy dashboard but the process is not clearly explained in GroupMe-specific documentation.

r993.riskReason: Privacy policy lacks specific detail on data types collected, retention periods, encryption practices, and COPPA/FERPA compliance despite serving K-12 students and requiring minimum age of 13.

The platform states it does not sell student data and only shares information with staff, the platform provider Cyber Skyline, or third parties with consent. However, the privacy policy is vague about specific protections, data retention, and lacks explicit COPPA or FERPA compliance statements despite serving students as young as 13.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: Privacy policy states they may update policies and indicates changes on the website, but does not specify advance notification to users or provide revision history.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: Privacy policy mentions personal information collection during registration and mentions cookies and usage data, but does not provide comprehensive list of all specific data types collected.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: Policy states information is collected when users register, contribute to or use site features, and mentions cookies, but lacks specific detail on collection methods.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: Privacy policy states NCL is the sole owner of all information collected on the site, not the user.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Privacy policy allows users to contact them to change information and states users can request changes, but does not clearly specify full deletion rights or process.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: Privacy policy does not specify any data retention period or timeline for how long student data is kept.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: Privacy policy mentions certain sections use encryption and cryptographic/hashing standards, and uses reasonable precautions, but does not list specific security measures.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: Policy states certain sections encrypt data using cryptographic and hashing standards but acknowledges no transmission over Internet is totally secure.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: Terms of use require users keep passwords confidential using credential management best practices, but does not specify enforcement of strong password requirements.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No mention of multi-factor authentication or SSO options in the privacy policy or terms of use.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: Privacy policy mentions cookies are used for traffic analysis and personalization and describes cookie purpose generally, but does not list all specific cookies.

complianceNotes.SHRQ2: Policy does not specify what particular data is shared with each third party category.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Privacy policy states they will only share contact details with third parties if user gives consent, suggesting opt-in model, but opt-out process is unclear.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: Privacy policy does not mention whether third-party vendors must follow contractual data protection agreements.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: Privacy policy states they may update from time to time and will indicate changes on website, but does not specifically address notification of third-party sharing changes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: No evidence of advertising displayed on the platform based on website review and privacy policy.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Privacy policy does not mention targeted advertising or behavioral tracking for ad purposes.

complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Privacy policy mentions cookies for website functionality and traffic analysis only, not for advertising purposes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: No advertising data sharing mentioned in privacy policy, making opt-out not applicable.

r1030.parentSummary: Canvas collects student names, grades, assignments, and activity data to provide learning management services. Instructure does not sell student data and has signed the Student Privacy Pledge. Data is encrypted and stored securely with Amazon Web Services. Schools can add third-party educational tools that may access student information, so parents should ask their school which integrations are enabled.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: Privacy Policy and Terms are updated with notice to users and previous versions are available for review.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: Comprehensive list of data collected including personal data, institutional data, user content, and usage analytics is provided in privacy policy.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: Privacy policy specifies data is collected directly from schools via SIS integration, from users directly, and automatically through platform usage.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: Terms explicitly state user content belongs to users and Instructure does not claim ownership of customer data.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users and schools can request deletion of accounts and data; administrators can delete user accounts at any time.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: General retention statement provided but no specific time period stated; data deleted upon request or contract termination.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: Detailed security measures listed including AWS hosting, encryption policies, access controls, DDoS protection, and SOC 2/ISO 27001 compliance.

complianceNotes.SECQ3: Passwords are encrypted using SHA512 with user-specific salt but policy does not specify strong password enforcement requirements.

complianceNotes.SECQ5: Cookies are listed and explained for functionality, security, and analytics purposes in privacy documentation.

complianceNotes.SHRQ2: AWS hosting relationship specified but individual LTI tool data sharing depends on school-configured integrations and is not fully detailed.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: No third-party data sales occur per policy; LTI tool sharing controlled by school administrators who configure integrations.

complianceNotes.ADVQ1: No advertisements displayed to students, parents, or educators per privacy policy and Free for Teacher terms.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: No targeted advertising to students; marketing privacy policy applies only to website visitors, not product users.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: No third-party tracking for advertising purposes within the Canvas product per privacy statements.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Cookies and analytics used only for platform functionality, security, and improvement, not for advertising.

complianceNotes.DCQ2: Policy specifies data is collected from schools via SIS integrations, OneSync automated syncs, OneRoster standard, and CSV uploads from educational institutions.

complianceNotes.DCQ3: Google Workspace for Education terms clearly state that Customer owns all Customer Data, and education organizations retain full rights over intellectual property in customer data.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users can delete data through Download Your Data, delete activity from My Activity, and have full control to delete content from Google Account at any time.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: Google's retention policy specifies various retention periods including up to 6 months for deleted data removal, up to 9 months for browser data, and indefinite retention for useful data with user control.

complianceNotes.SECQ2: Data is encrypted in transit and at rest as explicitly stated, but Google Chat does not offer end-to-end encryption which is a limitation.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: Google enforces strong password requirements and account security through age verification, password complexity requirements, and account security checks.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: Google accounts support 2-Step Verification and Advanced Protection Program, and can integrate with SSO via SAML for organizational accounts.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: Privacy Policy describes cookie usage including purposes for cookies, pixel tags, local storage, and provides user controls to manage cookie settings.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: Privacy Policy names specific third parties including affiliates, trusted service providers for data centers and operations, and security partners.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy provides general categories of what is shared with service providers but does not specify exact data types per individual third party.

complianceNotes.SHRQ4: Google requires service providers to process data based on Google's instructions and in compliance with Privacy Policy and appropriate confidentiality and security measures.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: Privacy Policy states it may be updated and users are notified of material changes, but does not specifically commit to notifying users of third-party relationship changes.

complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Not applicable as Google Workspace for Education does not serve ads to students, eliminating the need for opt-out mechanisms for advertising data sharing.

r178.riskReason: Candy Crush Saga is a consumer gaming app not designed for educational use that sells personal data to advertisers, displays personalized ads, uses extensive third-party tracking, and lacks COPPA compliance mechanisms required for K-12 educational settings.
r178.parentSummary: Candy Crush Saga collects extensive data including device information, gameplay activity, location, and personal identifiers to power targeted advertising and marketing. The app shares and sells this data with numerous advertising and marketing partners who track users across websites and apps. r251.riskReason: No account required, diagram data never stored on vendor servers, no tracking or cookies, data remains on user's device or chosen storage location, and vendor explicitly states they do not share or sell any information.
r251.parentSummary: Diagrams.net (draw.io) is a privacy-focused diagramming tool that requires no account or registration. When students use it, their diagram data stays only in their web browser while working and is saved to wherever they choose (Google Drive, local device, etc.), never passing through or stored on the vendor's servers. The service collects only minimal technical data (IP address and device info) stored in logs for 10 days for debugging purposes, with no tracking, cookies, advertisements, or data sharing with third parties.

r252.riskReason: Dictionary.com collects extensive data including biometric information, shares data with third-party advertisers and data brokers, displays targeted advertising, and lacks clear security and encryption disclosures while collecting data from children under 16 without robust parental consent mechanisms.
r252.parentSummary: Dictionary.com collects a wide range of personal information including names, emails, location data, browsing behavior, and even biometric data from users age 16 and up, and from younger students through its Academy Tutors program with school or parental consent. This data is shared with advertising partners, analytics providers, and the parent company IAC Group for targeted advertising and marketing purposes. While the platform claims data can be deleted upon request, the extensive data collection and third-party sharing for advertising purposes present significant privacy concerns for K-12 students.

r254.riskReason: Discord is not FERPA compliant, collects extensive personal data including message content and third-party demographic information, shares data with numerous third parties including for targeted advertising purposes, and is not designed for educational use with student records.

While Discord states it does not sell personal information, it shares data with service providers, analytics partners, measurement partners for advertising, and third-party developers. The platform has end-to-end encryption for voice/video and offers privacy controls, but is not FERPA compliant for educational records and has had security incidents including data breaches.

Data is encrypted in transit and at rest using TLS 1.2 and AES-256, and subprocessors are contractually bound with no independent right to use student data. Parents should be aware that older Boom Cards decks containing YouTube videos may expose students to YouTube's advertising tracking cookies if played.

complianceNotes.ADVQ5: No Privacy Policy exists at cadsnapcad.com, so there is no opt-out process described for data sharing with advertisers.

dataSharedWith: Social media platforms (Facebook, Twitter, YouTube, Instagram, SoundCloud)
r816.riskReason: Choral Tracks has no minimum age requirement, no COPPA or FERPA disclosures, uses advertising pixels and third-party tracking cookies that could profile students, and does not restrict data collection for users under 13.
r816.parentSummary: Choral Tracks collects personal information such as name, email, payment details, IP addresses, and browsing behavior through cookies and advertising pixels shared with third-party ad partners. The platform explicitly states it does not sell personal information for advertising, but it does allow third-party advertising partners to place tracking technologies on users' browsers. There is no mention of COPPA compliance, no minimum age requirement, and no specific protections for students or children under 13, making it a significant privacy concern for K-12 school use.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The Terms state material changes will be communicated via prominent notice or email, and the Privacy Policy references an effective date for tracking revisions, but no formal revision history archive is provided.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The Privacy Policy lists several categories of data collected (name, email, payment info, IP address, clickstream, cookies) but does not provide a comprehensive enumerated list of every data type collected.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy describes some collection methods (account registration, purchases, cookies, pixel tags, server logs, social media integration) but lacks a fully structured breakdown of active vs. passive collection.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The Privacy Policy does not explicitly state that users own their data; ownership language is absent and the policy implies Choral Tracks controls and retains data at its discretion.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users may request removal of their information by contacting the company, but the policy notes data may still be retained even after deletion requests for legal, fraud prevention, and liability purposes.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy states data is deleted or anonymized when no longer needed for a legitimate business purpose, but no specific retention timeframe (e.g., number of days or years) is provided.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The Privacy Policy acknowledges security measures exist but only offers a general caveat that no system is 100% secure, without listing specific safeguards such as encryption standards or access controls.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: No mention of HTTPS, SSL/TLS, or data encryption is made in Choral Tracks' Privacy Policy or Terms, leaving encryption status unconfirmed.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The Terms place password security responsibility entirely on the user with no mention of platform-enforced strong password requirements or complexity rules.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No multi-factor authentication, SSO, or LTI integration is mentioned anywhere in the Terms or Privacy Policy.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The Privacy Policy and separate Cookie Policy acknowledge use of cookies across four categories (necessary, analytical, functional, advertising/targeting) but do not list specific cookies by name or provide a granular cookie inventory.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The policy broadly references third-party payment processors, advertising partners, and fulfillment providers but does not name specific companies (e.g., Stripe, Google Ads).
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy groups data sharing by category of third party without specifying exactly which data elements are shared with each type of partner.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can opt out of marketing emails via unsubscribe links or by emailing the company, but no opt-out mechanism for third-party advertising cookie tracking is clearly described.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy states third-party service providers are contractually restricted to use data only per Choral Tracks' instructions, but advertising partners' obligations are described more vaguely.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The Privacy Policy states it may be modified at any time at Choral Tracks' sole discretion, with no specific commitment to notify users when third-party data-sharing relationships change.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: Choral Tracks explicitly enables third-party advertising partners to place pixels and tracking GIFs to manage online advertising, indicating advertising is present on the platform.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: The Privacy Policy confirms advertising partners use cookies to recognize users across sessions and serve targeted advertising, constituting user-level targeting.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Third-party advertising partners are permitted to place tracking pixels and cookies on users' browsers with no clear opt-out mechanism disclosed within the policy for this specific tracking.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The policy confirms use of pixels, transparent GIF files (web beacons), and cookies by advertising partners, with no indication these are limited to functional purposes only.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Users may opt out of marketing emails from Choral Tracks directly, but there is no clear process described for opting out of data sharing specifically with advertising partners or third-party trackers.

dataSharedWith: Technology service providers (web hosting, analytics, chat)
r1033.riskReason: Clever is a school-controlled SSO and data integration platform that explicitly prohibits student data sale, targeted advertising to students, and profiling, is FERPA/COPPA compliant, holds multiple independent privacy certifications, and gives districts granular control over all data sharing.
r1033.parentSummary: Clever collects student information (such as name, grade, and school ID) on behalf of schools to enable secure single sign-on to authorized educational apps, and does not use that data for advertising or sell it to third parties. All data sharing is controlled by the school district, which authorizes which applications can receive student data. Clever holds strong privacy certifications (Student Privacy Pledge, iKeepSafe, 1EdTech TrustEd Apps Seal, CommonSense 'Use Responsibly' rating) and encrypts data both in transit and at rest.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: Clever maintains a public change history page (clever.com/trust/privacy/change-history) and the privacy policy states at least 30 days advance notice will be given to schools for material changes.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy policy and DPA explicitly enumerate data types collected including student name, ID, grade, class roster, IP address, device data, usage logs, cookies, and location approximation via IP.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The privacy policy clearly distinguishes data collected directly from schools, data provided by students logging in, and data automatically collected via tracking technologies such as cookies and web beacons.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: Clever explicitly states schools own student data and that Clever does not own or control it; the TOS reinforces that schools remain responsible for student data.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Schools may request deletion of student data within 10 business days (except backups deleted within 60 days), and Clever states it will always delete district data upon request; however deletion of data already shared with third-party developers must be requested directly from those developers.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The security practices page states backups are stored no longer than 60 days; the privacy policy states student data is deleted promptly after school account termination, and inactive account data retention is addressed in the Additional Terms for Schools.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: Clever's security practices page lists AES256-GCM encryption at rest and in transit, TLS/HSTS, firewalls, physical access controls, logical separation, automated threat detection, third-party security audits, bug bounty program, criminal background checks for employees, and cyber liability insurance.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: Clever explicitly states it encrypts all PII in transit and at rest using AES256-GCM, uses SSL/TLS with an A-rated TLS configuration from SSLLabs, and enforces HSTS.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: Clever recommends strong passwords per CommonSense evaluation findings but does not appear to technically enforce complexity requirements on end users; SSO/badge login is available as an alternative that reduces password risk.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: Clever explicitly supports two-factor authentication for employee access and SSO for student and teacher authentication, meeting the intent of this requirement for a school-mediated platform.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: Clever publishes a dedicated subprocessors page (clever.com/trust/subprocessors) listing third-party processors with access to student PII, and the privacy policy names categories such as web hosting, chat, and analytics providers.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The subprocessors page lists vendors but does not granularly itemize exactly which specific data fields each subprocessor receives; data shared with school-authorized developer applications is authorized per-app by the district but not enumerated centrally by Clever.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Districts have full control via the Clever dashboard to authorize or revoke application access to student data, and an unsubscribe option exists for promotional emails; however opt-out from subprocessor sharing for core service delivery is not individually available.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: Clever requires all subprocessors to execute written agreements binding them to the same privacy and security protections, and all Clever Library apps must sign the Universal Data Sharing Agreement.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The privacy policy and change history page indicate Clever notifies schools of material policy changes with at least 30 days notice, and the subprocessors page notes the list may change as Clever grows, implying updates may occur without individual advance notice per change.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: Clever explicitly states it does not display advertising to students on Clever, and the compliance page confirms no ads are directed at authenticated student users.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Clever explicitly prohibits using student data for targeted advertising and does not permit third-party advertising networks to collect information about authenticated users for targeting purposes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Clever states it does not permit third-party ad networks to track authenticated service users, but acknowledges third-party partners may collect device and usage data from adult-directed public pages (e.g., support pages) for tracking and advertising purposes, with a Cookie Preference Center opt-out available.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Clever uses cookies, web beacons, and similar tracking technologies on its website including on adult-directed pages where third-party advertising partners may collect data, though authenticated student users are explicitly excluded from ad-purpose tracking.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Clever provides a Cookie Preference Center for opting out of targeted advertising/sales, a consumer rights form, and email contact (trust@clever.com) for privacy rights requests, including the right to opt out of data sharing for targeted advertising under applicable state laws.

r817.riskReason: CNN 10 is a general-audience commercial news platform that displays targeted, interest-based advertising supported by third-party trackers and cookies, with no K-12-specific data protections, no student data agreements, and no mechanisms designed to prevent data collection from minors in a school context.
r817.parentSummary: CNN 10 is a free, no-account-required video news platform widely used in classrooms, but it operates under CNN's general consumer privacy policy, which permits the collection of device identifiers, IP addresses, usage data, and browsing behavior through cookies and third-party tracking technologies for targeted advertising purposes. CNN states it does not knowingly collect personal information from children under 13 without parental consent, but since no account or age verification is required to access the site, there is no mechanism in place to prevent passive data collection from student visitors. Parents and educators should be aware that third-party ad trackers are embedded in the site and may collect and share student browsing data with advertising partners, and there are no FERPA or SOPIPA-specific protections or school data agreements in place.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: CNN's Terms of Use state that changes take effect upon posting with no advance notice to users, though some notification may appear on the homepage for the first week; there is no formal revision history available.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy policy lists broad categories of data collected (name, email, device data, usage data, location) but does not comprehensively enumerate all data types, particularly those collected passively via third-party trackers.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The privacy policy specifically describes how data is collected — directly from users, through the website and mobile app, via cookies and tracking technologies, and from third-party sources.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The privacy policy does not clearly assign data ownership to users; submitted user content is treated as non-confidential and CNN/Turner claims broad rights to use it, indicating company rather than user ownership.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users can submit deletion requests through the CNN Privacy Center (cnn.com/privacy), but the process is form-based and not immediate, representing a limited rather than full self-service deletion option.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The privacy policy does not specify a concrete data retention period; it contains only general references to retaining data as needed for business purposes without defined timeframes.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: CNN/WarnerMedia references encryption, access controls, and monitoring for unauthorized access in its privacy disclosures, but specific technical security standards or certifications are not detailed.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: CNN's website operates over HTTPS, providing encryption in transit; WarnerMedia's policy references encryption as a security measure, indicating at least baseline encryption is in place.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: No account is required to access CNN 10, so strong password enforcement is not applicable; this criterion is effectively met by the no-account-required access model.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No account or login is required to use CNN 10, making MFA and SSO requirements non-applicable; access is anonymous and requires no authentication.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The privacy policy mentions cookies and tracking technologies generally and references a cookie preference/opt-out mechanism, but does not provide a comprehensive list of all cookies by name and specific purpose.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The privacy policy references broad categories of third parties (ad networks, analytics providers, affiliates, partners) but does not name specific third-party companies in the main policy, though court documents have identified trackers like PubMatic and Magnite.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy groups data sharing by category of third party rather than specifying which precise data fields are shared with each named partner, making it difficult to assess per-party data exposure.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: An opt-out for targeted advertising is referenced (wbdprivacy.com/opt-out), but the opt-out is not prominently placed on CNN 10 itself and does not prevent all passive data collection by third-party trackers.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The privacy policy contains a general statement that third-party service providers are obligated to use data only for specified purposes, but no comprehensive vendor agreement framework or enforcement mechanism is described.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The Terms of Use state that changes take effect immediately upon posting with no advance user notification; there is no stated process for notifying users when third-party data-sharing arrangements change.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: CNN 10 displays advertisements as part of the broader CNN.com platform, including personalized/interest-based ads served via third-party ad networks, which are confirmed by CNN's own help page noting that 'we personalize some ad experiences on CNN.'
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: CNN's privacy policy and help documentation explicitly confirm interest-based (targeted) advertising is practiced on the platform using data collected from user behavior and third-party identifiers.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Third-party trackers (including ad platforms) are embedded in CNN's website and collect IP addresses and browsing data to serve targeted ads, with no automatic opt-out for K-12 users or students visiting the site.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: CNN's privacy policy and court filings confirm the use of web beacons, pixels, cookies, and SDKs by CNN and third-party ad partners to track user behavior for advertising measurement and ad delivery purposes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: An opt-out mechanism for targeted advertising exists at wbdprivacy.com/opt-out, but it is not clearly surfaced on the CNN 10 page itself and the process for exercising it is not straightforward for school-age users or educators.

r818.riskReason: Common Sense Education is a nonprofit platform that explicitly prohibits third-party advertising and data sales, supports COPPA, maintains a public Subprocessor List, and applies enhanced protections for minors including parental consent requirements and non-necessary cookie restrictions for logged-in teens and children.
r818.parentSummary: Common Sense Education (commonsense.org/education) collects basic account information such as name, username, email, age, and school details when educators or members register, and uses cookies and web beacons for site functionality and analytics. The platform explicitly states that no data is used for third-party advertising on its education domain, does not rent or sell personal information for profit, and requires third-party service providers to meet equivalent privacy standards. Parents of children under 13 are notified and asked for consent before their child's data is used, and accounts for children under 13 are being fully discontinued as of October 2025, further reducing risk for K-12 students.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The privacy policy has a published effective date (December 3, 2024) and a revision history is implied by the availability of a former version, but the policy does not clearly describe an advance notification process for users before changes take effect.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy policy enumerates specific categories of personal information collected including name, username, email, age, school information, SSO data, usage data, and cookies, providing a reasonably complete data inventory.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy specifically describes multiple collection methods including direct user input during registration, Single Sign-On services, cookies and web beacons, and third-party sources such as education partners and social media platforms.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The policy is ambiguous on ownership; users can edit or delete profile data, but the policy does not explicitly state that users own their data, and aggregated non-personal information may be used or disclosed for any purpose at Common Sense's discretion.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Members can change or remove profile information by logging in and accessing 'My Account,' and parents can request deletion of children's personal information, satisfying the full deletion standard.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy states data is retained while there is an ongoing legitimate business need and deleted or anonymized when no longer needed, but does not specify a concrete retention period in days or months, making this only a general retention statement.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The policy states that 'reasonable administrative, organizational, technical, and physical measures' are used to protect personal information, but does not enumerate specific security controls, protocols, or certifications.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The policy does not explicitly state that data is encrypted in transit or at rest; the site uses HTTPS (implied by the live domain), but encryption is not described in the privacy policy text itself.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: Single Sign-On (SSO) via services like Google is supported for educator members, and the platform does not describe a separate password creation process for educators using SSO, effectively meeting this standard through SSO availability.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: SSO/Single Sign-On authentication is explicitly supported for educator members, satisfying the MFA/SSO standard for account access.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: A dedicated Cookie Policy exists that lists cookie types and purposes, distinguishes between the education site (no advertising cookies) and the media site, and provides a Cookie Settings link for users to manage or opt out of non-necessary cookies.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The policy references a publicly available Subprocessor List for third-party service providers, and names specific third parties in the older policy version (e.g., Learning Locker for Digital Citizenship Quizzes), meeting the standard for named third-party disclosure.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy states third parties receive only the personal information needed to perform their functions, but does not provide a granular per-third-party breakdown of exactly which data fields are shared with each vendor; the Subprocessor List provides additional but incomplete detail.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can opt out of cookies via Cookie Settings, opt out of email marketing via unsubscribe links, and the education site explicitly does not use third-party advertising cookies, effectively eliminating the main opt-out concern for the education domain.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy explicitly states that third-party service providers are obligated to meet the same level of data privacy and protection as Common Sense, and are required to notify Common Sense if they can no longer meet those standards, with compliance monitored by Common Sense.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy does not explicitly commit to notifying users when specific third-party subprocessors are added or changed; the Subprocessor List is maintained but users are not described as receiving proactive notice of changes to it.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The privacy policy and cookie policy both explicitly state that no advertising or targeting cookies are placed on the education site (commonsense.org), and any advertising activities are confined to the separate commonsensemedia.org media site.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: The policy explicitly states that no data is used for third-party advertising or collected on Common Sense Education domains for such purposes, and the cookie policy confirms no targeting or advertising cookies are set on the education site.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: The cookie policy confirms that tracking to deliver targeted content does not occur on the education site (commonsense.org), and the only third-party tracking noted involves embedded YouTube links which redirect to YouTube's own platform.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The education site uses only functional/analytics cookies with no advertising or social media tracking cookies, and web beacons are referenced only in the context of cookie and analytics use as described in the Cookie Policy.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Users can manage and opt out of non-necessary cookies via the Cookie Settings link, and can unsubscribe from marketing emails; since no third-party advertising data sharing occurs on the education domain, the opt-out is effectively complete.
