r314.riskReason: FigJam's privacy policy explicitly permits third-party advertising partners to set tracking technologies and collect data for interest-based advertising, and automatically collects advertising identifiers and similar data even from children, creating significant COPPA compliance risk for K-12 deployments without a school institutional agreement.
r314.parentSummary: FigJam (operated by Figma, Inc.) collects account information, usage data, device identifiers, and user-generated content; it also allows third-party advertising partners to use cookies, pixel tags, and web beacons to track users for interest-based advertising. Students under 13 may only use the platform if their school signs a formal institutional agreement with Figma, which provides additional protections, but the general privacy policy permits extensive third-party data sharing and advertising tracking that is not appropriate for K-12 use without that agreement in place. Figma does offer strong enterprise-grade security (SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, encryption in transit and at rest) and states it will not sell customer personal data under its DPA, but schools should carefully vet whether an institutional DPA is in place before deploying FigJam with any students.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: Figma states it will notify users of significant privacy policy changes via the Services or email, but does not maintain a publicly accessible revision history with clear version dates for user review.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy policy provides a detailed and comprehensive list of all categories of personal data collected, including account info, automatic data, student account info, and user-generated content.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy clearly explains how data is collected — directly from users, automatically via cookies/tracking technologies, and from third parties — with specific examples for each method.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: For enterprise/school accounts, the DPA clarifies that the customer (school) acts as the Controller and Figma as the Processor; however, for standard consumer accounts the ownership relationship is less clearly stated in favor of users.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users may request deletion of personal information and account at any time per the privacy policy, and the DPA specifies Figma will delete customer data within 30 days of request, meeting deletion requirements.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy states data is retained as long as necessary to fulfill the purpose or comply with law, but does not specify concrete retention timeframes; the DPA references a 'data retention schedule' without publishing specific periods.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: Figma's security page and DPA describe specific technical and organizational measures including physical, administrative, and technical safeguards, SOC 2 Type II certification, ISO 27001/27018, and annual independent audits.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: Figma explicitly states customer data is encrypted in transit (TLS 1.2+) and at rest, with encryption keys protected from unauthorized use — confirmed across multiple policy documents.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The ToS requires unique user IDs per authorized user and prohibits credential sharing, but the general privacy policy does not explicitly state that strong passwords are enforced at the platform level.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: Figma supports SSO/LTI integrations for enterprise and education plans, and the SSA mentions unique user ID assignment; however, MFA is not explicitly described as enforced or universally available for all account types.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The privacy policy mentions cookies, pixel tags, web beacons, local storage, and analytics technologies, and references a 'Your Choices' section and EU cookie consent tool, but does not provide a complete enumerated list of all cookies with their individual purposes.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The privacy policy references categories of third parties (advertising partners, analytics providers, service providers, law enforcement) but does not name specific advertising or analytics partners beyond Google Analytics.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy groups data shared with third parties by category rather than specifying what data is shared with each named third party, making it unclear exactly what information each party receives.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can opt out of interest-based advertising via the 'Your Choices' section, browser settings, or industry opt-out programs; however, cookie-based opt-outs do not work on mobile apps, limiting the effectiveness of opt-out for all users.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The DPA and SSA explicitly require subprocessors to protect customer data with at least the same level of care as Figma itself, and Figma remains contractually responsible for subprocessor compliance.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: Figma's DPA states that prior to engaging new subprocessors, Figma will notify customers by posting proposed new subprocessors to its published subprocessors list, giving customers the right to object.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The privacy policy explicitly states that third-party advertising partners are allowed to set tracking tools within the Services and deliver targeted advertisements, which is not appropriate for a K-12 platform.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Figma's privacy policy confirms it allows third-party advertising partners to collect data for 'interest-based advertising' or 'personalized advertising,' meaning confirmed user targeting occurs.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: An opt-out for interest-based advertising is mentioned (via 'Your Choices' and industry opt-out programs), but it is not straightforward and cookie-based opt-outs are ineffective on mobile, limiting protection.

complianceNotes.ADVQ5: The Privacy Policy references opt-out options under 'Your Choices' (including Google Analytics opt-out and instructions to opt out of third-party advertising), but the process is scattered across multiple instructions rather than a single, clear centralized opt-out mechanism.

r317.riskReason: FlipHTML5 uses interest-based advertising via Google Ads, Bing Ads, and Facebook Ads with third-party tracking cookies and web beacons, makes no COPPA or FERPA-specific provisions, has no parental consent mechanism, allows policy changes without advance notice, and collects extensive behavioral and location data from all users including those as young as 13.
r317.parentSummary: FlipHTML5 collects a broad range of personal and behavioral data including email, location, device info, mouse movements, and session recordings, and shares this data with advertising platforms such as Google Ads, Bing Ads, and Facebook Ads for interest-based advertising. The platform sets a minimum age of 13 but has no COPPA-compliant parental consent process, no dedicated student data protections, and no FERPA compliance language. Parents and schools should be aware that targeted advertising tools actively track user behavior on this platform, and the privacy policy can be changed at any time without advance notice to users.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The privacy policy explicitly states changes are 'effective upon posting without notice' and users are merely encouraged to revisit the page periodically, with no advance notification process or revision history provided.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy policy enumerates a comprehensive list of collected data types including email, IP address, browser info, device type, location, cookies, clicks, session recordings, file metadata, and upload/download history.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy clearly describes multiple collection methods including direct registration forms, automatic log activity collection, third-party analytics services, web beacons, cookies, and session recording tools.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The policy does not explicitly declare user ownership of personal data; while it states data will not be transferred to unrelated third parties without permission, it also notes user data may be transferred as a business asset in a sale, leaving ownership ambiguous.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: The policy states users may delete and amend collected data and that account deletion initiates a data removal process, but acknowledges it is 'physically impossible' to remove data used collectively for research or accounting, limiting full deletion.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy references that disabled books are deleted after one year of inactivity but does not state a clear, specific retention period for personal data collected during account use, making the overall retention timeline vague.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The privacy policy lists specific security measures including access control, authentication, regular security assessments, encryption in transit and at rest, and use of Amazon S3/AWS infrastructure for secure hosting.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The policy explicitly states use of encryption technology during transmission and storage, and marketing materials reference TLS and 256-bit AES multi-layered encryption on paid cloud plans.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The Terms of Service and Privacy Policy make no mention of password strength requirements, enforcement of strong passwords, or equivalent SSO/MFA mechanisms that would substitute for this protection.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: The platform does not offer or mention multi-factor authentication, SSO, or LTI integration, and accounts require only a standard email/password login with no MFA option described anywhere in the policies.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The privacy policy mentions cookies and web beacons and references opting out of Google's cookie use, but does not provide a full list of all cookies used with individual purposes; a separate cookie policy page is linked in the site footer but details from it were not fully retrievable.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The privacy policy specifically names Google Ads, Bing Ads, Facebook Ads, and Google Tag Manager as advertising partners, and references Amazon S3/AWS and PayPal, satisfying the requirement for named third parties.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: While specific third-party names are provided, the policy groups data shared with analytics, advertising, and service providers broadly without specifying exactly which data fields are transmitted to each individual third party.

complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy states that third-party suppliers process data 'under obligations similar to those in this Privacy Policy' and that GDPR-compliant third parties are used for EU users, but does not reference formal data processing agreements or binding supplier contracts for all users.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy states changes are effective upon posting without notice, meaning users would not be notified if new third-party sharing arrangements are introduced, with no process described for notifying users of third-party changes.

complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The policy explicitly confirms use of web beacons ('clear gifs and pixel tags') in conjunction with cookies, and Google Tag Manager is used for advertising tracking purposes, confirming tracking methods beyond functional use.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: An opt-out for Google advertising cookies is referenced via an external Google page, but no clear, platform-level opt-out process covering all advertising data sharing (including Facebook and Bing) is described, making the opt-out process incomplete and unclear.

r318.riskReason: Flipsnack for Education claims FERPA and SOPIPA compliance and does not sell student data, but the general platform uses Google Ads, targeting/advertising cookies, and web beacons that pose residual risks for K-12 student users not on dedicated education accounts.
r318.parentSummary: Flipsnack collects personal information such as name, email, IP address, device data, and detailed usage/activity logs; for its Education tier, it states student data is used only to provide the service and not for advertising, and educational institutions retain full rights over student data. However, the broader platform deploys Google Ads, targeting cookies, and third-party tracking pixels, which may affect students on non-dedicated education accounts. Parents should confirm their school is using the Flipsnack for Education plan and has obtained required parental consent as mandated by Flipsnack's own privacy policy.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The privacy policy states material changes will be posted prominently on the site and/or emailed to account holders, and previous policy versions are archived and accessible.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy policy enumerates specific data types collected including name, email, phone, IP, browser, OS, device, location, cookies, chat activity, page visits, search terms, clicks, and session data.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy specifically describes data collected directly by Flipsnack, via third-party service providers, through social media login APIs, contact forms, and embed code interactions.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: Users retain ownership of their content per the Terms of Service, but Flipsnack is granted a broad license to use, display, and distribute content, making ownership partially unclear for data vs. content.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users may request full account and data deletion by emailing privacy@flipsnack.com, with data removed from systems and third-party processors within 30 days, though deletion is irreversible.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy states data is retained as long as the account is active but does not specify a fixed retention period in days or years beyond the 30-day post-deletion window, making this partially addressed.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: Flipsnack documents specific security measures including TLS encryption in transit, encryption at rest, RBAC, AWS infrastructure, penetration testing, SOC 2 audits, and ISO 27001 certification.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The platform uses TLS (SSL) for data in transit with 2048-bit keys and SHA-256/RSA encryption, and strong encryption standards for data at rest, confirmed by independent SSL testing.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The security page mentions strong password policies and hashed passwords, but the privacy policy does not explicitly state minimum password complexity requirements are enforced for standard accounts.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: Flipsnack supports SSO (SAML 2.0/OIDC) and multi-factor authentication, available on enterprise plans, meeting this requirement for institutions using those plans.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: Flipsnack has a dedicated cookie policy listing essential, performance, targeting/advertising, and social media cookie categories, but advertising and tracking cookies are present and active by default.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The privacy policy and third-party sources specifically name Google (Analytics, Ads, Tag Manager), AWS, HubSpot, Stripe, Mailgun, Atlassian, and advertising/analytics partners.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: While specific third parties are named, the policy does not clearly delineate exactly which data fields are shared with each individual third party, grouping them broadly by purpose.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can opt out of Google Analytics tracking via an official opt-out link, and browser-level cookie controls are referenced, but a comprehensive in-platform opt-out for all third-party sharing is not provided.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The Terms of Service note that third-party integrations are subject to that provider's own terms, but do not explicitly state that all sub-processors are contractually bound to Flipsnack's data protection standards.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The privacy policy states changes will be communicated via site notice or email, but does not specifically commit to notifying users when individual third-party data sharing relationships are added or changed.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: Flipsnack uses Google Ads on the general platform; however, the Education tier explicitly states student data is not used for advertising purposes, creating a partial compliance scenario depending on account type.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: The cookie policy confirms targeting and advertising cookies collect user browsing habits and share them with advertising technology providers and advertisers for interest-based targeting.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Targeting and advertising cookies share user data with ad technology providers and advertisers with no in-platform opt-out mechanism, only external browser-level controls referenced.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The cookie policy explicitly confirms use of web beacons (tracking pixels) by Flipsnack and its third-party partners for tracking and advertising purposes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: A Google Analytics opt-out link is provided, but there is no clear, centralized opt-out mechanism within the platform for all advertiser data sharing, making this only partially addressed.

r319.riskReason: Floor Plan Creator displays Google AdMob ads (including ad cookies), collects advertising IDs for third-party advertising purposes, has no minimum age requirement, no COPPA or FERPA disclosures, no parental consent mechanism, and no student data protections whatsoever — making it unsuitable for K-12 deployment.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The privacy policy does not describe any advance notification process for policy changes or maintain a visible revision history.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The policy lists email, anonymized IP, and ad/device identifiers, but does not comprehensively enumerate all data collected (e.g., app interaction telemetry disclosed only via Amazon Appstore listing).

complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users may request full account deletion at any time, and the Terms state the operator shall delete the account within 3 business days of the request.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy states email is stored until account deletion and server logs are deleted after three months, but does not specify retention periods for ad/analytics data or device identifiers.

complianceNotes.SECQ5: The policy names session/login cookies and Google ad cookies, but does not provide a full cookie inventory with purpose descriptions for each cookie type.

complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy does not include any statement requiring third-party recipients (Paddle, Google, hosting provider) to adhere to equivalent data protection obligations.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy does not describe any process for notifying users if third-party partners change or if new third parties are added.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The platform is explicitly supported via Google AdMob advertising, which displays ads to users including in the Android app.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Google AdMob is used for targeted advertising; while some U.S. state residents get non-personalized ads, the default for most users involves ad personalization.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Ad cookies are used by Google AdMob for advertising purposes and no general opt-out from third-party ad tracking is offered to users outside specific U.S. states.

complianceNotes.ADVQ5: No clear opt-out process for data sharing with advertisers is described in the privacy policy; the state-specific non-personalized ad provision is not a user-initiated opt-out.

complianceNotes.SHRQ3: No opt-out mechanism for third-party data sharing is described; users' only recourse is to stop using the service entirely.

r321.riskReason: Flowlab uses remarketing advertising cookies, shares data for third-party marketing, and deploys web beacons and advertising/targeting cookies — practices that are problematic under COPPA and SOPIPA for K-12 student users.
r321.parentSummary: Flowlab (flowlab.io) is an online game-making platform used in K-12 classrooms that collects account information (username, email), device data, and usage data, and uses Google Analytics, web beacons, and advertising/remarketing cookies. While the platform has a Children's Privacy Notice and requires parental or school-official consent for children under 13, it discloses that personal data is shared for third-party marketing and uses targeting cookies — practices that raise significant concerns under COPPA and state student privacy laws like SOPIPA. Common Sense Media has given it a 'Warning' privacy rating due to issues with data use for advertising and non-educational profiling.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The privacy policy states it may be updated but does not clearly commit to advance notification before changes take effect, nor is a revision history or changelog publicly available.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy policy and children's privacy notice enumerate specific data types collected including username, email, password, IP address, device identifiers, browser type, and usage/activity data.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy specifically states data is collected at user registration, when purchasing products, automatically from the browser/device, and via cookies and web beacons.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The policy does not explicitly state that users own their data; data ownership is ambiguous, and the policy reserves the right to transfer personal data in a merger or acquisition.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Teacher accounts can delete student accounts and project data via the dashboard, but it is unclear whether individual users can fully delete all their own personal data on demand.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The privacy policy does not state a specific or general data retention period, making it impossible for schools or parents to assess how long student data is stored.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The policy makes only general references to security practices without enumerating specific technical or organizational security measures in place.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: No explicit mention of encryption (in transit or at rest) is made in the flowlab.io privacy policy; the policy is silent on this control.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The policy does not mention password strength requirements or enforcement; no SSO or equivalent is described for student accounts.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No mention of multi-factor authentication or SSO/LTI integration for school accounts is made in the Terms of Service or Privacy Policy.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The policy lists cookie categories (session, persistent, media, advertising/targeting) with general descriptions but does not provide a full named-cookie inventory with specific purposes.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The policy references broad categories of third-party service providers (payment processors, analytics companies, email providers) but does not name specific vendors except Google Analytics.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy groups third-party sharing into general categories without specifying what particular data fields are shared with each named or unnamed third party.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can opt out of advertising/remarketing cookies via the Network Advertising Initiative link, but no clear in-platform opt-out mechanism is provided for general third-party data sharing.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy states employees and contractors must comply with Google API Services User Data Policy but does not make a broader commitment requiring all third-party vendors to contractually protect user data.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy does not state that users will be notified if third-party service providers change or if new data-sharing relationships are established.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The policy explicitly discloses use of remarketing advertising services that show targeted ads on third-party websites, confirming ads are displayed beyond the platform context.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: The policy confirms use of remarketing to build browsing interest profiles and serve targeted advertisements on other websites, which constitutes user-level ad targeting.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Remarketing companies read cookies from users' browsers to enable targeting; an opt-out link (networkadvertising.org/choices) is provided, but it is external and non-trivial for K-12 contexts.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The policy confirms use of web beacons, advertising/targeting cookies, and remarketing technologies for ad tracking purposes, which are confirmed tracking methods for ads.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: An opt-out mechanism for remarketing cookies is referenced via the NAI opt-out tool, but no clear in-policy or in-product opt-out process is described for all forms of advertiser data sharing.

r322.riskReason: Fluency Matters acknowledges COPPA and FERPA and limits student data collection to teacher-provided information, but lacks a standalone Terms of Service, does not explicitly name third-party vendors, omits data retention timelines, does not address encryption or MFA, and the privacy policy has not been visibly updated since 2020.
r322.parentSummary: Fluency Matters collects only the student data provided by teachers or group leaders, such as names (which can be pseudonyms), usernames, and optionally email addresses, along with grades and course progress. There are no known third-party data sharing arrangements associated with this product, making it highly appropriate for classroom use.

complianceNotes.DCQ3: Because no data is collected, there is no ownership concern; users implicitly retain all rights to their information by default.

complianceNotes.SECQ2: Encryption practices are not mentioned in any accessible documentation for this specific app.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: No account creation is required to use the app, satisfying this requirement by design.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No account or login is required to play, which eliminates the need for MFA entirely and satisfies this criterion.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The app has no links to external sites, no advertising, and no tracking technologies as explicitly stated, meaning no cookies or web beacons are used.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: Halfbrick explicitly states no third-party data sharing occurs for this child-safe app, satisfying disclosure requirements.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: No data is shared with any third party per Halfbrick's child-safe app designation, so no data-per-third-party disclosure is needed.

complianceNotes.SHRQ4: There are no third parties involved in data sharing for this app, satisfying the vendor agreement requirement by default.

complianceNotes.ADVQ4: No web beacons, tracking pixels, or similar technologies are used in the app per Halfbrick's child-safe app policy.

r331.riskReason: Fun Run 3 explicitly serves third-party behavioral advertising, shares advertising IDs and IP addresses with multiple ad networks, has confirmed data sales/sharing with third parties per Common Sense Media, sets a minimum age of 13 with no verifiable parental consent mechanism for younger users, and is not designed as an educational tool, making it unsuitable for K-12 school use under COPPA, FERPA, or SOPIPA.
r331.parentSummary: Fun Run 3, developed by Dirtybit, collects device identifiers, IP addresses, advertising IDs, location data, and in-game behavioral data, and shares this information with multiple third-party ad networks (including Google AdMob, Meta, and Unity) to serve targeted in-game advertisements. The app requires users to be at least 13 years old and does not offer a child-safe or school-managed mode, nor does it provide verifiable parental consent mechanisms required under COPPA for children under 13. Common Sense Media has flagged this product with a 'Warning' rating, noting that data is sold or rented to third parties and used for behavioral ad targeting, making it a high-risk choice for any K-12 school environment.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The Dirtybit privacy policy includes a changelog with past update dates and states that appropriate measures will be taken to inform users of changes, but does not specify advance notification before changes take effect.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy policy lists several categories of data collected (IP address, device ID, advertising ID, location, game data), but does not provide an exhaustive itemized list of all personally identifiable data fields collected.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy specifically describes both automatic collection from device/app usage and voluntary collection via social login (Facebook, Google, Apple, WeChat), meeting this requirement.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The policy does not assert user ownership of data; Dirtybit claims broad rights to process, share, and transfer user data, with no explicit statement that users own their information.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: The Dirtybit privacy policy explicitly states users can delete their player account directly within the app under Settings > 'Delete Account', meeting this requirement.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy states data will be retained until 'no ongoing legitimate business need' exists, but does not specify any concrete retention period in days or months, making this vague.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The policy mentions 'appropriate technical and organisational measures' to protect data but does not enumerate specific security controls (e.g., encryption standards, firewalls, access controls).
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The Dirtybit privacy policy does not mention encryption of data in transit or at rest; no encryption standard is referenced anywhere in the policy.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The Terms of Service and Privacy Policy make no mention of password strength requirements or enforcement of strong passwords for user accounts.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: There is no mention of multi-factor authentication or SSO/LTI integration in any of Dirtybit's published policies or the funrun3.com terms.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The privacy policy mentions cookies and advertising IDs are used but does not provide a comprehensive cookie list with individual purposes; cookie usage is addressed only in general terms.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The Dirtybit privacy policy specifically names third-party ad partners including IronSource/Unity LevelPlay, Google AdMob, Meta, Unity, Applovin, AdColony, and Vungle, meeting this requirement.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy groups data shared with ad partners (advertising ID and IP address) without specifying exactly which data fields go to each named third party individually.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can opt out of targeted advertising via device-level settings (iOS 'Limit Ad Tracking' or Android 'Opt out of Interest-Based Ads') or an in-app toggle, but this opt-out is limited and does not prevent all third-party data sharing.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy states third-party service providers process data 'for purposes described in this Privacy Notice,' implying contractual limits, but does not explicitly claim vendor agreements require the same privacy standards as Dirtybit itself.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy's changelog shows ad partner lists have been updated multiple times without any stated process for notifying users in advance of changes to third-party sharing relationships.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The Dirtybit privacy policy explicitly confirms that third-party behavioral and contextual advertisements are displayed within the app, funded by advertising revenue.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: The policy confirms that advertising IDs and IP addresses are sent to ad networks to serve targeted (interest-based) advertisements, constituting confirmed user-level behavioral targeting.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Third-party ad tracking is confirmed, but a partial opt-out is available via device privacy settings or an in-app toggle to disable targeted ads, though third-party SDKs may still collect some data.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The policy confirms advertising IDs are shared with multiple ad networks and third-party SDKs (e.g., IronSource, Google AdMob) are integrated, constituting tracking for ad purposes beyond functional use.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: An opt-out of targeted advertising is available via device settings or an in-app toggle, but the process is not prominently disclosed, and opting out of all advertiser data sharing is not fully possible given the number of integrated ad SDKs.

r333.riskReason: Fusion 360 is a general-interest adult platform that requires a minimum age of 13, has a DPA and FERPA terms available for K-12 schools, and explicitly prohibits selling student data, but its general privacy policy permits targeted advertising and third-party ad tracking that applies to non-student accounts, and COPPA compliance for under-13 students depends entirely on school-initiated DPA execution rather than built-in platform controls.
r333.parentSummary: Autodesk Fusion 360 collects account information (name, email, birthdate), device and usage data, and geolocation from users, and shares data with advertising partners and analytics providers for adult users. For K-12 use, schools must sign a Data Privacy Agreement (DPA) with Autodesk, under which student data cannot be sold or used for advertising; however, these protections are contractual and require proactive action by the school. Parents should confirm their school has executed a DPA before allowing student use, and should be aware that accounts managed outside a school DPA are subject to Autodesk's standard commercial privacy practices, including behavioral advertising.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: Autodesk provides advance notice of material Terms changes via email or in-service notification and maintains a publicly accessible Privacy Statement Changes revision history page.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The Privacy Statement enumerates specific categories of data collected including identifiers, device data, usage data, geolocation, professional info, commercial info, financial info, and education information.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The Privacy Statement explicitly describes three collection methods: directly from users during account creation/use, automatically via cookies and tracking technologies, and from third parties including affiliates and business partners.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The General Terms state users retain ownership of their files and designs, but Autodesk retains broad rights to collect and process user-generated metrics and content for business purposes, making ownership only partially clear for student-generated content outside a DPA context.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users can delete their account and personal data through self-service account settings, and Autodesk offers a deletion request form for non-account holders, with processing completed within 45 days.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The Privacy Statement states data is retained 'as long as reasonably necessary or permitted and proportionate to the purpose' but does not specify a fixed retention period in days or months, making this a general rather than specific retention statement.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The General Terms reference 'administrative, technical, and physical safeguards' and the Trust Center references an industry-standards-based security framework, but specific technical measures beyond encryption in transit are not enumerated in the public-facing privacy policy.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: Autodesk explicitly states all collected analytics data is encrypted, and authentication enforces HTTPS with TLS 1.2 encryption in transit for all user sign-ins.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: Autodesk requires each user to have a unique email and password for authentication, and SSO integration with SAML-based identity providers is available, satisfying strong authentication requirements for institutional deployments.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: Autodesk supports optional multi-factor authentication for organizations and SSO/SAML integration, meeting the requirement for MFA availability even if not mandatory for all individual accounts.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: Autodesk maintains a detailed Cookie Statement listing cookie categories (functional, analytics, advertising) with purposes, and provides a cookie preference management tool; a third-party cookie list is also published.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: Autodesk's third-party services page names specific partners including Google Analytics, Twitter/X, Marketo, Yahoo Japan, Qualtrics, Salesforce Live Agent, Khoros, LaunchDarkly, and Upsellit.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: While specific third parties are named, the exact data elements shared with each individual third party are described only at a category level (e.g., IP address, behavioral data) rather than per-field disclosures for each named partner.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can manage cookie preferences and opt out of behavioral advertising via the Digital Advertising Alliance's AdChoices tool, but the opt-out is cookie-based and must be renewed per browser/device, making it limited and not persistent.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: Autodesk's Privacy Statement and Data Privacy Framework certification state that Autodesk remains liable if third-party agents process data inconsistently with its policies, indicating contractual accountability for subprocessors.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The Privacy Statement may be updated periodically and Autodesk notifies users of material changes, but the policy does not guarantee specific notice when individual third-party ad or analytics partners are added or replaced.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: Autodesk's Privacy Statement and Cookie Statement confirm that advertising cookies are used to serve personalized ads and track marketing campaign results, including on the main Autodesk platform, not only on pre-login pages.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: The Cookie Statement explicitly states that advertising cookies collect data based on user activities and interests to show targeted ads, and third-party ad partners may further combine this data for behavioral targeting.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Autodesk offers opt-out via the Digital Advertising Alliance AdChoices tool, but this opt-out is not persistent across browsers or devices and third-party ad partners may still track independently, limiting effective opt-out.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Autodesk's Cookie Statement confirms the use of pixels, web beacons, and cookies for advertising purposes, including sending data to third-party ad partners to deliver personalized advertising.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Autodesk provides a 'Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information' link and the AdChoices opt-out tool for advertising data sharing, but the process requires per-browser/device renewal and is not a single persistent opt-out.

r335.riskReason: While G-W explicitly prohibits selling student data and acknowledges FERPA obligations, the policy permits third-party companies to collect behavioral data via cookies and web beacons for targeted advertising purposes, creating meaningful risk for K-12 student users.
r335.parentSummary: G-W Online, operated by Goodheart-Willcox Publisher, collects student personally identifiable information and education records (provided by schools), as well as usage data such as IP addresses, pages visited, and cookie data. G-W states it does not sell or rent personal information and treats student data as confidential, used only to provide and improve its services. However, the privacy policy permits third-party companies to collect behavioral and click-stream data via cookies and web beacons for targeted advertising, and does not specify a minimum age or explicitly state COPPA compliance, which are notable concerns for parents of K-12 students.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The G-W Learning legacy terms state changes may be made by updating the posting without advance notice to users, though the main g-w.com terms do not detail a revision history or proactive notification process.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy policy lists specific data types collected including IP address, pages viewed, time on site, referring URLs, student PII, education records, cookie data, and click-stream information.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy explains data is collected via user-submitted forms, automatically through web server logs and cookies, and through schools/districts providing student education records.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The policy states student data is considered confidential and used only for service purposes, but does not clearly assert that users own their data; ownership language is ambiguous.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: The policy directs students and parents to contact their school or educational institution to review, modify, or delete student information, rather than providing a direct deletion mechanism with G-W.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The privacy policy does not state a specific data retention period or general retention timeframe for any category of user or student data.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The policy states G-W strives to take appropriate security measures and uses commercially acceptable means to protect data, but does not enumerate specific technical security measures beyond SSL/TLS for payment processing.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: Encryption (SSL/TLS) is mentioned only in the context of third-party payment processor transmissions; encryption of general student or user data at rest or in transit is not explicitly confirmed.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The platform requires account registration with a username and password, but the policy and terms do not specify enforcement of strong password standards or complexity requirements.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: The G-W Online Textbooks platform shows two-factor authentication is available as an option, but it is not confirmed as mandatory or universally enforced across all users.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The policy mentions cookies and web beacons are used and that browsers can disable cookies, but does not provide a comprehensive list of specific cookies, their names, or their individual purposes.

complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy groups data sharing by category of third party rather than specifying which data elements are shared with each individual third-party vendor.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: The only opt-out mechanism described is configuring the browser to disable cookies, which impairs platform functionality; no direct opt-out from third-party data sharing is offered.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy states G-W enters into contracts with third-party hosting vendors requiring adequate security, but does not make a general statement requiring all third parties to follow vendor data protection agreements.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy does not describe any process for notifying users when third-party service providers or data-sharing relationships change.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The policy explicitly states G-W will not provide third parties with personal information for targeted advertising purposes, but separately permits third-party companies to collect behavioral data via cookies for ad targeting.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: The policy contradictorily disclaims targeted advertising using personal information while simultaneously permitting third-party companies to collect click-stream and behavioral data to serve targeted advertisements to users.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: The policy allows third-party companies to use cookies and web beacons to collect behavioral data for targeted advertising with no opt-out mechanism provided beyond browser-level cookie disabling.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The policy explicitly acknowledges third-party companies use cookies and web beacons to collect click-stream, browser type, and ad interaction data for targeted advertising purposes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: No clear opt-out process from third-party advertising data collection is provided; only browser-level cookie disabling is mentioned, which is not a user-friendly or complete opt-out solution.

r336.parentSummary: Gale In Context: Opposing Viewpoints, operated by Cengage, collects limited usage and technical data (such as IP address, session activity, and device identifiers) primarily to deliver the research service to schools. Cengage explicitly states it does not sell student data, does not use K-12 student data for its own purposes, and prohibits targeted advertising to students. Data is owned by the school and access for young students is facilitated through school consent in line with COPPA requirements.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The privacy policy notes that changes will be posted on the website but does not explicitly commit to advance notification or maintain a visible revision history for users.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: Usage data, IP addresses, device identifiers, and session activity are listed, but the full enumerated list of all data types collected through the Gale platform specifically is not comprehensively detailed in one place.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The privacy policy specifically states data is collected via cookies, web beacons, server logs, browser analysis tools, and directly from users or LMS integrations, clearly explaining collection methods.

complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy groups data sharing by category of recipient (service providers, analytics, advertisers) rather than specifying what data is shared with each named third party.

complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The K-12 Privacy Notice explicitly states that Cengage discloses student data only to third parties that are contractually obligated to maintain confidentiality and security, meeting this requirement.

r337.parentSummary: Gameplan collects student names, email addresses, usage/activity data, and grade/roster information through integrations with school LMS and SIS platforms like Google Classroom and PowerSchool. The platform states it adheres to CIS Critical Security Controls, uses AWS infrastructure, and supports SSO via Clever, but its public-facing privacy policy does not explicitly name all third parties, define data retention periods, or clearly prohibit sale of student data. Parents and administrators should request a signed Data Privacy Agreement before deploying this platform with students under 18.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The privacy policy states changes may be communicated via email or in-service notice, but no commitment to advance notice timelines or a publicly maintained revision history was found.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The trust and privacy pages reference general categories (usage data, roster data, log files, cookies) but do not provide a comprehensive enumerated list of all data types collected from students.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy generally states data is collected via account registration, LMS/SIS integrations, and log files, but does not specifically describe every collection mechanism used within the student-facing platform.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The Terms of Service grant Gameplan a broad license to use, process, and store submitted content, making data ownership ambiguous; no explicit statement that students or schools own their data was found.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: The privacy policy allows consent withdrawal and references GDPR/CCPA deletion rights, but does not provide a clear, simple self-service deletion mechanism for K-12 users or their schools.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy states retention is 'only as long as reasonably required,' which is a general retention statement but lacks a specific defined period, making this only a partial meet.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The trust page references CIS Critical Security Controls, role-based access management, and regular external security testing, but the publicly available privacy policy itself only states 'physical, electronic and/or procedural safeguards' without specifics.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The platform uses AWS infrastructure and SSO, and the site appears to use HTTPS, but no explicit statement confirming end-to-end encryption of student data at rest and in transit was found in the policy documents.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: Gameplan supports SSO via Clever and LMS-based single sign-on, which meets this requirement through federated identity management rather than standalone password policies.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: The trust page explicitly states Gameplan implements 2FA via SSO through Clever, meeting the MFA requirement for authenticated access.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The career site cookie policy lists functional and analytics cookies with vendor (Teamtailor), but the main gameplan.com privacy policy only mentions cookies generally without a comprehensive categorized cookie list for the student platform.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: LMS/SIS integrations with Clever, Edlink, Canvas, Google Classroom, PowerSchool, and Infinite Campus are named, but other third-party service providers (analytics, security vendors) are not specifically identified in the privacy policy.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy does not specify what data categories are shared with each named or unnamed third party; data sharing is described only in general terms.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Consent withdrawal is mentioned and CCPA opt-out rights are referenced, but no clear, easy opt-out process specifically for third-party data sharing in the K-12 context is documented.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy makes a general statement about not being responsible for third parties but does not explicitly state that third-party vendors are contractually bound to the same data protection standards.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy reserves the right to modify terms at any time and mentions possible email notification, but does not specifically commit to notifying users when third-party sharing relationships change.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The gameplan.com platform pages do not show advertising to students, but the trygameplan.com privacy policy references third-party ad servers and advertising partner policies, creating ambiguity about ad exposure across platform variants.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: The main K-12 platform (gameplan.com) does not appear to display targeted ads to students, but a related Gameplan privacy policy (trygameplan.com) references personalized advertising content, making targeted advertising status unclear across all platform surfaces.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: The trygameplan.com privacy policy explicitly states third-party ad servers use cookies and web beacons to track users and that Gameplan has no control over these cookies, with no opt-out mechanism provided within the platform.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The trygameplan.com privacy policy confirms use of web beacons and JavaScript by third-party ad networks for ad effectiveness measurement, which is a confirmed tracking method for advertising purposes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: CCPA 'Do Not Sell My Personal Information' rights are mentioned, but no clear, dedicated opt-out process for data sharing with advertisers is provided within the platform interface itself.

r338.riskReason: Gamestar Mechanic is a legacy, unsupported platform explicitly designed for children aged 7–14 that lacks specific encryption disclosures, no-longer-active moderation, vague data retention periods, and allows third-party cookies/web beacons with only general descriptions, creating meaningful gaps in COPPA and FERPA compliance for K-12 schools.
r338.parentSummary: Gamestar Mechanic collects minimal personal data from children — primarily a username, password, and birthdate — and explicitly states it does not collect email addresses from users under 16 or share personal data for advertising purposes. However, the platform is a legacy application that is no longer actively moderated or supported, third-party service providers may place cookies and web beacons on users' devices, and the privacy policy does not specify encryption methods or precise data retention timelines. Schools should be aware that educator-mediated consent is used in lieu of direct parental consent, and that no new data privacy agreements can be entered into with E-Line Media.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The policy states changes will be posted and users will be notified for significant changes, but no revision history or change log is provided.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The policy describes major data categories (username, birthdate, email, usage data, cookies) but does not enumerate a complete exhaustive list of all data fields collected.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy provides a general statement that data is collected during registration and through cookies/web beacons but lacks specific technical detail on each collection mechanism.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The Terms of Service explicitly state users have no ownership rights in their account or account-related data, assigning effective control to E-Line Media.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: The privacy policy states that at a user's request, E-Line will provide a copy of their data, correct errors, or remove it from Gamestar, indicating full deletion is available upon request.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The privacy policy does not specify any concrete data retention period or schedule, providing no guidance on how long user data is stored after account inactivity or deletion.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The policy states 'reasonable measures' are used to protect data from unauthorized access but does not enumerate specific security controls or protocols in use.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: No mention of encryption (in transit or at rest) is made anywhere in the privacy policy or terms of service.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The policy and terms of service make no mention of password strength requirements or enforcement of strong passwords.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No mention of multi-factor authentication or SSO/LTI integration is made in any policy or help documentation.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The policy mentions cookies and third-party web beacons in general terms but does not provide a detailed list of cookies, their names, or specific purposes.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The policy acknowledges sharing with vendors and technology service providers but does not name any specific third-party companies.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy groups data shared with service vendors and payment processors together without specifying which data elements are shared with each category.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can opt out of marketing emails and social network sharing; however, no explicit opt-out from sharing with operational vendors is described.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy states E-Line takes steps to ensure vendors treat personal data consistently with their own privacy practices, but no formal supplier agreement or specific contractual obligation is described.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy does not mention any process for notifying users when third-party service providers change or when new vendors are onboarded.

complianceNotes.ADVQ2: The policy explicitly states it does not use personal data to engage in behavioral or targeted advertising.

complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Third-party cookies and web beacons are acknowledged as used to support internal operations, but the specific tracking methods and their purposes are not fully itemized.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Because the platform explicitly states no data is shared with advertisers, the opt-out question is effectively resolved — no advertiser data sharing occurs to opt out of.

r339.riskReason: Gamma is not designed for K-12 use, sets a minimum age of 16, explicitly excludes personal data of children under 13 in its DPA, collects extensive personal and behavioral data, engages in targeted advertising, does not respond to Do Not Track signals, and lacks any COPPA, FERPA, or SOPIPA compliance statements.
r339.parentSummary: Gamma (gamma.app) is an AI-powered presentation platform that collects a wide range of personal data including names, emails, usage behavior, device information, and user-generated content, and shares this data with affiliates, service providers, and marketing partners. The platform states it is not intended for anyone under 16 years of age, expressly prohibits customer submission of personal data from children under 13 in its Data Processing Addendum, and makes no claims of COPPA or FERPA compliance. Parents and school administrators should be aware that Gamma may use personal information for targeted advertising purposes and does not respond to browser Do Not Track signals, making it a high-risk platform for K-12 student use.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The privacy policy states Gamma reserves the right to modify it at any time and will notify users by updating the date and posting the modified version, but no advance notification process or full revision history archive is provided.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy policy enumerates specific categories of personal data collected including contact data, profile data, demographic data, transactional data, marketing data, user-generated content, usage/device data, and third-party sourced data.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy clearly describes data collected directly from users, automatically via cookies and tracking technologies, and from third-party sources such as social media platforms and data licensors.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The policy does not explicitly state that users own their data; user-generated content ownership is not clearly assigned, and Gamma's use of content for service improvement creates ambiguity about effective data ownership.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Gamma's help documentation states users can delete their account from the profile menu, which permanently removes content and personal data, indicating full deletion is available.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy states data is generally retained to fulfill collection purposes and satisfy legal or accounting requirements, but no specific retention period (in days or months) is defined, making this only a general retention statement.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The policy states Gamma employs technical, organizational, and physical safeguards, but does not enumerate specific measures beyond HTTPS encryption; the help center confirms HTTPS encryption is in use.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: Gamma's help center explicitly confirms all requests and interactions are encrypted using HTTPS and secure communication protocols.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: Neither the Terms of Service nor the Privacy Policy mention password strength requirements or enforcement of strong passwords.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No mention of multi-factor authentication or SSO/LTI integration for K-12 is found in the Terms of Service or Privacy Policy.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The privacy policy references a separate Cookie Notice for full cookie details but does not list all cookies with individual purposes inline; users are directed to a Cookie Preference Center, indicating partial but not fully transparent cookie disclosure.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The privacy policy broadly categorizes third parties (service providers, affiliates, payment processors, marketing partners) but does not name most specific vendors; Stripe is the only third party named explicitly.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy groups data sharing by third-party category rather than specifying what data is shared with each individual vendor, resulting in only a general disclosure.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: A Cookie Preference Center is mentioned for opting out of targeted advertising, and users can opt out of marketing emails, but no comprehensive opt-out from all third-party data sharing is clearly provided.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The DPA includes provisions requiring sub-processors to apply security measures no less protective than Gamma's own, but the public-facing privacy policy does not make a clear general statement that all third parties must follow a vendor agreement.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The privacy policy does not mention any process for notifying users when third-party sub-processors or data-sharing partners are added or changed.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The Terms of Service explicitly references Third-Party Ads served within the platform, and the privacy policy confirms personal information may be used for targeted advertising purposes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: The privacy policy states personal information may be used for targeted advertising, which constitutes confirmed user-level targeting beyond first-party platform ads.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Gamma explicitly states it does not respond to Do Not Track signals, and while a Cookie Preference Center exists for opting out of some tracking, third-party tracking appears to be active without a robust opt-out mechanism.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Cookies and similar tracking technologies are used and referenced in the policy; the Terms of Service confirm Third-Party Ads exist within the service, indicating tracking for advertising purposes beyond functional use.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: A Cookie Preference Center is mentioned as a mechanism to opt out of targeted advertising data use, but the process is not clearly described in the main privacy policy text, making the opt-out only partially accessible.

r340.minAge: Under 18 with parental consent (account creation requires 18+ or parental/guardian consent)
dataSharedWith: GCF subsidiaries (for business and marketing purposes with consent)
