r369.riskReason: Grammarly's consumer product requires users to be at least 13 and does not sell student data, but its standard privacy policy permits targeted advertising using hashed email identifiers and third-party advertising cookies, and it lacks explicit COPPA/FERPA compliance statements for individual (non-enterprise) K-12 deployments — schools must execute a separate Student Data Privacy Agreement (DPA) to obtain those protections.
r369.parentSummary: Grammarly collects account information (name, email), the text students write while using the service, usage data, and device/browser identifiers in order to provide grammar and writing assistance, improve its product, and (on its marketing websites) serve ads promoting Grammarly. Grammarly states it does not sell student content and encrypts data in transit (TLS) and at rest (AES-256), and schools can sign a separate Student Data Privacy Agreement (DPA) to lock in FERPA/COPPA protections. However, without a school-executed DPA, the standard consumer privacy policy allows advertising-related tracking cookies and hashed-email targeted advertising on Grammarly's marketing sites, which is a concern for K-12 deployments.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: Grammarly/Superhuman provides at least 30 days advance notice of Terms of Service changes via email or in-product notification, posts updated versions with a 'Last Updated' date, and historically has notified active users 60 days in advance of privacy policy changes.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The Privacy Policy lists specific categories of data collected including account information, user text content, usage data, device/browser identifiers, cookie IDs, inferred location, inferred attributes, and (for paid users) payment information.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The Privacy Policy explicitly states data is collected directly from users at account creation, automatically during product use (including via cookies and tracking technologies), and from third-party partners.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: Grammarly explicitly states users retain all rights to their text content and that Grammarly does not claim ownership, though it licenses a limited right to process content for service delivery.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users can delete their account and all associated data at any time; users can also request deletion of specific data via privacy settings, and opting out of a feature triggers deletion of data stored for that feature.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The Privacy Policy states data is retained 'as long as necessary' for service provision and legal obligations with retention varying by data type and settings, but does not specify concrete retention periods for most data categories — this is a vague general statement rather than a specific timeframe.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: Grammarly specifies multiple security measures including TLS encryption in transit, AES-256 encryption at rest, bcrypt password hashing, network segregation, principle-of-least-privilege access controls, SOC 2 Type 2 certification, and ISO 27001/27017/27018 certifications.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: Grammarly explicitly confirms data is encrypted in transit using TLS and at rest using AES-256, representing full encryption coverage for stored and transmitted data.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: Grammarly does not explicitly enforce strong password requirements in its public policies; while bcrypt hashing is mentioned for stored passwords, there is no stated enforcement of complexity rules — the ToS and Privacy Policy are silent on password strength enforcement.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: Multi-factor authentication is available as an optional feature (referenced in third-party security reviews and account settings), but the policy does not mandate MFA nor is SSO/LTI for institutional deployment explicitly described in public-facing terms.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: Grammarly references cookies and tracking technologies (web beacons, pixels, advertising cookies) and provides a Cookie Preferences tool via OneTrust for EU/UK users and a 'Your Privacy Choices' footer link for US users, but does not publish a comprehensive cookie-by-cookie list with individual purposes for all users.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The Privacy Policy broadly categories third-party recipients (corporate affiliates, LLM service providers, analytics/advertising companies, marketplace apps) but does not publish a named list of specific third-party vendors in the consumer-facing policy.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy groups data sharing by recipient category (e.g., LLM providers receive prompt text and context; advertising partners receive hashed emails and cookie IDs) but does not enumerate exactly which data fields go to each specific named vendor.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can opt out of targeted advertising and data sharing via the 'Your Privacy Choices' footer link and in-account settings, but the opt-out is browser-specific, must be renewed across devices, and does not cover all forms of data sharing with third parties.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: Grammarly explicitly states that trusted service providers (including LLM providers and AWS) are bound by contractual agreements requiring them to follow data privacy and security requirements and use data only as directed.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The Privacy Policy states Grammarly may update the policy and will provide notice of material changes, but does not specifically commit to notifying users whenever the list of third-party sub-processors changes — a dedicated sub-processor change notification process is not described in consumer-facing terms.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: Grammarly does not display third-party ads within its product to users, and states it does not help third parties advertise to its users; however, Grammarly itself uses advertising partners and tracking technologies on its marketing websites to promote its own product to users on other sites.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Grammarly does not allow third parties to target ads to users within the product, but the Privacy Policy acknowledges that sharing hashed email identifiers and advertising cookies with partners for cross-site promotion of Grammarly may constitute 'targeted advertising' under certain state privacy laws.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Grammarly uses advertising cookies, web beacons, and pixels on its marketing websites that are set by third-party advertising partners; opt-out is available via cookie preferences and the 'Your Privacy Choices' link but is browser-scoped and requires manual renewal per device.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Grammarly's Privacy Policy explicitly confirms the use of cookies, web beacons, pixels, and unique device/browser identifiers by advertising partners on marketing websites, which constitutes tracking for advertising purposes and cannot be characterized as purely functional tracking.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: An opt-out mechanism for targeted advertising/sharing exists via 'Your Privacy Choices' footer link and in-account settings, and Global Privacy Control signals are honored, but the process is browser-scoped, requires renewal on new devices/browsers, and the policy language describing how to exercise it is spread across multiple support pages rather than consolidated in one clear location.

dataCollected: Student attributes (e.g., academic proficiency, gender, leadership traits)
r370.riskReason: Grouper.school explicitly prohibits advertising, does not sell student data, claims COPPA and FERPA compliance, encrypts data in transit and at rest, and limits data collection to what is necessary for educational use.
r370.parentSummary: Grouper.school collects teacher and student roster data (names, attributes like reading level or leadership traits) to help teachers form classroom groups. The platform explicitly states it does not display ads, does not sell student data, and does not use student records for commercial purposes. Data is encrypted in transit and at rest, and parents or schools can request deletion of student records by contacting the platform directly.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The policy states material changes will be communicated and the date updated, but does not specify advance notification timelines or provide a revision history archive.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy policy lists specific categories of data collected including name, email, class and student data, usage data, and cookies, with a stated commitment to collecting only what is necessary.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy clearly explains data is collected through account creation (email, Google, Clever), teacher-entered roster data, and automatically via cookies and similar technologies.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The policy notes student data may remain under school control but does not clearly and explicitly affirm user ownership of all personal data; ownership language is ambiguous for teacher-provided data.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users can request deletion by emailing support@grouper.school or privacy@grouper.school, and student records can be deleted by contacting the school, satisfying the deletion requirement.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy states data may be retained beyond account termination for legal or compliance reasons and anonymized data may be retained longer, but does not specify a concrete retention period in days.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The policy explicitly states reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards are implemented, with data encrypted in transit and at rest as a specific example.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The privacy policy explicitly states all data is encrypted in transit and at rest, fully meeting the encryption requirement.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: Account creation is supported via Google SSO or Clever (which enforce strong credentials), but the policy does not explicitly state password strength requirements for email-based accounts.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: The platform supports Google and Clever SSO which may include MFA, but there is no explicit mention of native MFA support within Grouper itself.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The privacy policy distinguishes between necessary cookies and analytics cookies, explains their purposes, and provides guidance on managing cookie preferences including a settings page for registered users.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The policy acknowledges data is shared with third-party vendors for service delivery and mentions Google and Clever integrations, but does not enumerate all third-party vendors by name.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy groups third-party sharing broadly under 'service delivery' without specifying which data types are shared with which specific vendors.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: The policy states no advertising or targeted tracking is performed and student data is not used commercially, effectively making third-party data sharing for advertising a non-issue; unsubscribe is available for teacher marketing emails.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy states data is shared with vendors who process information to help provide services, implying contractual relationships, but does not explicitly confirm third parties are bound by data protection agreements.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy states it may be updated at any time with notification for material changes, but does not specifically commit to notifying users about changes to third-party vendor relationships.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The privacy policy explicitly states the service is free from any advertising, including contextual or personalized advertising.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: The policy explicitly states no data is collected or processed for the purpose of tracking for personalized advertising and student records are never used for advertising.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: The policy explicitly states Grouper does not track users across third-party websites to provide targeted advertising and does not respond to DNT signals as a result.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Cookies are described as functional and analytics-only with no mention of advertising tracking technologies such as web beacons or pixel trackers for ad purposes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Because no advertising or third-party ad sharing occurs, there is nothing to opt out of; the platform's no-advertising stance meets this requirement by design.

r372.riskReason: Gynzy demonstrates strong GDPR compliance and offers a data processing agreement aligned with educational privacy covenants, but lacks explicit COPPA compliance statements, does not clearly specify a minimum age, and uses external third-party AI model providers whose data handling is not fully transparent to end users.
r372.parentSummary: Gynzy is a Dutch-based interactive whiteboard platform used by K-12 teachers that collects account information, usage data, and user-created content in order to deliver its educational services. Gynzy positions itself as a GDPR-compliant data processor, places data ownership with the school (customer), and offers a data processing agreement for schools; it also states it does not sell personal data. However, the platform uses third-party AI models and integrations (such as YouTube) whose data practices are governed separately, and Gynzy's public policy does not explicitly address COPPA compliance or set a minimum age for student users, which may require additional due diligence by U.S. schools serving students under 13.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The Terms of Use mention that updated versions of the data processing agreement may be declared applicable by sending them to customers, but there is no clearly stated advance notification process or publicly accessible revision history for the privacy policy itself.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: Gynzy's privacy policy confirms collection of personal data for service operation and improvement, but the public-facing policy page renders minimal detail; specific enumerated data types (e.g., IP address, usage logs, account info) are partially implied rather than comprehensively listed.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy generally states that data is collected through use of the platform and website visits, but does not provide a specific, itemized description of all collection mechanisms such as cookies, server logs, or third-party integrations.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The Terms of Use explicitly designate the customer (school/institution) as the data controller and Gynzy as the data processor, clearly placing data ownership and control with the school rather than Gynzy.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: The GDPR page confirms users have the right to access, correct, and delete their information, and the Terms of Use permit account deletion; deletion rights are acknowledged in line with GDPR obligations.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy references retention in the context of GDPR compliance and data processing agreements, but does not state a specific retention period (e.g., number of days or years) in its public-facing documentation.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: Gynzy states that data is secure and accessible only to authorized personnel and maintains a responsible disclosure program with a dedicated security contact, but specific technical security measures (e.g., encryption standards, access controls) are not enumerated in the public policy.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The platform is web-based and uses HTTPS (implied by the responsible disclosure and infrastructure references), but the privacy policy does not explicitly state that data is encrypted in transit or at rest.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The Terms of Use require customers to keep login credentials confidential and manage account security, but there is no explicit statement that the platform enforces strong password requirements for teacher or student accounts.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: The platform supports Google account integration (implied by Google Drive and Google Classroom integrations), which may support SSO, but MFA is not explicitly mentioned or confirmed as available in the public documentation.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The privacy page is titled 'Privacy and cookie statement,' indicating cookies are addressed, but the publicly indexed content does not enumerate specific cookie categories, names, or purposes in detail.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The Terms of Use acknowledge use of third-party applications (e.g., YouTube) and external AI model providers, but do not provide a named, comprehensive list of all sub-processors or third-party data recipients.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: Third-party sharing is acknowledged in grouped terms (AI providers, payment processors, sub-processors under DPA), but the specific data fields shared with each individual third party are not disclosed publicly.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: The GDPR rights page confirms users can object to data processing, but there is no clearly described self-service opt-out mechanism for third-party data sharing specifically for U.S. users or parents.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The Terms of Use require all data processing to occur under a formal data processing agreement with the customer, and Gynzy references the education privacy covenant model DPA, indicating sub-processors are held to contractual data protection obligations.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The Terms of Use state Gynzy may declare updated versions of the data processing agreement applicable by sending them to customers, which provides some notification, but it is not clear that customers can object to changes in sub-processors prior to implementation.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: There is no indication in any Gynzy documentation that ads are displayed to students or teachers within the platform; Gynzy is a subscription-based service with no ad-supported tier described.

r375.parentSummary: HatchXR (kids.hatchxr.com), operated by K 12 Innovations Private Limited, collects personal information such as name, email, phone number, usage data, and cookies from users who register on its platform, and by registering, users authorize the company and its business partners to contact them for promotional purposes via email, phone, or SMS. While the platform is explicitly marketed as a K-12 coding and AR/VR tool for students as young as Grade 1, the privacy policy states that no personal data is collected from minors under 18 — a contradictory claim that suggests the policy is designed for parent/teacher accounts rather than students, yet provides no clear parental consent workflow. The company states it does not sell personal data, allows parents to request deletion of their child's data by contacting hello@hatchxr.com, and claims COPPA and FERPA compliance on its marketing pages, but the actual policy text lacks the specific disclosures, consent mechanisms, and third-party safeguards required to substantiate those claims.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The Terms of Use note that HatchXR may revise policies at its sole discretion, and the Privacy Policy states continued use constitutes acceptance, but there is no stated process for advance notification or a maintained revision history.

complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy broadly states data is collected via registration, site usage, cookies, and analytics platforms like Google, but does not provide a detailed breakdown of exactly how each data type is collected.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The policy does not explicitly assign data ownership; it states HatchXR will not sell data and that users can request deletion, but does not affirmatively state that users own their data, leaving ownership ambiguous.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Parents may contact hello@hatchxr.com to request deletion of a child's data, but the policy notes deletion may result in account termination and does not specify a timeframe or guarantee full deletion across all systems.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy states data is retained 'so long as it is necessary to fulfil the purposes for which it was collected' — a vague general statement without a specific retention period or schedule.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The policy references 'appropriate and adequate administrative, technical and physical safeguards' against unauthorized access, but does not list specific security measures such as encryption standards, audits, or access controls.

Parents should be aware that third-party advertising partners may collect data for their own purposes, and the sale or non-sale of user data to third parties is not explicitly addressed.

r387.parentSummary: Hudl collects extensive personal and athletic data about student athletes, including name, contact details, video footage, biometric data, and AI-derived performance data. This data may be shared with advertising partners such as Facebook, Google, and Twitter for targeted advertising purposes, and with recruiters if a student opts into recruiting features. Schools are responsible for obtaining parental consent for students under 13, but Hudl itself does not strongly gate COPPA compliance at the platform level, making careful school-level oversight essential before deploying this tool with minors.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: Hudl states the current policy is always available at hudl.com/privacy and that users will be notified of material changes via email or prominent notice, but there is no revision history or changelog publicly available.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: Hudl's privacy policy and student athlete privacy statement enumerate specific categories of data collected, including identifiers, biometrics, video, messages, health info, device data, and geolocation.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy specifically describes how data is collected — through account registration, website visits, wearable devices, cookies/web beacons, coach uploads, and third-party SSO logins.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: Ownership is not explicitly stated as belonging to the user; Hudl grants itself broad licenses to use and aggregate data, and the organization terms grant Hudl sublicensable, royalty-free rights to content — leaving data ownership ambiguous.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users can access, correct, or delete personal data via their account profile, and state-specific rights (including deletion) are provided with a formal request mechanism and Do Not Sell/Share form.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy states data is kept only as long as necessary to fulfill collection purposes or legal requirements, but does not specify a concrete retention period in days or years for most data types.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: Hudl's security page lists specific measures including role-based access control, least-privilege principles, employee confidentiality agreements, security awareness training, audit logging, and a zero-trust network strategy.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: Hudl states that all data processed, transmitted, and stored is encrypted using the latest industry standards, and authentication credentials are encrypted in transit with passwords salted and hashed.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: Hudl requires customers to use a unique email and strong password by default, and supports SSO; strong password enforcement is explicitly stated for all Hudl user accounts.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: MFA is available upon request for customers who wish to enhance account security, but it is not enforced by default — making this only partially met for standard K-12 deployments.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The policy mentions cookies, web beacons, and advertising/analytics cookies generally, and names some advertising partners, but does not provide a fully categorized cookie list with individual purposes for each cookie type.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: Hudl specifically names major advertising partners including Facebook, Google, Twitter, LiveRamp, and Amobee, as well as categories of other third parties such as affiliates, contractors, and service providers.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: While advertising partners are named, the specific data fields shared with each individual third party are not enumerated — only general categories or grouped descriptions are provided.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Opt-out mechanisms exist for specific partners (Facebook, Google, Twitter, LiveRamp, Amobee) and a state privacy rights form is available, but the opt-out process requires navigating multiple third-party platforms, making it limited in practice.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy states disclosures to third parties will comply with applicable law and purposes listed, but does not explicitly require all third-party partners to sign a vendor agreement or assert contractual responsibility for all categories of partners.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy notes that it may be updated periodically and users will be notified of material changes, but does not specifically commit to notifying users when third-party sharing partners change.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: Hudl explicitly uses targeted advertising cookies and web beacons, and personalizes advertising content for logged-in users — meaning targeted ads are displayed to users including potentially student athletes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Hudl confirms use of targeted advertising via named ad partners (Facebook, Google, Twitter, LiveRamp, Amobee) and uses web beacons to personalize advertising, constituting confirmed user targeting.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Third-party tracking for ads is confirmed, but Hudl provides opt-out links for each named advertising partner, resulting in limited but available opt-out rather than no tracking.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Hudl explicitly uses web beacons and tracking technologies to monitor traffic, conversion patterns, and ad performance, and these are used for advertising rather than functional purposes only.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: A Do Not Sell/Share request form is available and state-specific opt-out rights are described, but the process requires submitting a formal request rather than providing a simple in-product toggle, making this only partially accessible.

r388.riskReason: Huion is primarily a consumer hardware brand with no dedicated K-12 or FERPA/COPPA compliance framework, collects extensive personal and device data, shares it with numerous unnamed third parties, updates its privacy policy without advance user notice, and is governed by Chinese law with disputes resolved in Chinese courts.
r388.parentSummary: Huion collects a wide range of personal data including name, email, address, device identifiers, IP address, location, and usage information when users register or use Huion products and apps. While Huion states it does not sell personal data and uses TLS encryption to protect it, it shares data with payment processors, analytics services (including Google Firebase and Umeng), resellers, and shipping companies, and does not provide advance notice before updating its privacy policy. Huion is not designed as an educational platform and has no stated COPPA, FERPA, or SOPIPA compliance, making it unsuitable as a school-deployed EdTech tool without additional vetting and legal review.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The privacy policy explicitly states it may be updated at any time without separate notice to users, with changes taking effect immediately upon publication.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The app-agreement and download-clause pages list several data types (name, email, address, device IDs, IP, location, usage), but the primary huion.com/privacy-policy page is vague and does not enumerate all collected data in one place.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: Huion provides a general statement that data is collected when registering, using products, or downloading software, but does not give a complete or specific breakdown of every collection method (e.g., cookies, pixel tags, SDKs).
complianceNotes.DCQ3: Huion's policies do not clearly affirm user ownership of data; the HiNote policy grants Huion broad rights to use user-posted content 'for any legal purposes on both the application and beyond,' suggesting company claim over content.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users can request deletion via support contact, but some policies note that certain data may not be removable, and there is no self-service deletion mechanism described; the process requires contacting Huion directly.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The Keydial policy states data is retained 'no longer than is necessary,' and the download-clause mentions responding to data requests within 30 days, but no specific retention periods in days or years are defined.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The download-clause references TLS encryption and 'a variety of security technologies and procedures,' but the main huion.com privacy policy only states 'technical and security measures' without any specifics.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The Keydial privacy policy states data is encrypted before sending to hosting organizations 'if possible,' and the download-clause confirms TLS encryption, but this is not universally stated across all Huion policy pages.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: No mention of password strength requirements or enforcement is found in any of Huion's publicly available privacy or terms pages.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No mention of multi-factor authentication, SSO, or LTI integration is found in any of Huion's publicly available policies.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The HiNote and Huion Note policies acknowledge that third-party cookies and tracking pixels may exist on linked sites, but Huion does not provide a dedicated cookie policy listing all cookies used and their purposes.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: Some specific third parties are named in certain sub-policies (e.g., payment processors: Digital River, BlueSnap, PayPal, Stripe; analytics: Umeng, Firebase/Google), but the main privacy policy only references third parties generically.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: Grouped disclosure exists (e.g., payment data goes to payment processors, analytics to Umeng/Firebase), but no policy page provides a comprehensive table of exactly what data is shared with each named third party.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: The app-agreement page mentions users can adjust analytics settings within the application, but opt-out procedures are not clearly or consistently described across all Huion policy pages.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The Keydial policy states Huion signs NDAs and data processing clauses requiring third parties to comply with its privacy policy, but other Huion policy pages offer only general statements or disclaim responsibility for third-party actions.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: No policy page states that users will be notified if Huion's third-party service providers change; the main privacy policy is updated without separate user notice.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The app-agreement page references identifiers for advertising (IDFA for iOS, GAID for Android) collected from devices, indicating advertising-related data collection beyond simple platform analytics.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Advertising identifiers (IDFA, GAID) are explicitly collected per the Keydial privacy policy, indicating the potential for user-level targeted advertising, which is a significant concern for minors.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: No opt-out from advertising identifier collection or third-party ad tracking is described in any of Huion's policies, and third-party services like Firebase may conduct their own tracking.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: HiNote and Huion Note policies acknowledge that 'Cookie or tracking pixels may exist' on third-party sites accessible through their platforms, but Huion does not fully disclose its own use of such tracking methods.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Users can opt out of marketing emails per the download-clause page, but there is no clear opt-out mechanism described for advertising data sharing or behavioral tracking by third-party ad networks.

dataCollected: Video viewing history (show titles, episode names)

r389.riskReason: Hulu is a consumer entertainment streaming platform that actively uses targeted advertising, sells/shares user data with third parties under California law, collects extensive personal and behavioral data, and has no K-12 educational purpose, FERPA compliance, or SOPIPA commitments whatsoever.
r389.parentSummary: Hulu collects a wide range of personal data including name, email, birth date, location, device identifiers, and detailed video viewing history, which is used to serve targeted advertisements and shared with numerous third parties including advertisers, analytics providers, and Walt Disney family companies. Hulu explicitly acknowledges selling or sharing user data under California privacy law definitions, and the platform is designed for adult consumers, not K-12 students. Hulu is not an educational platform and lacks any FERPA, COPPA (for under-13), or SOPIPA compliance commitments, making it highly inappropriate for use in a school environment.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The subscriber agreement states changes are effective 30 days after notice is posted or emailed, but no publicly accessible change log or revision history of prior policy versions is maintained.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: Hulu's privacy policy and California state disclosures provide a detailed enumeration of collected data categories including identifiers, demographic info, commercial info, geolocation, internet activity, and inferences.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The privacy policy specifically describes collection methods including direct user input at registration, automated usage and log data collection, cookies, local storage, web beacons, pixels, mobile device SDKs, and third-party sources.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: Hulu's Media Feed Terms explicitly state that all user activity data collected via its player is owned exclusively by Hulu, and the consumer privacy policy does not assert user ownership over personal data.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users can submit deletion requests via email to privacy@hulu.com, but there is no self-service instant deletion tool, and the process involves contacting Hulu directly without a guaranteed timeframe.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The privacy policy states data is retained 'for the length of time needed to fulfill the purposes outlined in this privacy policy,' which is a general statement without specific retention periods defined.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The privacy policy references 'technical, administrative, and physical security measures' to protect user data but does not enumerate specific security technologies or frameworks employed.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: No explicit mention of end-to-end or at-rest encryption is made in the consumer privacy policy; the policy only provides a general security statement without confirming encryption standards.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The subscriber agreement and privacy policy contain no mention of password strength requirements or enforcement of strong passwords for user accounts.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: Hulu does not offer or mention multi-factor authentication (MFA) for standard consumer accounts, and no SSO or LTI integration for educational use is available.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The privacy policy references use of cookies, local storage, web beacons, pixels, and SDKs for advertising and analytics, but does not provide a comprehensive list of each cookie's name and specific purpose.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The privacy policy broadly categorizes third parties as business partners, social networking services, service providers, advertisers, and corporate owners, but does not name specific companies.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy describes categories of data shared with grouped third-party types rather than specifying which exact data elements are disclosed to each individual third party.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: California residents have opt-out rights for data sale/sharing via state privacy rights tools, but opt-out is not universally available to all users and the process requires navigating state-specific rights pages.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The advanced TV advertising terms include data-handling representations from advertisers, but the consumer privacy policy only broadly states that third parties are bound by applicable law without detailing specific contractual prohibitions.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The privacy policy does not specifically commit to notifying users when new third-party data sharing relationships are added or existing ones materially change.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: Hulu offers ad-supported subscription tiers where targeted advertisements from third-party companies are displayed to users during content playback.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Hulu's privacy policy confirms it uses collected user data including behavioral and demographic information for interest-based and online behavioral advertising targeting.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Hulu uses cookies, web beacons, pixels, and mobile SDKs from third-party advertising partners to track user behavior, with only limited opt-out mechanisms available primarily for California residents.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Hulu explicitly uses web beacons, pixels, cookies, device identifiers, and SDKs to facilitate third-party advertising and track user activity across platforms for ad measurement purposes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: California residents can opt out of data sale/sharing for advertising via the state privacy rights page, but this opt-out is not clearly available or straightforward for users outside California.

dataCollected: Support/feedback contact information (if user initiates contact)
r390.riskReason: The HumanWare explorē Magnifier app explicitly states it does not collect or share any personal information during use, requires no account, and only collects anonymous device telemetry — presenting minimal K-12 privacy risk, though the lack of explicit COPPA/FERPA declarations and a dedicated K-12 policy introduces minor compliance uncertainty.
r390.parentSummary: The HumanWare explorē Magnifier is a mobile assistive-technology app for iOS and Android that requires no account or login to use. According to HumanWare's mobile app privacy policy, the app does not collect or share any personal information; it only collects non-personal device data (such as device ID, OS version, and build number) to improve the product, and contact information only if a user voluntarily reaches out for support. There are no ads, no third-party data sharing, and no student data sold, making it a low-risk tool for K-12 use, though HumanWare has not published an explicit COPPA or FERPA compliance statement specific to this app.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The mobile app privacy policy states it is updated 'from time to time' but provides no advance notification process or revision history; the store-level policy does mention email notification for material changes.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The mobile app privacy policy explicitly states no personal information is collected during use, and lists only non-personal device data (device ID, OS, build number) — a clear and complete disclosure.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy specifically states data is collected passively from device usage and only voluntarily if the user contacts support, clearly describing the collection mechanism.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: Because the app collects no personal information and only anonymous device telemetry, there is effectively no user-owned personal data at stake; the policy implies data is used solely to improve the service.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: No deletion mechanism is described in the mobile app privacy policy, likely because no personal data is retained, but the omission of any deletion process leaves this criterion unmet.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: No data retention period or general retention statement is provided in the mobile app privacy policy.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The mobile app privacy policy does not describe specific security measures; the broader HumanWare store policy references vulnerability scanning and 'commercially acceptable means' but is not app-specific.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: No mention of encryption is made in the mobile app privacy policy or the app store listings.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: No account creation is required to use the app, eliminating password-related risks entirely.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No account or login is required, so MFA and SSO are not applicable and the risk is fully mitigated.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The mobile app privacy policy does not address cookies or in-app tracking technologies; the app store listing (Apple App Store) confirms no data is collected, but no formal cookie/tracking policy exists for the app.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The mobile app privacy policy states no personal information is collected or shared, effectively disclosing that there are no third-party data recipients for personal data.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: Because no personal data is shared with third parties per the mobile app policy, there is nothing to disclose on a per-third-party basis — this criterion is met by virtue of no sharing occurring.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: No third-party data sharing of personal information takes place per the app policy, so no opt-out is needed; this criterion is satisfied.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The mobile app privacy policy makes no mention of supplier agreements, data processing contracts, or third-party vendor accountability obligations.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: There is no stated process for notifying users if third-party data sharing practices change in the future.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: Neither the app store listings nor the privacy policy indicate that any advertisements are displayed within the app.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: No targeted advertising is referenced anywhere in HumanWare's mobile app privacy policy or app store descriptions.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: No third-party tracking for advertising purposes is mentioned or evidenced in the app's privacy documentation.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: No web beacons, tracking pixels, or ad-related tracking methods are mentioned; only functional device telemetry is described.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Because no advertising or advertiser data sharing occurs, no opt-out mechanism is needed and this criterion is fully satisfied.

r391.riskReason: The privacy policy excludes under-13 users without a COPPA-compliant parental consent mechanism, makes no mention of FERPA, does not name specific third-party vendors, lacks a stated data retention period, provides no explicit data deletion process for users, and offers only a general 'commercially acceptable' security statement — all significant gaps for a K-12 deployment.
r391.parentSummary: Hypatia (hypatiasys.com) is a math editor used in K-12 classrooms that collects names, email addresses, IP addresses, and device/usage log data. The platform states it does not knowingly serve children under 13 and will delete their data if discovered, but provides no parental consent workflow required by COPPA for school use. Data is shared with unnamed third-party service providers for analytics and error tracking, and no explicit data deletion rights, retention timelines, or FERPA commitments are described.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The policy states it may update the Privacy Policy and advises users to review the page periodically, but does not commit to advance notification or maintain a revision history.

complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The policy acknowledges third-party code may use cookies to collect information but does not clarify whether web beacons or pixel tracking are used or excluded.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: No opt-out process for data sharing with advertisers or marketing partners is described anywhere in the policy.

r392.riskReason: iAnnotate's privacy policy contains no mention of COPPA, FERPA, or SOPIPA compliance, no minimum age requirement, no prohibition on targeted advertising, and no explicit student data protections, making it unsuitable for K-12 use without further institutional vetting.

r393.riskReason: IBM Watson is explicitly not designed for children or minors, has no COPPA or FERPA compliance disclosures, engages in targeted advertising and third-party data sharing for marketing purposes, and its Terms of Use state that policy changes may occur at any time without notice to users.

The platform collects extensive personal data including names, email addresses, IP addresses, geolocation, and behavioral/usage data, and shares this with advertising partners, analytics providers, and social networks for targeted marketing. There are no disclosed COPPA or FERPA compliance commitments, and the Terms of Use allow policy changes at any time without advance notice, making this platform unsuitable and potentially non-compliant for K-12 school use.

complianceNotes.SECQ3: IBM's Terms of Use and Privacy Statement make no mention of strong password enforcement requirements for Watson service accounts.

complianceNotes.SHRQ4: IBM states it shares data with suppliers and partners on a need-to-know basis and references contractual controls (e.g., Standard Contractual Clauses), but does not explicitly claim responsibility for third-party compliance in the main privacy statement.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: IBM's Terms of Use state that terms may be revised at any time without notice, meaning third-party relationship changes may occur without user notification.

complianceNotes.ADVQ2: IBM explicitly states it delivers targeted advertisements using data collected about user interactions, hashed email addresses, and authorized third-party data, confirming user-level targeting.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: IBM uses advertising partners and third-party tracking technologies (cookies, web beacons, pixels) for targeted advertising across IBM and third-party sites with limited opt-out options via Cookie Manager.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: IBM's privacy statement confirms use of web beacons, pixels, tags, cookies, HTML5, and Local Storage for tracking user behavior, including for advertising purposes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: IBM provides opt-out options via the Cookie Preferences manager and email unsubscribe, as well as a Global Privacy Control (GPC) signal, but the opt-out process is fragmented and not clearly comprehensive for all advertising data sharing.

r399.riskReason: iNaturalist collects geotagged observation data and PII, shares user data with Google Analytics for advertising on third-party websites, uses third-party tracking that cannot be fully opted out of, and most user-submitted content is public by default — creating significant privacy risks for K-12 students.
r399.parentSummary: iNaturalist collects personal information including name, email, location data, and photos when students create accounts and post nature observations, and most of this content is public on the internet by default. The platform shares data with third parties including Google Analytics, which can use information to serve ads on external websites, though iNaturalist states it does not sell personal data for marketing purposes. Children age 12 and under require parental consent to participate, but the platform lacks a formal FERPA or SOPIPA school agreement, and its public-by-default data model and third-party ad-tracking integrations present notable concerns for classroom use.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The policy states changes are posted when material updates are made and are effective immediately upon posting, but no advance notification to users is provided and no revision history or changelog is maintained.

r404.riskReason: InThinking allows student access to selected pages via teacher accounts but does not specify a minimum age, lacks explicit COPPA/FERPA compliance statements, and its combined ToS/Privacy page lacks detailed data retention periods, MFA, and granular cookie disclosures required for K-12 environments.
r404.parentSummary: InThinking collects only names and emails from registered users (primarily teachers), stores data on an encrypted server in Ireland compliant with GDPR, and states it does not sell or share user information with third parties (except sharing workshop participant details with the International Baccalaureate Organization). Students can be granted access to selected pages by their teachers but cannot hold their own subscriptions, and users may request access, correction, or deletion of their data by contacting InThinking directly. However, the platform does not explicitly address COPPA or FERPA compliance, does not specify data retention periods, and uses Google Analytics and third-party cookies without a detailed cookie inventory.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: InThinking states it will notify Account Managers by email of material changes to its Privacy Policy and Terms, but there is no mention of a revision history or versioned archive of past policies.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The policy lists name, email, and optional fields (country, years teaching, student count), plus Google Analytics usage data and session cookies, but does not explicitly enumerate all data types collected from student users granted access by teachers.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy generally states that data is collected upon registration and through Google Analytics usage tracking, but does not detail how data is collected from students who access pages via teacher-shared credentials.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The policy does not explicitly address data ownership; it states data is stored on InThinking's private server, leaving ownership ambiguous between the user and InThinking.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users can exercise their right of erasure by contacting InThinking directly, which satisfies the deletion requirement, though it requires manual contact rather than a self-service mechanism.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: No specific data retention period is stated anywhere in the legal/privacy page; there is no mention of how long subscription or personal data is kept after account termination.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The policy states data is stored on a private server using encryption and GDPR compliance, but does not list specific security measures such as firewalls, access controls, or security audits.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The legal page explicitly states the server uses encryption and the site uses HTTPS, satisfying basic encryption requirements.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The policy requires a unique email and password per user but makes no mention of strong password enforcement rules or complexity requirements.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: There is no mention of multi-factor authentication or SSO/LTI integration options anywhere in the legal or terms documentation.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The policy mentions session cookies and third-party Google Analytics cookies, but does not provide a full enumerated list of all cookies, their purposes, or their lifespans.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: Google Analytics and the International Baccalaureate Organization are named as parties with whom data or usage information is shared, but no other third parties are disclosed.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy notes that anonymized usage data goes to Google Analytics and workshop participant details go to the IBO, but does not detail exactly what data fields are shared with each party.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can contact InThinking to exercise data rights, but there is no explicit opt-out mechanism for Google Analytics data sharing or IBO sharing for workshop participants.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy makes no mention of data processing agreements, contractual obligations, or requirements imposed on third parties such as Google Analytics or the IBO to protect user data.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: There is no statement about notifying users if new third-party data sharing arrangements are added or existing ones change beyond the general policy-change email notification.

complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Session cookies and Google Analytics tracking are used for functional and analytical purposes respectively, but the policy does not clearly delineate whether any tracking extends beyond functional use.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: There is no described opt-out process for the Google Analytics data sharing, only a link to Google Analytics' own privacy information, which is insufficient as a clear user opt-out mechanism.

r405.riskReason: iScanner collects device advertising identifiers, shares cookie and behavioral data with third-party ad networks for targeted advertising, builds data profiles for personalized ads, and has no stated COPPA compliance, no minimum age requirement, no children-specific privacy section, and no FERPA commitments — making it inappropriate for K-12 deployment without significant policy safeguards.
r405.parentSummary: iScanner collects account email addresses, device identifiers, usage/log data, and location-related information, and shares this data with third-party advertising and analytics partners who may use it to build behavioral profiles and deliver targeted ads. While documents themselves are stored locally by default and iScanner states personal data is not sold, the app does not include any COPPA-specific protections, has no minimum age requirement, and Common Sense Media's evaluation flagged that personal information is shared for third-party marketing and personalized advertising. Schools and parents should be cautious about deploying this app with students under 18, particularly under 13, given the absence of child-directed privacy safeguards.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The Privacy Policy states that new processing purposes will result in policy updates, but there is no explicit advance notification mechanism or published revision history for users.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The Privacy Policy enumerates specific categories of data collected including email, device details, IP address, location-related data, advertising identifiers, log files, and optionally user photos for ML improvement.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy specifically describes how data is collected — automatically via analytics SDKs, via account registration, via support contact forms, and via optional user submission for ML purposes.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The policy does not clearly state that users own their data; it implies company control over collected behavioral/device data, though user-generated documents are stated to remain under user control.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users can delete their iScanner account via in-app or web settings, which permanently deletes all associated account data with no possibility of restoration.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: Some retention periods are mentioned (e.g., ConvertAPI deletes files within 3 hours post-conversion), but there is no comprehensive, explicit data retention schedule for all categories of user data collected.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The policy references GDPR and CCPA adherence and AWS cloud storage security, but does not enumerate specific technical security measures such as encryption standards or access controls within the privacy policy text itself.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: Common Sense Media's evaluation confirmed that all data in transit and at rest are encrypted, consistent with AWS hosting standards.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The privacy policy and terms of use do not mention password strength requirements or enforcement of strong passwords for account creation.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: There is no mention of multi-factor authentication (MFA) or support for SSO/LTI in the privacy policy or terms of use.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The policy references categories of third-party service providers (advertising networks, analytics tools, ConvertAPI, AWS, email marketing tools) but does not name all specific vendors explicitly within the main policy text.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy groups data shared with third parties broadly rather than specifying exactly what data each named third party receives, making it difficult to assess on a per-vendor basis.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can opt out of advertising identifier tracking via iOS ATT settings or device settings, and can contact iScanner to cease personal data processing, but the opt-out process is not a simple in-app toggle.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy states that third parties are service providers acting under agreement and for business purposes only, but does not detail contractual data protection obligations imposed on those third parties.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy does not state that users will be notified if specific third-party service providers change or are added; updates to the overall policy are mentioned but not specifically tied to third-party changes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: Common Sense Media's evaluation confirmed that personalized advertising is displayed within or associated with the app, and the privacy policy acknowledges third-party ad networks delivering targeted ads.

complianceNotes.ADVQ5: An opt-out form exists for ceasing personal data processing, and device-level advertising ID opt-out instructions are provided, but the process is not a clear, simple in-app opt-out from advertiser data sharing specifically.

r408.riskReason: Jotform is a general-purpose form builder with no explicit COPPA or FERPA compliance commitments, no stated minimum age, third-party tracking cookies and web beacons in use, and terms that allow policy changes without advance notice — all of which create significant compliance risks for K-12 deployments.
r408.parentSummary: Jotform collects account registration details, form submission data, billing information, usage/device data, and tracking data via cookies and web beacons, some of which may be processed by third-party cloud and analytics providers. Jotform states it does not sell customer form data, and data is deleted after account closure or one year of inactivity, but the platform does not explicitly claim COPPA or FERPA compliance and sets no minimum age for account holders. Schools deploying Jotform should be aware that third-party tracking is active on the platform, that Jotform's terms do not include a student data protection addendum, and that the responsibility for lawful use of collected data largely falls on the form creator (i.e., the school).

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The Terms of Use state Jotform may modify terms at its sole discretion and that continued use constitutes acceptance, but no advance notification process or public revision history for the policy itself is specified.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The Privacy Policy lists multiple categories of data collected (registration, billing, usage, form responses, device, referral, page tags) but notes this is explicitly 'not an exhaustive list,' leaving the inventory incomplete.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The Privacy Policy specifically describes how data is collected — directly from account creation, via form submissions, through billing, via third-party tracking services using cookies and page tags, and from third-party accounts if linked.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The Privacy Policy states that form data is owned and managed by the Customer (form creator), and Jotform does not claim ownership of user-submitted form data, satisfying the user-owns-data standard.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users can close their account and make forms unavailable, after which personal data is deleted within one month; users also have stated rights to access, amend, delete, and request data portability.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The Privacy Policy states data is retained for as long as the account is active or necessary for service, deleted one month after account closure, or held encrypted for one additional year after one year of inactivity before deletion — a clear and specific retention policy is present.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: Jotform explicitly lists security measures including 256-bit SSL encryption, PCI DSS Level 1 compliance, SOC 2 compliance, form-level encryption, password protection, reCAPTCHA, and annual security audits.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: Jotform uses SSL encryption for data in transit and encryption at rest, and offers optional end-to-end form encryption; however, file uploads are noted by third-party reviewers as not encrypted, representing a partial gap.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The Privacy Policy and Terms do not explicitly state that strong passwords are enforced for all account types; password protection is available as a feature but mandatory enforcement standards are not described.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: Multi-factor authentication is not explicitly mentioned as available or required in the publicly accessible Terms or Privacy Policy, though SSO is available via Enterprise plans only.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The Privacy Policy mentions use of cookies and page tags (web beacons) by third-party tracking services, but does not provide a detailed list of all cookies by name and purpose as required for a full 'Meets' rating.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The Privacy Policy names Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud as third-party server providers and references third-party payment processors and tracking services, but does not provide a comprehensive named list of all third parties.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The Privacy Policy groups data shared by category of recipient (cloud providers, payment processors, analytics) rather than specifying exactly which data elements are shared with each named third party.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users have the right to withdraw consent and request data deletion, and some opt-out mechanisms exist under GDPR/CCPA rights, but a simple, universal opt-out from all third-party data sharing is not clearly described in the policy.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The Privacy Policy states Jotform does not sell form data and uses third-party providers to deliver services, implying contractual relationships, but the policy does not explicitly state that all third-party vendors are contractually bound to follow Jotform's data protection standards.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The Terms of Use state Jotform may update terms at its sole discretion with no obligation to notify users of changes to third-party relationships, meaning users may not be informed when third-party data processors change.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: Jotform's Privacy Policy does not explicitly state that no ads are shown to users; the free tier includes Jotform branding on forms, and third-party tracking services are used, suggesting some form of advertising infrastructure may be present.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: The Privacy Policy does not clearly state that targeted advertising is prohibited; third-party tracking services collect usage and user statistics, which could support behavioral targeting, though no explicit targeting program is confirmed.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: The Privacy Policy confirms use of third-party tracking services employing cookies and web beacons to collect aggregated and anonymized data about visitors, with no clearly described opt-out mechanism available to users or form submitters.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The Privacy Policy explicitly states use of page tags (web beacons) and third-party tracking cookies to collect usage data and user statistics, which goes beyond purely functional tracking.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: No clear, easy opt-out process for data sharing with advertisers or tracking third parties is described in the Privacy Policy or Terms of Use for standard (non-Enterprise) users.
