r477.riskReason: Mendeley is a graduate/researcher-oriented platform with no stated minimum age, no explicit COPPA or FERPA compliance, collects extensive personal and behavioral data, delivers targeted advertising, shares data broadly across Elsevier affiliates and third parties, and is wholly inappropriate as a K-12 EdTech tool without significant vetting and institutional agreements.
r477.parentSummary: Mendeley, owned by Elsevier, collects a wide range of personal data including names, email addresses, usage activity, uploaded research content, and device/location information, primarily to personalize research services and deliver targeted advertising across the Elsevier product ecosystem. Data is shared with Elsevier affiliates, institutional administrators, sponsors, and third-party service providers, though Elsevier states it does not sell personal information for commercial purposes. The platform is designed for university researchers and professionals, has no stated minimum age restriction suitable for K-12 use, and makes no mention of COPPA or FERPA compliance, making it a high-risk tool for use with students under 18.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The privacy policy states changes will be posted with an updated revision date and material changes will be notified through the service or other means, but no formal advance notification window or revision history archive is explicitly provided.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The Elsevier privacy policy provides a detailed enumeration of personal data types collected, including contact details, account credentials, educational/professional background, uploaded content, device data, IP address, usage activity, and location data.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy clearly states data is collected in three ways: directly from user input, from third-party sources, and through automated technologies such as cookies, web beacons, and servers.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: Mendeley Data's FAQ states users retain ownership of uploaded data, but the main Elsevier privacy policy describes Elsevier as the 'primary controller' of personal information, creating ambiguity around full user data ownership in the context of account and usage data.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: The U.S. Consumer Privacy Notice explicitly grants users a right to request deletion of personal information, and Mendeley Data allows deletion of draft datasets directly and published datasets via contact, satisfying the deletion requirement.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy mentions data retention in the context of specific operational needs (e.g., IP data retained up to 13 months for COUNTER compliance), but does not provide a comprehensive, clearly stated general retention schedule for all data categories.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: Elsevier references a 'defense-in-depth security methodology,' penetration testing, and use of Amazon Web Services infrastructure, but does not publish a detailed list of all specific technical security controls in the consumer-facing privacy policy.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: Data is stored on Amazon Web Services infrastructure (noted for Mendeley Data in Ireland), implying encryption at rest and in transit, but the main Elsevier privacy policy does not explicitly state end-to-end encryption for all data in transit.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The Terms of Use and Privacy Policy make no mention of password strength requirements or enforcement policies, leaving this compliance point unaddressed.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: The platform supports SSO via institutional credentials and allows sign-in via third-party accounts, but there is no explicit mention of multi-factor authentication (MFA) being available or required for standard user accounts.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: Mendeley provides a detailed Cookie Notice at mendeley.com/terms/cookie-policy that categorizes cookies (strictly necessary, performance, functionality, and advertising) with descriptions of each type and available opt-out tools.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The policy identifies broad categories of third parties (affiliates, service providers, sponsors, joint venture partners, societies) but does not name specific third-party companies or vendors receiving personal data.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy groups data sharing by third-party category rather than specifying exactly which data types are shared with each individual third party, making it difficult to determine precise data flows.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can manage communication preferences and opt out of certain data uses via the Elsevier Privacy Center and cookie settings, but opt-out from all third-party sharing is not clearly or easily accessible in a single process.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: Elsevier's FAQ explicitly states that all third parties processing data on behalf of Elsevier must agree to the RELX Privacy and Data Protection Requirements for Suppliers or comparable terms, satisfying contractual responsibility requirements.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The privacy policy states it will be updated from time to time and material changes will be communicated, but does not specifically commit to notifying users when third-party data-sharing relationships change.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The Elsevier privacy policy explicitly lists 'deliver targeted advertisements, promotional messages, and other information related to the Service and to your interests' as a purpose for data use, confirming targeted ads are served.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Elsevier confirms use of personal data to deliver targeted advertisements based on user interests and activity across their product ecosystem, which constitutes confirmed user-level targeting.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: The Cookie Notice mentions advertising cookies and references consumer opt-out tools such as YourAdChoices and Your Online Choices, offering limited opt-out options but confirming third-party tracking for ads occurs.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The Elsevier Researcher Academy privacy policy confirms use of web beacons and similar tracking technologies, and the Cookie Notice confirms advertising/marketing cookies are used, indicating tracking beyond functional purposes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Users can opt out of cross-contextual behavioral advertising via cookie settings or by sending an opt-out preference signal per the U.S. Consumer Privacy Notice, but the process is not prominently surfaced and requires navigating multiple policy documents.

r478.riskReason: Common Sense Media rates Mentimeter with a Warning due to confirmed third-party behavioral/targeted advertising, data collection by third-party tracking services, and use of data to target ads on other websites, which are incompatible with K-12 student privacy requirements under COPPA and SOPIPA.
r478.parentSummary: Mentimeter collects personally identifiable information including names, email addresses, IP addresses, and usage/behavioral data from account holders, and participants' responses are also recorded. While data is stated to not be sold, it is shared with third-party advertising and tracking services and used to serve targeted ads on other websites, which poses significant privacy risks for student users. Mentimeter has a 'Privacy Principles for Kids' page and requires users to be at least 13, but lacks explicit COPPA or FERPA compliance statements, and COPPA/parental consent processes are unclear.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The privacy policy indicates an effective/version date, but Common Sense evaluation notes that advance notification of material changes and a changelog of past versions were not clearly evaluated or confirmed.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: PII is confirmed as collected (name, email, IP address, browser, usage data), but a full enumerated list of all collected data categories is not clearly disclosed in a single consolidated location per Common Sense evaluation.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: Some information on how data is collected (account registration, voting participation, cookies, third-party trackers) is referenced, but the policy provides only a general rather than comprehensive description of each collection method.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: Common Sense evaluation notes user data ownership was not evaluated; the policy does not clearly and explicitly state that users own their data, leaving ownership ambiguous.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Common Sense evaluation confirms that processes for schools, parents, or students to delete data are available, satisfying the deletion requirement.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: Third-party sources note participant IP addresses are stored for 12 months and presenter IP addresses stored until revoked, indicating some retention information exists but a comprehensive, policy-stated retention schedule for all data types is not clearly published.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: Mentimeter states it uses industry best practices to protect data and both data in transit and at rest are encrypted, but specific technical security measures (e.g., SOC 2, ISO 27001 certifications) are not confirmed in publicly available policy text.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: Common Sense evaluation confirms all data in transit and all data at rest are encrypted, meeting the encryption requirement.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: Common Sense evaluation does not confirm strong password enforcement, and no evidence of enforced password complexity requirements was found in publicly available documentation.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: Common Sense evaluation did not confirm two-factor authentication is available, and no evidence of MFA or SSO/LTI support for K-12 was found in publicly available documentation.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: Mentimeter has a dedicated Cookie Policy page (https://www.mentimeter.com/trust/legal/cookie-policy), but search results confirm third-party advertising and tracking cookies are used, and a full enumerated list of cookies with purposes was not confirmed from available sources.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: Common Sense evaluation confirms collected information is shared with third parties and categories are indicated, but specific named third-party companies are not confirmed as publicly listed in the policy.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: Categories of information shared with third parties are indicated per Common Sense evaluation, but specific data fields shared with each individual third party are not clearly delineated.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: No evidence of a clear or easy opt-out process from third-party advertising data sharing was found; data is confirmed to be shared with advertising/marketing third parties without an apparent straightforward opt-out for K-12 users.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: Common Sense evaluation confirms contractual limits are placed on third-party data use, partially satisfying this requirement, though third-party security protections were not evaluated.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: No evidence was found that users are notified of changes to third-party sharing arrangements; Common Sense evaluation did not confirm this practice.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: Common Sense evaluation confirms behavioral or targeted advertising is displayed to users, which is not appropriate for K-12 student use.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Common Sense evaluation confirms data is used to track and target advertisements on other third-party websites or services, confirming cross-site targeted advertising.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Common Sense evaluation confirms data is collected by third-party advertising or tracking services with no confirmed opt-out mechanism available to K-12 users.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Common Sense evaluation confirms third-party advertising or tracking services collect data, indicating web beacons or similar tracking methods are in use for advertising purposes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: No clear opt-out process from advertiser data sharing was identified in publicly available documentation; Common Sense evaluation did not confirm this capability.

r479.riskReason: The free, ad-supported version of Merriam-Webster displays behavioral/targeted advertising, allows third-party tracking across sites, collects data beyond educational purposes, and has received a 'Warning' rating from Common Sense Media for K-12 use.
r479.parentSummary: Merriam-Webster collects personal information such as name, email, age, and device/usage data, and its free service is supported by behavioral advertising that uses third-party trackers to target users across the web. While the platform states it does not sell personal data and offers COPPA/FERPA-compliant institutional subscription options, the free consumer-facing product used by most students displays targeted ads and shares data with advertising networks, posing notable privacy risks for K-12 students. Schools should consider using only the paid, ad-free institutional subscription if deploying this platform.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The privacy policy notes it will be updated from time to time and states amended terms take effect 30 days after posting, but no proactive advance notification process or revision history/changelog is clearly provided; prior versions require an email request.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The policy lists common data types (name, email, city, state, age, phone, usage/behavioral data, device identifiers) but acknowledges data received from third parties may extend beyond what is explicitly enumerated, leaving the full scope partially unclear.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy specifically describes multiple collection methods including registration forms, cookies, pixel tags, web beacons, device identifiers, server logs, and third-party data providers.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The policy does not explicitly affirm user ownership of data; Merriam-Webster claims rights to use data for its business purposes and data may be transferred in a merger or acquisition, leaving ownership unclear.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users can request correction or deletion of personal data by emailing dpo@m-w.com, but there is no self-service deletion portal and the process, timeline, and scope of deletion are not clearly defined.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: No specific data retention period or general retention timeline is stated in the publicly available privacy policy; this topic is not substantively addressed.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The policy states only that 'industry best practices are used to protect data' without enumerating specific technical or organizational security measures.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: Encryption is not explicitly confirmed for data in transit or at rest in the policy; Common Sense Media flagged encryption status as unclear.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: No mention of password strength requirements or enforcement is made in the Terms of Use or Privacy Policy.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No mention of multi-factor authentication or SSO/LTI integration for K-12 institutional use is found in the public policies.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: A Cookie Policy exists and lists cookie categories and opt-out options, but it groups many third-party advertising cookies together without naming all individual third parties or fully detailing each cookie's purpose.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The policy references third-party service providers and advertising networks (mentioning Google, DoubleClick, Heap, and Google Analytics by name) but does not provide a comprehensive named list of all third parties.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy describes categories of data shared with third parties generally but does not provide a granular breakdown of exactly which data elements go to each specific named third party.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Opt-out mechanisms for behavioral advertising are mentioned (IAB opt-out, Google Ads Settings, Google Analytics opt-out add-on), but these are external browser-level tools rather than a simple in-product opt-out, making the process burdensome.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy makes a general statement that third parties facilitating service delivery must handle data appropriately, but does not describe specific contractual security or privacy obligations imposed on third-party vendors.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The cookie policy states it may be updated periodically without prior notice, and no process for notifying users of new third-party relationships is described.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The free, ad-supported version of Merriam-Webster displays behavioral and targeted advertisements, which is confirmed by the policy and third-party evaluations including Common Sense Media.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Common Sense Media confirmed that behavioral/targeted advertising is displayed and data is used to track and target ads on other third-party websites and services.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Third-party advertising networks (including Google/DoubleClick) collect tracking data, but opt-out options via IAB framework and Google Ads Settings are referenced, providing limited user control.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The policy and cookie policy confirm use of web beacons, pixel tags, device identifiers, and third-party advertising cookies for ad targeting purposes on the free service.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Opt-out options for behavioral advertising are mentioned (IAB, Google Ads Settings, browser settings) but the process is fragmented across multiple external platforms rather than a single, clear in-product opt-out mechanism.

r480.minAge: 13 (parental consent required for under 13 if registering)

r480.riskReason: Word Central is a children's vocabulary site that expressly prohibits collecting data from under-13 users and does not sell data, but third-party tracking and advertising services are present alongside unclear FERPA and SOPIPA compliance posture and an outdated, minimally detailed privacy policy.
r480.parentSummary: Merriam-Webster Word Central may collect a child's first name and email address for newsletters or contest entry, and uses cookies and third-party tracking technologies on the site. Data is not sold to third parties, and only first-party (Merriam-Webster merchandise) advertisements appear on the site; however, third-party tracking services are confirmed to collect data, and the site's privacy policy is dated and lacks specifics around K-12 school data protections such as FERPA or SOPIPA compliance. Parents of children under 13 have the right to review, delete, or restrict collection of their child's data by submitting a written request to Merriam-Webster.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The policy indicates an effective/update date and notes changes take effect 30 days after posting, but there is no explicit advance notification method or publicly accessible changelog of past versions beyond emailing the company.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The policy lists some data types collected (name, email, city, state, age, IP address, usage data via cookies), but the WordCentral-specific policy is sparse and largely redirects to the broader Merriam-Webster policy, leaving children's data categories incompletely disclosed.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: Collection methods are partially described (voluntary form submissions, automated cookie/tracking collection), but the WordCentral-specific policy does not clearly enumerate all automated collection methods in one place.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The policy does not explicitly assert user ownership of data; Merriam-Webster retains data for its own purposes including service delivery and demographic analysis, making ownership ambiguous.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Parents of children under 13 are explicitly granted the right to request review, deletion, or cessation of collection of their child's personal information via a provided parental letter form, satisfying a deletion mechanism.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The broader Merriam-Webster policy states data is retained 'as long as necessary to permit us to use it for the purposes communicated,' which is a vague general statement without a specific timeframe.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The policy references physical, technical, and administrative safeguards and states security technology is updated on an ongoing basis, but does not name specific security measures or frameworks.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: No explicit mention of encryption (at-rest or in-transit) is made in the WordCentral or applicable Merriam-Webster privacy policy; a third-party audit found the site's SSL certificate had expired as of 2019.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The site does not appear to require user account creation to access core dictionary and game features, so strong password enforcement is effectively a non-issue for the majority of users.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No account is required to use core features, eliminating MFA concerns for most users; optional newsletter/sweepstakes registration does not mention MFA but the risk is low given the minimal data collected.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The policy references cookies and similar technologies (pixel tags, web beacons) and links to a separate Cookie Policy, but the WordCentral-specific page does not enumerate all cookies by name or purpose.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: DRH Internet Inc. is specifically named as the third-party email/newsletter provider, and Encyclopaedia Britannica is identified as the parent company, but other third-party advertising and tracking services are not individually named.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy notes that email addresses are shared with DRH for newsletter delivery and payment information with processors, but data shared with unnamed advertising/tracking third parties is not itemized per party.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can unsubscribe from newsletters at any time, and parents can opt out of all data collection for under-13 children; however, opt-out from third-party tracking cookies requires browser-level controls rather than an in-product mechanism.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy states third-party providers are given data solely for the purpose of providing services on Merriam-Webster's behalf, implying contractual limits, but no explicit vendor agreement or data processing agreement terms are described.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy reserves the right to update third-party relationships without specific advance notice to users beyond the general 30-day policy change posting notice, with no dedicated notification process for third-party changes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: Common Sense Media reviews confirm that the only advertisements on Word Central are for Merriam-Webster's own merchandise, not third-party commercial ads, which represents a low-risk advertising posture.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: While first-party ads are platform-only, third-party tracking services are confirmed to be present on the site, and the policy does not explicitly rule out behavioral profiling for advertising on other platforms.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Third-party tracking/advertising services do collect data on the site, but the policy references opt-out tools (e.g., Google Ads Settings) and IAB TCF consent management via OneTrust, providing partial but incomplete opt-out coverage.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The policy and Cookie Policy acknowledge use of web beacons, pixel tags, and JavaScript tracking in addition to cookies, but do not clearly confirm these are used solely for functional purposes versus ad targeting.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: An opt-out pathway exists via the IAB Transparency & Consent Framework (OneTrust CMP) and Google Ads Settings for analytics/advertising tracking, but the process is not prominently described or easily accessible within the WordCentral-specific policy.

r481.riskReason: Meta Quest for Business is a consumer-grade commercial VR platform not designed for K-12 use, collects extensive biometric and behavioral data, explicitly disclaims fitness for regulated educational fields, relies on a fragmented web of overlapping privacy policies with no FERPA or COPPA-specific commitments, and broadly shares data across the Meta ecosystem and third-party advertising partners.
r481.parentSummary: Meta Quest for Business collects a wide range of data including biometric-adjacent information (head/body movement, eye tracking, facial expressions), voice audio, device identifiers, location, and detailed usage logs, which flow into Meta's broader advertising and analytics ecosystem. While Meta states it does not sell customer data or use it to personalize consumer Meta products in a business-managed account context, data is still shared with third-party developers, analytics partners, and law enforcement. This platform was not designed for K-12 schools, explicitly disclaims suitability for the educational sector, and provides no COPPA or FERPA-specific protections, making it a high-risk choice for student use.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The Meta Privacy Policy states users will be notified before material changes are made and will have an opportunity to review the revised policy, but a full public revision history is not maintained or linked.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The Supplemental Meta Platforms Technologies Privacy Policy and related disclosures list many data categories (device info, voice, biometrics, profile, usage, location), but the data is spread across multiple overlapping documents making a complete enumeration difficult to ascertain.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: Meta's policies specifically describe how data is collected — through device sensors, account registration, voice services, developer APIs, crash logs, cookies, and third-party partners — satisfying this criterion.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: Meta's commercial terms indicate that customer data is logically separated and not used for advertising, but Meta retains broad licensing rights over content shared on the platform and does not clearly affirm that users or organizations own their data outright.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users can delete their Meta Horizon profile via Accounts Centre, but managed Meta accounts can only be deleted by the organization's admin, not by individual users, limiting self-service deletion rights.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: Meta states data is retained as long as necessary to provide products or comply with legal obligations and references case-by-case retention decisions, but no specific retention period (e.g., 90 days, 1 year) is clearly defined for most data categories.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: Meta for Work's trust page details specific security measures including sandboxing, encryption, malware detection, vulnerability scanning, PIN requirements, remote wipe, SSO integration, and SOC 2 and ISO audits.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: Meta explicitly states it leverages Android encryption features for operating system security and implements encryption as part of its device and data security infrastructure.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: Meta Quest for Business supports SSO (single sign-on) and identity provider integrations, and the managed account system enforces organizational authentication standards, satisfying this criterion.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: Meta for Work explicitly supports two-factor authentication and SSO/identity provider integrations as part of its enterprise security controls for managed deployments.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: Meta provides a cookie help page for Quest devices and a Meta Cookies Policy referencing specific cookies (e.g., '_fbp' for advertising), but the full list of cookies with individual purposes is not presented in a single, consolidated disclosure specific to the Business platform.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: Meta's policies broadly categorize third-party recipients (analytics partners, advertisers, developers, vendors, law enforcement) but do not name specific third-party companies by name in a centralized list for the Business product.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: Data shared with third parties is described in grouped or general terms across multiple policy documents rather than specifying exactly which data categories are shared with each named third party.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Some opt-out controls exist (e.g., ad preferences, cookie management, off-Meta activity settings), but opt-outs are limited in scope — they affect ad personalization rather than stopping data collection, and managed-account users have reduced individual control.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: Meta states it requires developers to comply with Meta Platform Terms and Developer Policies and reserves the right to remove non-compliant apps, representing a general contractual accountability claim but not a specific vendor data protection agreement.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: Policy change notifications are promised for material changes to the main Meta Privacy Policy, but no specific process is described for notifying users when new third-party data-sharing relationships are added.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: Meta's cookie policy for Quest explicitly states cookies are used to show relevant ads and measure ad campaign performance, including on third-party websites, confirming ads are displayed on the platform.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Meta uses device advertising IDs, behavioral data, and off-platform activity to enable targeted advertising, with third-party apps also permitted to run ads based on user advertising IDs depending on ad preferences.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Users can adjust some ad preferences and use opt-out tools (e.g., Google Analytics opt-out, Facebook ad settings), but these controls are fragmented, do not stop underlying data collection, and are described as limiting personalization rather than blocking third-party tracking.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Meta uses cookies (including advertising cookies like '_fbp'), pixel tracking, and third-party analytics integrations on Quest devices for advertising and measurement purposes, constituting confirmed tracking beyond functional needs.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Meta provides ad preference controls and links to industry opt-out tools, but these mechanisms only limit how data is used for ad targeting rather than providing a clear, comprehensive opt-out from data sharing with advertisers entirely.

Schools should not deploy this platform until verified privacy documentation meeting COPPA, FERPA, and SOPIPA requirements is available and reviewed.

r483.riskReason: Mindomo has meaningful child privacy protections and ISO 27701/GDPR compliance, but it is a Romanian-based platform that does not explicitly claim FERPA or COPPA certification, uses third-party service providers who may set their own cookies and collect data independently, and lacks specific data retention timeframes or a named list of all third-party vendors.
r483.parentSummary: Mindomo collects personal information such as names, email addresses, IP addresses, and usage data from users, and students can only join via a teacher or school account rather than registering directly. The platform states it does not sell personal data, does not permit third-party targeted advertising, uses 256-bit SSL encryption, and allows parents or guardians to request deletion of a child's data by contacting support. However, Mindomo is a European company (Romania) without explicit COPPA Safe Harbor certification, and some third-party service providers may independently collect data through cookies and tracking technologies on the platform.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The Terms of Use state Mindomo will inform users of amendments 'in good time' and that silence within 14 days constitutes acceptance, but no formal revision history or changelog is publicly maintained.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy policy lists major data categories (name, email, IP, usage/analytics, grades, payment info) but does not provide an exhaustive enumeration of every data field collected, leaving some ambiguity.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The privacy policy specifically describes data collected directly at registration, through third-party integrations (Google, LTI), through automatic tracking technologies (cookies, log files), and via payment processors.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The Terms of Use explicitly state 'You retain all ownership rights you have in any User Submissions' and 'Mindomo does not claim any ownership rights in the User Submissions.'
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users can delete their accounts and all associated data through in-app settings, and parents/guardians can request deletion of a child's data via email to support; deletion is processed within 14 days.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy states data is deleted upon user request or end of service, and logs are kept 'as long as the logs are kept,' but no specific numeric retention periods (e.g., 90 days, 1 year) are stated for different data types.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The security page details specific measures including 256-bit SSL encryption, bcrypt password hashing, SSH key server access, ISO 27001-certified data center, full-disk encryption on workstations, and periodic disaster recovery testing.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: Mindomo explicitly uses 256-bit SSL/TLS encryption over public networks and bcrypt hashing for passwords, with SSL certificates from Sectigo RSA and RapidSSL CA.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The Terms of Use mention passwords and user responsibility for credentials, but the privacy and security documentation does not explicitly state that strong password complexity rules are enforced on users.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: Mindomo supports LTI and Google SSO integration which can provide SSO-level access control, but no explicit multi-factor authentication (MFA) option for standard accounts is documented in the available policies.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The privacy policy mentions cookies, log files, Local Storage Objects (HTML5), and tracking technologies generally, but does not provide a comprehensive named cookie list with individual purposes.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: Stripe, PayPal, and Amazon AWS are named; Google Drive, OneDrive, and Dropbox are mentioned as optional integrations, but other third-party service providers who may collect data via cookies are not individually named.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: Payment data shared with Stripe/PayPal is implied by context, but the policy does not specify exactly which data fields are shared with each named or unnamed third-party service provider.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can opt out of cookie-based tracking via browser settings as noted in the policy, but there is no dedicated opt-out mechanism for third-party data sharing beyond browser-level controls.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy states that in merger/acquisition scenarios, the acquiring entity must be 'bound by the same commitments,' and that no data is transferred unless the recipient 'has agreed to comply with our Privacy Policy,' but broader third-party vendor contractual obligations are not described.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy states Mindomo will 'always notify users before any transfer takes place' in a merger/acquisition, but does not explicitly commit to notifying users when third-party service providers change.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The privacy policy explicitly states 'We do not permit third parties to collect information from our website for the purpose of sending targeted advertisements on our site or on other websites.'
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Mindomo does not use targeted advertising based on user data, as confirmed by the explicit statement prohibiting third-party targeted ad data collection on their platform.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: While Mindomo prohibits third-party targeted ad tracking, third-party service providers may still place their own cookies and tracking technologies independently, which Mindomo states it does not participate in or control.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The policy acknowledges third-party service providers may use cookies, web beacons, and LSOs to collect data directly and automatically, and Mindomo states it does not participate in these transmissions, creating some ambiguity about the scope of tracking.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Users can adjust browser settings to refuse cookies per the policy, but there is no explicit dedicated opt-out mechanism or process described for opting out of any residual data sharing with third-party service providers.

r484.riskReason: Minecraft (via the Microsoft Privacy Statement) permits interest-based advertising, third-party ad tracking, and broad data sharing for non-educational purposes for non-student general users, and Microsoft was fined $20M by the FTC in 2023 for COPPA violations related to Xbox/gaming account sign-ups of children under 13 — raising significant concerns for K-12 deployment outside of the dedicated Minecraft Education product.
r484.parentSummary: Minecraft collects a broad range of personal data including name, email, date of birth, device identifiers, gameplay data, and communications, governed by the Microsoft Privacy Statement. While Minecraft Education claims COPPA, FERPA, and GDPR alignment and pledges not to use student data for advertising, the standard consumer Minecraft product (minecraft.net) does allow interest-based advertising and third-party ad tracking for general users, and Microsoft was fined $20 million by the FTC in 2023 for illegally collecting children's data through Xbox accounts without adequate parental notice or consent. Parents should be aware that the consumer version of Minecraft carries materially higher privacy risks than the dedicated Minecraft Education edition, and schools should use only Minecraft Education with a formal Data Protection Agreement in place.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The EULA states Microsoft will inform users of changes before they take effect, but the policy also notes that continued use constitutes consent to changes, making advance notification only partially robust for K-12 contexts.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The Microsoft Privacy Statement lists many categories of data collected (name, email, device IDs, usage data, diagnostics, advertising ID), but the Minecraft-specific data collection disclosures are distributed across multiple documents, making comprehensive review difficult.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The Microsoft Privacy Statement specifically describes how data is collected — directly from users, through product interactions, via cookies and web beacons, and from third parties — meeting this standard.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: Data ownership is ambiguous: Microsoft states user content belongs to the user, but Microsoft claims broad rights to use collected data for advertising and product improvement, making data ownership unclear for student users.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Microsoft provides a privacy dashboard for users to access, view, and delete personal data, and parents can manage child account data, satisfying the deletion requirement.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The Privacy Statement mentions data retention criteria and states advertising data is retained no more than 13 months, but lacks specific retention schedules for all data categories, making this only partially addressed.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: Microsoft explicitly states it uses strong security and encryption to protect user data, and references enterprise-grade security infrastructure across its services.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: Microsoft's privacy principles explicitly commit to encryption throughout its services, and the platform uses HTTPS; encryption is addressed in its privacy commitments.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: Microsoft accounts require passwords and Microsoft enforces account security standards including account recovery procedures; SSO via Microsoft accounts is available for school deployments.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: Microsoft accounts support multi-factor authentication (MFA) and organizations using Minecraft Education can enforce MFA via Microsoft Entra ID / Azure AD.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The Microsoft Privacy Statement describes cookies and web beacons generally and lists purposes, but does not enumerate all individual cookies with specific purposes in a granular cookie table, making this only a partial disclosure.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The Privacy Statement names some third-party ad partners (e.g., AppNexus, Facebook, Media.net in historical versions) and references analytics and advertising partner categories, but a current complete named list is not consistently maintained in the live policy.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy groups data sharing by category of third party rather than specifying exactly which data elements are shared with each named third party, falling short of full per-party disclosure.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Microsoft provides an opt-out page for interest-based advertising and a privacy dashboard, but opting out of advertising does not stop underlying data collection, making the opt-out only partial.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: Microsoft states it requires third parties to protect data per its policies and agreements, but provides only a general statement of responsibility rather than specific contractual accountability terms in the public-facing policy.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy reserves the right to update third-party partnerships and notes users should check back; it does not commit to proactive notification of changes to specific third-party sharing arrangements.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The Microsoft Privacy Statement confirms that interest-based advertising is served to general (non-child) users of Microsoft and Minecraft-related web properties, which is incompatible with K-12 deployment standards.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Microsoft explicitly uses data to target advertising to general users, including combining data across products and contexts; while children under 13 are excluded from interest-based ads, teen users (13–17) in the consumer product are not fully protected.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Third-party ad companies (e.g., AppNexus, Facebook) may place tracking cookies and collect data across sites; an opt-out mechanism exists but tracking is not disabled by default.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Microsoft explicitly uses web beacons and advertising IDs alongside cookies for ad targeting; third-party advertisers may embed their own tracking pixels, confirming ad-related tracking is present.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: An opt-out page for interest-based advertising exists, but opting out does not stop data collection — it only stops the use of data for ad targeting — making the opt-out process incomplete for K-12 privacy standards.

dataSharedWith: Vivendi Group entities (parent company, for targeted advertising partnerships)
r485.riskReason: Minion Rush is a consumer entertainment game with no FERPA compliance, third-party advertising SDKs, confirmed data sales to Vivendi Group and ad partners, third-party ad targeting for users 16+, a documented 2018 COPPA compliance concern, and no school data processing agreement — making it wholly unsuitable for K-12 classroom use.
r485.parentSummary: Minion Rush, developed by Gameloft, collects device identifiers, IP-derived location, usage data, and (if an account is created) name, email, and date of birth; for children under 13, only limited data such as age status, coarse location, and device identifiers are collected, and behavioral advertising is replaced with contextual advertising only. However, Gameloft explicitly states it may sell user data to Vivendi Group entities and select third-party advertising partners, and third-party ad networks use cookies, pixels, and SDKs for ad targeting (restricted to users 16+). This game was not designed for educational or school use, has no FERPA provisions, and has previously been flagged in academic research for potential COPPA issues.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: Gameloft re-posts updated policies with a modification date and maintains a public revision history page, but relies on continued use as acceptance rather than providing advance notice to users before changes take effect.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy policy lists several categories of data collected (device IDs, IP, usage, coarse location, age status), but the full list of third-party SDK data collected on behalf of ad partners is not comprehensively enumerated in one place.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy clearly states data is collected directly from the user, automatically through use of Services, and from third-party partners including advertisers, billing providers, and social networks.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: Gameloft explicitly states it may sell user data to Vivendi Group entities and select third-party ad partners, indicating the company asserts commercial control over user data rather than treating users as data owners.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users can request deletion of personal data via a webform; the policy confirms deletion will occur within one to two months, though a retained anonymous archive is reserved and game progress will be reset upon deletion.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy states data is retained while the user is active and for five years after inactivity for regulatory reasons, with children's data specifically retained for five years post-play per the Children's Privacy Policy.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The policy references general safeguards and secure operating environments accessible only by authorized employees, but does not enumerate specific technical security measures such as encryption standards, penetration testing, or SOC certifications.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: Industry-standard encryption is mentioned for financial/credit card data in the online store, but the policy does not confirm end-to-end encryption for all personal data transmitted during gameplay.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The Terms of Use advise users to keep passwords confidential and enable device-level password protection, but there is no mention of enforcing password complexity or strength requirements on Gameloft accounts.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No multi-factor authentication option is mentioned anywhere in Gameloft's Terms of Use or Privacy Policy for player accounts.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: A separate Cookie Policy exists and describes cookie categories and opt-out mechanisms, but it does not provide a granular per-cookie or per-vendor listing with specific purposes for each tracking technology used.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: Third-party categories are described broadly (advertising networks, analytics, billing, fraud prevention, Vivendi entities) but specific vendor names are only accessible via a separate consent management form rather than being listed directly in the policy.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy groups data shared with third parties by category of partner rather than specifying exactly which data fields are shared with each named third party.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can opt out of targeted advertising via in-app settings ('Manage My Choices') and via a webform, but the process requires affirmative action and is not straightforward; children under 16 are excluded from targeted advertising by default.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy states partner contracts are 'strictly drafted to protect personal information' and that partners cannot reuse data beyond the contracted purpose, representing a general contractual obligation rather than a named DPA framework.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy states the list of third-party partners 'may be updated from time to time' without committing to notifying users proactively when specific partners are added or removed.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The game contains third-party advertising; both the Apple App Store listing and Google Play Store listing explicitly state the game contains ads for Gameloft products and third parties that may redirect users to external sites.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Gameloft confirms it uses cookies, pixels, and SDKs with ad partners for targeted/interest-based advertising for users aged 16 and over, and children under 16 receive only contextual advertising — but targeted ads are present for older minors (16-17).
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Third-party ad tracking via SDKs, pixels, and cookies is confirmed; users can opt out via in-app 'Manage My Choices' or device-level ad ID settings, but opt-out is not automatic and tracking occurs by default until disabled.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The policy confirms use of cookies, pixels, SDKs, and similar technologies by Gameloft and its ad partners to collect advertising-related data including mobile ad IDs, browsing activity, and purchase history.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: An opt-out mechanism exists via in-app settings and a webform (DataProtectionSupport@gameloft.com), but the process is not clearly prominent or simple, and the policy does not guarantee a specific response timeline for ad data opt-outs.

r486.riskReason: Miro explicitly prohibits use by anyone under 16, uses interest-based and cross-context behavioral advertising trackers, shares data with marketing and advertising partners, does not have a dedicated K-12 or COPPA compliance policy, and places the burden of age verification on the school customer rather than enforcing it at the platform level.
r486.parentSummary: Miro is a visual collaboration platform that collects account information, usage data, board content, and cookie/tracking data, and may use that data for personalized and interest-based advertising via third-party analytics and advertising partners. The platform explicitly states it is not intended for users under age 16, which excludes most K-12 students, and there is no separate privacy policy or COPPA compliance framework for educational use. While Miro states it does not sell student data for marketing and offers a data deletion mechanism, its use of behavioral advertising trackers and third-party data sharing raises significant concerns for K-12 deployment.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The Privacy Policy states Miro will take 'commercially reasonable efforts' to notify users of material changes, but no formal advance notification timeline or revision history archive is explicitly provided.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The Privacy Policy lists multiple categories of data collected (account info, usage data, cookies, billing, content, AI interaction data), but the enumeration is grouped broadly and not exhaustively itemized for all scenarios.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The Privacy Policy specifically describes how data is collected — directly from users, automatically via cookies/trackers, through third-party integrations, and via third-party service providers — meeting this criterion.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The TOS states 'Customer maintains sole control' over Customer Content, but Miro retains broad rights to use Services Data (usage data, account info) for its own legitimate business purposes, creating ambiguity over data ownership.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Account deletion is supported and the Privacy Policy states that deletion of a Customer's account may result in deletion of associated personal data, satisfying the full deletion requirement.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The Privacy Policy states Miro retains data 'as long as necessary for the purposes described' and may retain some data after account deactivation for audits and legal compliance, but no specific retention periods in days or months are stated.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: Miro's security FAQ confirms the use of TLS 1.2+ for data in transit and AES-256 encryption at rest, restricted production environment access, and references a published Security Policy, meeting this criterion.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: Miro explicitly confirms TLS 1.2 or higher for transit and AES-256 at rest, meeting the encryption requirement.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The TOS requires users to keep login credentials confidential but does not explicitly state that strong password complexity rules are enforced at the platform level; SSO is supported on higher-tier plans only.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: Multi-factor authentication and SSO are available but appear to be limited to Enterprise plan tiers, not all plans, making MFA only partially available across the platform.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: Miro maintains a dedicated Cookies Policy and a Cookie List page that categorizes cookies (essential, performance, analytics, advertising) with descriptions of their purpose, meeting this criterion.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The Privacy Policy references a published subprocessors list (updated March 2026) naming specific vendors such as Amazon Web Services and Anthropic, but the main policy text describes third parties only in broad categories rather than naming them inline.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The Privacy Policy groups data shared with third parties by category (vendors, partners, advertising/analytics) without specifying which exact data fields are shared with each named subprocessor.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Miro provides a 'Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information' opt-out page for advertising/analytics cookies, but opt-out from all forms of third-party data sharing is not uniformly available or easy to exercise across all contexts.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The Customer Data Processing Addendum requires subprocessors to comply with data protection obligations, but the main Privacy Policy for third-party service integrations merely advises users to check those third parties' own policies, offering only a general assurance.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The Privacy Policy states Miro 'will take commercially reasonable efforts to notify you' of material changes, which would include third-party changes, but there is no explicit commitment to advance notice specifically for subprocessor or third-party changes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: Miro's Privacy Policy confirms it may deliver 'interest-based, targeted, or cross-context behavioral advertising' using cookies and trackers, meaning targeted ads can be displayed to users.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: The Privacy Policy explicitly acknowledges the use of advertising and analytics services for delivering targeted and cross-context behavioral advertising to users, confirming third-party user targeting.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: A 'Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information' opt-out mechanism is available, but it relies on a cookie to remember the preference and must be re-set per device/browser, making it only a partial opt-out from third-party tracking.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The Privacy Policy confirms the use of cookies, web beacons, pixels, tags, and a tracking GIF in emails specifically for advertising and analytics purposes, constituting confirmed tracking for ads.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: An opt-out link is available via the 'Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information' page, but the process is device- and browser-specific, cookie-dependent, and not persistent, making it only a partial opt-out mechanism.

r487.riskReason: Mission US is operated by a public media nonprofit (THIRTEEN/WNET), explicitly prohibits advertising and student data sales, collects minimal student data, limits use to educational purposes only, and expressly claims COPPA and FERPA compliance with data deleted within 365 days.
r487.parentSummary: Mission US collects limited student data including first name, partial last name, school, grade, and gameplay/coursework data, used solely for educational purposes under school authorization. The platform contains no third-party advertising or targeted advertising, and does not sell student data. Data is deleted within 365 days or at end of school year, and schools can request deletion at any time.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The privacy policy states THIRTEEN reserves the right to change it at any time with changes applied prospectively, and encourages users to periodically review it, but does not commit to advance notification before changes take effect.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy policy enumerates specific categories of data collected including teacher names and emails, student first name, partial last name, school, grade range, city/state, gameplay data, coursework responses, IP address, and clickstream data.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy clearly explains data is collected through direct user input (account registration, surveys), automatically via clickstream and cookies, and through third-party analytics tools like Google Analytics.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The policy explicitly states that as between THIRTEEN and its Educational Customers, all Personal Information subject to FERPA and COPPA is the property of the Educational Customer.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Educational institutions may direct THIRTEEN to delete Student Data at any time by emailing missionus@thirteen.org, and student accounts can be deleted by teachers through the Dashboard.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy states personal information from Educational Customers is deleted within 365 days of receipt, with renewed permission required annually, and student accounts are cleared each July at year-end.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The data retention policy details specific security measures including technical due diligence, data security and privacy trainings, oversight, audits, periodic tests, scans, risk assessments, and audit trails.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The policy does not explicitly mention encryption of data in transit or at rest; it acknowledges no method of safeguarding is completely secure but does not specify encryption standards in the main privacy policy.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The help page mentions students are recommended to change passwords on first login and teachers may be prompted to create passwords meeting new security requirements, but strong password enforcement is not explicitly stated as mandatory.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: The policy and help documentation do not mention multi-factor authentication or SSO/LTI integration options for login.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The privacy policy mentions Google Analytics cookies and clickstream data collection generally, but does not provide a full enumerated cookie list with individual purposes for each cookie type.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The privacy policy specifically names Google Analytics as a third-party analytics provider; however, other third-party service providers used for operational support are described only in general categorical terms without specific names.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: Google Analytics is named with IP address and usage data identified as shared, but data shared with other unnamed operational service providers is described only generally without per-party specifics.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: The policy states student data is used only for educational purposes and not for commercial purposes, and there is no third-party advertising; users can opt out of marketing emails via unsubscribe, and schools can refuse further data collection.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The data retention policy states THIRTEEN requires any service provider processing Personal Information to comply with and maintain a data security policy consistent with ISO 27001, NIST, or SOC 2 Trust Service Principles.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The privacy policy does not include a provision to notify users when third-party service providers change; it only encourages users to periodically review the policy.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The privacy policy explicitly states the Services do not contain third-party advertising or targeted advertising, and the platform does not send marketing communications to students.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: The policy unambiguously states no targeted advertising is present within the Services, and student data is not used for any commercial purposes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: The policy states Google Analytics is used for website analytics only, and for Educational Customers this data is used solely for school-authorized educational purposes, with no tracking for advertising.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Cookie and tracking use is limited to functional and analytical purposes (Google Analytics); the policy explicitly states the Services contain no third-party advertising, indicating no ad-related web beacons or tracking.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Because no advertising data sharing occurs for students, there is no opt-out needed; teachers and non-dashboard users can opt out of marketing emails via unsubscribe link or email request.

r488.riskReason: Moodle explicitly pledges never to collect, monetize, or sell student data from LMS sites, provides robust GDPR-aligned privacy tools, and supports DPAs with institutions, but COPPA and FERPA compliance is largely delegated to the deploying institution rather than guaranteed at the platform level.
r488.parentSummary: Moodle is an open-source learning management system that collects student account information (name, email), course activity, grades, submissions, and usage logs to deliver educational services. Moodle HQ explicitly states it does not collect, use, or monetize personal data from the thousands of Moodle LMS sites worldwide, and does not run ads within the LMS. However, because each school or district operates its own Moodle installation, the specific data practices, retention periods, and third-party integrations depend heavily on how each institution configures and manages their site, so parents should also review their school's own Moodle privacy policy.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: Moodle's Privacy Notice states a 'last updated' date is shown and significant changes trigger direct notification (e.g., a prominent website notice), satisfying advance notification and revision history requirements.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The Privacy Notice lists general categories of data collected (name, email, activity data, cookies, location identifiers) but does not provide a fully exhaustive enumerated list of every data field collected across all Moodle products and deployments.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The Privacy Notice describes that data is collected when users interact via websites, phone, in person, or when registering for events, but lacks a granular breakdown of automated vs. user-provided collection methods within the LMS itself.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The Terms of Service explicitly state that 'any and all Data you submit via the Moodle App Plans Services and Website are your sole and exclusive property,' clearly affirming user data ownership.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Moodle provides built-in GDPR tools including data export and deletion request workflows; users can request deletion via their profile or by emailing privacy@moodle.com, satisfying full deletion capability.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The Privacy Notice states data is retained 'for as long as necessary to fulfill the purposes outlined' and 'for the shortest amount of time possible,' but does not specify concrete retention periods (e.g., 90 days, 1 year) for different data types.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The Privacy Notice references 'physical, organisational and technical safeguards' but does not enumerate specific security measures (e.g., SOC 2, penetration testing, access controls) at the corporate policy level, leaving specific measures to hosting documentation.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: Third-party compliance guides note that server-level encryption (TLS, AES-256) is expected but responsibility is delegated to the hosting provider; Moodle's own privacy notice does not explicitly confirm encryption in transit and at rest for all deployments.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: Moodle supports configurable password policies and SSO/LTI integrations that can enforce strong passwords, but the default platform does not universally mandate strong password enforcement without administrator configuration.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: Moodle supports SSO and LTI integrations which can provide MFA at the institutional level, but MFA is not a built-in default requirement and depends on the institution's configuration.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: Moodle maintains a separate Cookies Policy at moodle.com/cookies-policy/ listing cookie categories (functional, tracking, optimization, partner) and third-party cookies, but does not enumerate every individual cookie with its specific purpose in the publicly accessible summary.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The Privacy Notice mentions passing data to 'third-party service providers' (e.g., video conferencing) and notes Google Analytics is used on public marketing sites, but does not publish a complete named list of all third-party sub-processors.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The Privacy Notice groups data sharing with third parties broadly around 'necessary service delivery' without specifying which data fields are shared with each individual third party, constituting a grouped rather than granular disclosure.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can withdraw consent at any time via 'delete my data' in the service or by emailing privacy@moodle.com, and Google Analytics behavioral tracking on marketing sites is separate from LMS data; opt-out pathways exist.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: Moodle explicitly states it 'seeks to enter into Data Processing Agreements with third-party service providers to ensure they only process your data as instructed,' satisfying the vendor agreement responsibility requirement.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The Privacy Notice states changes are communicated when made but does not specifically commit to proactive notification when third-party sub-processors are added or changed, leaving this only partially addressed.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: Moodle explicitly pledges it does not display ads within the LMS and does not monetize student data from any Moodle LMS sites; the platform is ad-free by design.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Moodle states it does not collect, use, or monetize personal information from Moodle LMS sites for any purpose including targeted advertising, fully meeting this standard.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: No third-party advertising tracking occurs within the Moodle LMS; Google Analytics behavioral tracking is limited to the public moodle.com marketing website and is explicitly separated from LMS learner data.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The Cookies Policy acknowledges web beacons are used on Moodle's public marketing websites for tracking site usage and marketing conversion, but these are limited to the corporate marketing site and not within the LMS student environment.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Users can opt out of data sharing and withdraw consent via profile settings or by contacting privacy@moodle.com; the Privacy Notice explicitly describes this right, satisfying the opt-out requirement.

r490.riskReason: MuseClass is explicitly designed for grades 6-12 (which includes students under 13) but relies on parent-company Muse Group's general consumer privacy policy that sets a minimum age of 16, contains no COPPA-specific parental consent mechanisms, permits sharing aggregate/anonymous data for advertising purposes, and uses advertising tracking technologies including cookies and marketing analytics — none of which are appropriately scoped for a K-12 student audience.
r490.parentSummary: MuseClass collects student names, email addresses, audio/video assignment recordings, AI-analyzed performance data, device information, and usage data through the platform operated jointly by Hal Leonard and Muse Group. While third-party sources describe the platform as compliant with US student privacy regulations, the publicly accessible privacy policy is a broad consumer-facing document that does not address COPPA, FERPA, or SOPIPA by name, and the governing Terms of Service set a minimum age of 16 — creating a mismatch with the platform's target audience of grades 6-12. Parents should request a copy of any school-specific Data Processing Agreement or DPA before allowing student use, as the public-facing policies do not provide sufficient K-12-specific privacy protections.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The Muse Group Terms of Service reserves the right to modify or discontinue the service 'with or without notice,' and no advance notification process or revision history mechanism is described for privacy policy changes.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The parent Muse Group privacy policy lists broad categories of data collected (contact info, technical data, usage data, social media data) but does not enumerate MuseClass-specific data such as student audio/video recordings or AI-graded performance data.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy describes data collection via direct interaction, automated technologies, and third parties in general terms, but does not specifically address how student assignment recordings or AutoGrade AI data are collected and processed.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The policy does not make an explicit statement that users own their data; Muse Group is identified as the data controller under GDPR, but no K-12-specific ownership or school/district data ownership clause is present.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: The Muse Group privacy policy allows users to contact privacy@mu.se to request deletion, but deletion requires deleting the entire account and may be refused if data accuracy would be affected — no streamlined school-directed deletion process is described.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: No specific data retention period is stated in the publicly accessible Muse Group privacy policy for MuseClass user or student data.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The policy makes only a general statement about taking privacy seriously; no specific technical security measures (e.g., encryption standards, access controls, SOC 2) are enumerated in the public-facing policy.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The main MuseClass site uses HTTPS, suggesting transport-layer encryption, but the privacy policy does not explicitly mention encryption of data at rest or in transit for student data.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: No mention of password strength requirements or enforcement is found in the public-facing Terms of Service or Privacy Policy.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No mention of multi-factor authentication or SSO/LTI integration is found in the public-facing legal documents, though the platform may support Google/Clever SSO in practice.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The website uses a cookie consent banner stating cookies are used for navigation, analytics, and marketing, but no detailed cookie inventory or categorized cookie policy listing specific cookies and their purposes is publicly available.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The privacy policy references broad categories of third parties (analytics providers, advertising networks, sub-contractors, data brokers) but does not name specific vendors used by MuseClass.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy groups third-party data sharing by category without specifying which data types are shared with each individual third party.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: No opt-out mechanism for third-party data sharing is described in the public-facing policy beyond contacting privacy@mu.se, with no easy or automated opt-out process for schools or students.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy states third-party service providers are not permitted to use collected data except to help conduct and improve business, but no explicit contractual accountability or vendor management clause is described for MuseClass specifically.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: No notification process for changes to third-party relationships or data sharing arrangements is described in the public policy documents.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The Muse Group cookie banner explicitly states cookies are used to 'assist in our marketing efforts,' indicating marketing/advertising cookies are active on the MuseClass domain.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: The parent company's data practices include sharing aggregate/anonymous data for advertising and marketing purposes, and advertising network third parties are listed as data recipients without excluding student users.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: No opt-out from third-party advertising tracking is offered within the MuseClass platform; only browser-level cookie control is mentioned.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The Muse Group policy and related properties reference use of cookies, pixels, and similar technologies for advertising and analytics with no indication that these are disabled or excluded for student users of MuseClass.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: No clear opt-out process for data sharing with advertisers is described in any publicly available MuseClass policy document.

dataSharedWith: Digital Advertising Alliance (DAA) participating third parties
r491.riskReason: MuseScore.com explicitly features interest-based advertising, shares personal data with third-party advertisers to build user profiles, sets a minimum age of 13 with no COPPA parental consent mechanism, does not claim COPPA or FERPA compliance, and is a general consumer platform not designed for K-12 school use.
r491.parentSummary: MuseScore.com collects account information (name, email), usage and behavioral data, device/browser identifiers, and cookies, and explicitly uses this data to enable interest-based (targeted) advertising — including sharing your information with third-party advertising companies to build advertising profiles. The platform requires users to be at least 13 years old and does not offer COPPA-compliant parental consent mechanisms, making it inappropriate for use with students under 13 without significant caution. There is no stated FERPA or COPPA compliance, and opt-outs for targeted advertising are available but are cumbersome, device-specific, and cookie-dependent.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: A privacy policy history page exists at musescore.com/legal/privacy/history and dates are shown, but the ToS;DR analysis notes terms may update with only continued-use acceptance rather than advance explicit notification.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The Muse Group privacy policy describes categories of data collected including usage, cookies, device, and social data, but the musescore.com-specific policy page does not render its full text in search results, leaving some uncertainty about completeness.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The parent Muse Group privacy policy clearly describes active collection (account registration, forms), passive collection (cookies, trackers), and third-party collection (social media logins), meeting this criterion.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The Terms of Service do not clearly affirm that users own their data; the company's broad data-use rights for advertising and profiling suggest the company effectively claims significant control over user data.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: The CCPA 'Do Not Sell' page and GDPR references indicate some deletion rights exist for qualifying residents, but no universal, straightforward account deletion process is clearly described for all users.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: A general retention statement exists referencing anonymization after a retention period, but no specific retention duration (e.g., number of days) is explicitly stated in accessible policy excerpts for musescore.com.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The Muse Group privacy policy references 'appropriate technical and organisational measures' but does not enumerate specific security controls such as encryption standards, firewalls, or audit procedures.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The site uses HTTPS (standard transport encryption), but the privacy policy does not explicitly confirm encryption of data at rest or specify encryption standards used.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: No information was found in the accessible policy text regarding password strength enforcement requirements for musescore.com accounts.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No mention of multi-factor authentication, SSO, or LTI integration for school use was found in the Terms of Service or Privacy Policy.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: A dedicated cookies policy page exists at musescore.com/legal/cookies, and the Muse Group privacy policy categorizes cookies into Essential, Analytics, and Third-Party Marketing cookies with descriptions of each.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The privacy policy references categories of third parties (analytics providers, advertising networks, social media platforms) and names Google Analytics as an example, but does not provide a comprehensive named list of all third-party partners.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy groups data shared by third-party category rather than specifying exactly which data fields are shared with each individual named third party.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Opt-out tools are referenced via the DAA WebChoices Tool and device-level ad tracking settings, but opt-outs are cookie-based, device-specific, and MuseScore disclaims responsibility for their operation.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy does not contain a clear statement requiring third-party vendors to adhere to a data protection agreement or equivalent contractual obligations aligned to user privacy rights.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: No specific notification process for changes in third-party sharing arrangements is described; policy updates are inferred from continued use rather than proactive notification.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: MuseScore.com explicitly features interest-based advertising, and the 'Do Not Sell My Personal Information' page confirms targeted ads are displayed on the platform and third-party sites.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: The platform explicitly confirms interest-based (targeted) advertising based on user activity and data shared with third-party advertising companies to build user profiles.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Third-party tracking for ads is confirmed; an opt-out is available via the DAA WebChoices Tool, but it is cookie-based, device-specific, and MuseScore disclaims control over the mechanism.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The privacy policy confirms use of third-party marketing cookies that 'collect information on your activities on the Site and other sites to display targeted marketing,' confirming cross-site tracking for advertising.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: A 'Do Not Sell My Personal Information' page exists with opt-out instructions via DAA tools, but the process is cumbersome, cookie-dependent, requires per-device action, and MuseScore disclaims responsibility for honoring it if cookies are cleared.
