r492.riskReason: Students access MusicplayOnline exclusively via anonymous teacher-generated class codes and provide no personal information, and the platform explicitly states it does not collect student PII, though teacher/educator account data is shared with several third-party analytics and service vendors.
r492.parentSummary: Music Play Themes and Variations (Musicplay, by Themes & Variations Inc.) does not collect any personal information from students — students access content only through an anonymous class code provided by their teacher and never create accounts or submit any personal data. Personal data (name, email, payment info, device/usage data) is collected only from registered adult educators and is shared with service providers including Stripe for payments, Google Analytics for usage tracking, and video-hosting platforms. The platform explicitly references COPPA, FERPA, SOPIPA, FOIPP, CIPA, and SOPPA compliance standards, and states it does not sell user data to third parties for promotional purposes.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The policy states it will be updated with a revised date and may notify users of material changes by notice or direct notification, but advance notification before changes take effect is not clearly guaranteed, and no revision history archive is provided.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy policy clearly lists all categories of data collected from educators (name, email, payment data, IP address, device/browser info, usage data, OAuth data) and explicitly states no personal information is collected from students.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy specifically describes how data is collected — voluntarily by users upon registration, automatically via browser/device tracking, and through third-party OAuth logins — satisfying this requirement.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The policy does not explicitly state that users own their data; it describes how the company processes and stores data but is silent on user data ownership rights, creating ambiguity.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users can request account deletion by contacting support or via account settings, and the policy states accounts and active database records will be deleted upon request, though some data may be retained for legal/fraud purposes.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy does not specify a defined retention period (e.g., 90 days or a specific number of years); it only states some data 'may be retained' for legal compliance and fraud prevention without a concrete timeframe.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The policy references general security efforts (fraud monitoring, breach notification within 72 hours) but does not enumerate specific technical security measures such as encryption standards, access controls, or penetration testing.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The site appears to use HTTPS, and payment data is handled by Stripe (which uses encryption), but the privacy policy itself does not explicitly state that data is encrypted at rest or in transit.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The policy does not describe or enforce password strength requirements; account creation requirements are mentioned (age verification, email restrictions for student domains) but password standards are not addressed.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No mention of multi-factor authentication or SSO/LTI integration for educator accounts is made in the policies reviewed; student access via class code bypasses this concern but teacher accounts lack MFA documentation.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: A detailed cookie policy exists listing individual cookies by name, purpose, provider, and expiration (including Google Analytics, PHP session, WordPress, and DigitalOcean cookies), satisfying the requirement for specific cookie disclosure.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The privacy policy names specific third parties including Stripe, Google Analytics, YouTube, Vimeo, SproutVideo, and DigitalOcean, meeting the requirement for named third-party disclosure.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: While third parties are named and grouped by category (payment, content optimization, analytics), the specific data fields shared with each individual third party are not fully enumerated on a per-vendor basis.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can contact the company to revoke consent for data processing, but a clear, self-service opt-out mechanism for third-party sharing (beyond browser cookie controls) is not explicitly described.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy states contracts are in place with data processors and affiliates must honor the privacy policy, indicating vendor agreements exist to govern data handling responsibilities.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy states it may update the privacy policy and may notify users of material changes, but does not commit to proactively notifying users specifically when third-party data-sharing arrangements change.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The cookie policy references third-party advertising tracking cookies and states third-party companies 'may use information about your visits to provide relevant advertisements,' suggesting some advertising presence exists for non-student users.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: The cookie policy acknowledges that third-party tracking technologies may be used to deliver relevant advertisements, though Google Analytics remarketing (Signals) is explicitly disabled on MusicplayOnline, indicating partial targeting controls.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Web beacons and third-party tracking cookies (Google Analytics NID cookie) are documented and used, and while some controls exist (e.g., remarketing disabled on MusicplayOnline), a comprehensive opt-out mechanism from all third-party ad tracking is not clearly provided.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The cookie policy explicitly discloses the use of web beacons ('tracking pixels' or 'clear gifs') for monitoring traffic patterns and measuring ad effectiveness, but it is unclear whether this applies within the student-accessible MusicplayOnline environment.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: No clear, step-by-step opt-out process for users who wish to stop their data from being shared with advertisers is described in the privacy policy or cookie policy beyond generic browser cookie settings.

r494.riskReason: The app is explicitly designed for infants and young children, displays third-party ads (including to babies), provides only a minimal multilingual privacy policy with no COPPA compliance statement, no parental consent mechanism, no data retention policy, no security details, no deletion rights, and no Terms of Service whatsoever.

NCES's official website collects no personal information from general visitors; only session cookies used for navigation are employed, and these do not store personal data. Any student data collected through official NCES research studies is governed by strict federal law, never sold, and may only be used for statistical purposes, with contractors required to sign nondisclosure agreements.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The IES/NCES privacy and security policy page does not explicitly describe an advance notification process or maintain a publicly visible revision history for policy changes.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The IES privacy policy clearly states that no personal information is collected from general website visitors; only session cookies and network monitoring data (non-PII) are captured, and voluntary form submissions are explicitly noted.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy specifically describes how data is collected — via session cookies, automatic server logs, network monitoring software, and voluntary email/form submissions — with clear explanations for each method.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: As a federal government agency, user data is not claimed as owned by a commercial entity; the policy states data is only used for the purpose provided and is destroyed after correspondence is complete, indicating user-protective ownership principles.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: No explicit user-facing data deletion mechanism is described in the public website privacy policy; however, Privacy Act rights allow individuals to request access to and correction of federal records, though this process is not clearly outlined on the IES privacy page itself.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy mentions session cookies are destroyed when the browser is closed and references a 90-day persistent survey cookie, but does not provide a comprehensive data retention schedule for all collected information.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The IES privacy policy lists specific security measures including SSL/128-bit encryption for survey portals, network traffic monitoring software, protected data files, separation of PII from descriptive data, and NIST-level security standards.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: Survey data portals explicitly state data is collected over SSL/128-bit encrypted connections, and the site uses HTTPS as a federal .gov website requirement.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: No account or password is required to access the public NCES website, which eliminates this concern for general visitors; restricted-use data portals use institutional access controls.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No user account is required for the public website; restricted-use data access requires formal application and institutional credentials, effectively functioning as a controlled-access system without consumer-style MFA.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The policy mentions session cookies and one persistent survey cookie with purpose described, but does not provide a comprehensive enumerated cookie list with all cookies, their names, and specific individual purposes.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The policy references Google Universal Analytics as a third-party analytics provider by name, and federal contractor names are published in Federal Register notices, but the public-facing privacy policy does not enumerate all third parties in one place.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: Google Analytics is described as receiving only aggregated, non-PII data; however, the specific data shared with each individual contractor/third party is not fully detailed within the main public privacy policy page.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: The policy explicitly states users can opt out of or disable cookies via browser settings and will still have full access to all content, providing a clear opt-out mechanism for the only significant third-party data sharing (analytics).
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: Federal contractors are legally required to sign Confidentiality Agreements and Affidavits of Nondisclosure, and NCES staff and contractors face severe fines and possible imprisonment for unauthorized disclosure.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The privacy policy does not explicitly commit to notifying users if third-party analytics or contractor arrangements change, though federal regulatory processes (Federal Register) govern major changes to data systems.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: No advertisements of any kind are displayed on the NCES/IES website, which is a federal government platform with no commercial advertising.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: As a federal government agency with no advertising model, there is no targeted advertising; the policy explicitly states data is not sold, rented, or exchanged.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Google Analytics is used only in an aggregated, non-PII manner and is explicitly prohibited from combining NCES data with other information; no user-level ad tracking occurs.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Only functional session cookies and one survey-avoidance persistent cookie are used; no web beacons or tracking pixels for advertising purposes are described or evident.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: No data sharing with advertisers occurs; the policy states 'we do not sell, rent, exchange, or otherwise disclose this information to persons or organizations,' making an opt-out moot.

dataSharedWith: Walt Disney Family of Companies affiliates
r504.riskReason: The site is explicitly child-directed and holds PRIVO COPPA Safe Harbor certification through Disney, but it displays interest-based ads, employs third-party tracking technologies (cookies, web beacons, pixels, Nielsen measurement), and data may flow broadly across the Walt Disney Family of Companies with limited transparency about specific third-party ad targeting of children.
r504.parentSummary: National Geographic Kids (kids.nationalgeographic.com) is operated by National Geographic Partners, a member of the Walt Disney Family of Companies, and does not require account creation for basic browsing. The site collects automatic technical data such as IP addresses, device identifiers, browser information, and usage patterns via cookies, web beacons, pixels, and similar trackers, and this data is shared with Disney affiliates, service providers, and third-party advertising/measurement partners including Nielsen. The site does maintain a dedicated Children's Online Privacy Policy and participates in PRIVO's COPPA Safe Harbor certification program, but the presence of interest-based advertising and broad data sharing within the Disney ecosystem warrants careful review before school-sanctioned use.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The Disney/NatGeo privacy policy states it may be amended at any time by posting the updated notice, without advance notification to users, which falls short of a full advance-notification standard.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The Children's Online Privacy Policy identifies categories of automatically collected technical data (IP address, device ID, browser, usage frequency) but does not provide a fully exhaustive enumerated list of every data type collected from child visitors.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy specifically states that data is collected via cookies, pixels, tags, SDKs, APIs, web beacons, and other unique identifiers, clearly describing the methods of collection.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: Ownership of data is not explicitly assigned to the user; the policy describes Disney/NatGeo Partners as the data controller with broad rights to use and share information across the Walt Disney Family of Companies, leaving ownership ambiguous.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Parents may submit requests to access or delete their child's data by contacting Disney directly, but the process requires contacting the company and is not a self-service deletion option, making it limited in practice.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy references retention in general terms tied to operational necessity and legal requirements but does not specify concrete retention periods for children's data, making this vague rather than fully defined.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The Walt Disney privacy policy references technical, administrative, and physical security measures but characterizes them only in general terms without listing specific technologies or protocols used to protect children's data.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The NGS policy mentions encryption for credit card data, and Disney states security measures are implemented, but end-to-end encryption for all children's data is not explicitly confirmed.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: No account is required to browse the site, and where accounts exist, Disney's system enforces age-gating and parental consent processes that effectively substitute for password enforcement requirements.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: Account creation is not required for basic use, and where it exists, Disney applies age-gating and parental consent controls; no standalone MFA is described but the overall gated model meets this criterion.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The policy mentions multiple categories of cookies (essential, analytics, personalization, targeted advertising) and refers users to a cookie banner and separate tracking page, but does not provide a fully itemized list of every cookie by name and purpose.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The policy references broad categories such as 'Walt Disney Family of Companies affiliates,' 'service providers,' and 'third-party advertising or tracking services' but does not name specific third-party companies receiving children's data.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy groups data sharing by category of recipient (affiliates, service providers, advertisers) rather than specifying exactly what data each third party receives, making the disclosure incomplete.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: A 'Do Not Sell My Info' link is present on the site and opt-out controls are described in the Disney Privacy Choices portal, but the process involves multiple steps and is not uniformly straightforward for all tracking activities.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The Disney Children's Online Privacy Policy states that service providers are contractually bound and that PRIVO COPPA Safe Harbor certification governs third-party data practices, meeting the vendor-agreement standard.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy reserves the right to update privacy practices and third-party arrangements by posting revised policies without advance notice, meaning users are not proactively notified of changes to third-party sharing arrangements.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The kids.nationalgeographic.com homepage explicitly lists 'Interest-Based Ads' as a footer link, and Common Sense Media's evaluation confirmed that behavioral or targeted advertising is displayed on the platform.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Common Sense Media's privacy evaluation confirmed that targeted/behavioral advertising is displayed and that third-party tracking services collect data on the platform, indicating user-level ad targeting is occurring.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: A 'Do Not Sell My Info' link and Disney Privacy Choices opt-out mechanism exist, providing some control, but third-party tracking (including Nielsen measurement) is active by default, placing the burden of opt-out on the user.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The policy confirms use of cookies, Flash cookies, pixels, tags, SDKs, APIs, and web beacons for advertising and tracking purposes, meaning tracking for ads is confirmed and not limited to functional purposes only.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: An opt-out mechanism ('Do Not Sell My Info' / 'Your Privacy Choices') is present and linked from the site, but it is a multi-step process tied to the broader Disney Privacy Center and may require separate opt-outs per device or browser, making it only partially accessible.

r506.riskReason: The platform explicitly acknowledges FERPA compliance and limits public student data, but shares student data with Lingco Language Labs and collects minor PII (name, address, grade level) with only vague parental consent language, uses cookies and conversion pixels without a detailed cookie policy, has no specific data retention timeline, and allows policy changes without advance notice.
r506.parentSummary: The National Spanish Exam (NSE), operated by AATSP Exams, collects student names, grade levels, addresses, and exam performance data submitted by teachers for the purpose of administering the Spanish language competition; individual student scores are kept private and only shared with the registered teacher and Lingco Language Labs (the exam delivery platform). The platform states it is bound by FERPA and does not publicly publish individual student names without written authorization, and students' exam data is wiped from teacher accounts each summer. However, the privacy policy uses general language around parental consent for minor data collection, does not specify a precise data retention period, and allows data to be shared with advertiser and vendor partners if members opt in, which may concern some parents.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The Terms and Policies page explicitly states that content 'may be changed at any time without notice' and users agree to changes by continued use, with no advance notification or revision history provided.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy policy lists several categories of personal data collected (name, address, phone, email, DOB, demographics, IP, OS, browsing data, credit card, student grade level) but does not provide a fully exhaustive enumeration of all data fields collected through Lingco Language Labs.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The privacy policy provides a general statement that data is collected during registration, membership, and browsing, and mentions cookies/pixels, but does not specifically describe the technical mechanisms or forms through which each data type is collected.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The policy does not explicitly state who owns the data; it refers to data as belonging to 'members and customers' but does not formally disclaim organizational ownership, leaving data ownership ambiguous.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: The privacy policy states there is 'a limited right to request deletion of personal data' directed to a designated contact, indicating deletion is possible but restricted and not guaranteed, constituting only partial deletion rights.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy states data 'may be retained for so long as necessary or useful to pursue the legitimate interests of NSE/AATSP,' which is a vague standard without a specific retention period, though the registration guide notes student data is wiped from teacher accounts each summer.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The privacy policy mentions general safeguards such as storing data in secure offsite facilities and limiting access to authorized employees, but does not list specific technical security measures such as encryption standards or security certifications.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The Terms page acknowledges that unprotected email communications are not confidential, implying email is not encrypted, while the payment page redirects to Authorize.net for secure payment processing; no explicit site-wide encryption statement is made.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The privacy policy and terms make no mention of password strength requirements or enforcement policies for user accounts on the platform.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: The platform uses Lingco Language Labs which supports LMS integrations (Canvas, Schoology, Clever, Blackboard) that may enable SSO, but no explicit MFA or SSO requirement is stated in the NSE's own policies.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The privacy policy mentions use of cookies and conversion pixels for tracking and personalization and notes users can disable cookies in browser settings, but does not provide a detailed list of each cookie type, its purpose, or its duration.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The privacy policy and a separate policies page name Lingco Language Labs, SHH, SHA, and AATSP as parties receiving teacher/school data, and Lingco as receiving student data, but third-party analytics tools used for web traffic are not named.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy distinguishes between what is shared with exam-affiliated organizations versus opt-in advertiser/vendor partners, but does not provide a granular breakdown of exactly which data fields are shared with each named third party.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can opt out of third-party marketing data sharing by unchecking boxes during/after account creation and can unsubscribe from broadcast emails, but there is no stated opt-out for data shared with Lingco Language Labs as the operational test provider.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The privacy policy does not state that third-party recipients are bound by a vendor agreement, data processing agreement, or any contractual obligation to protect shared data, though schools can separately request a privacy agreement from Lingco.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The Terms and Policies page states content may be changed at any time without notice, and there is no specific provision for notifying users when third-party data sharing arrangements change.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The privacy policy references sharing data with 'vendors and advertiser partners related to our mission' only for members who opt in, suggesting ads or advertiser partnerships may exist but are not displayed to general platform users without consent.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Data sharing with advertiser and vendor partners is conditional on member opt-in permission, which partially limits targeting, but the policy does not explicitly prohibit the use of user data for targeted advertising by those partners once shared.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: The privacy policy states third-party analytics tools are used for web traffic measurement and that conversion pixels are used; no opt-out mechanism for this third-party tracking is described.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The use of conversion pixels is explicitly mentioned alongside cookies, which are tracking technologies commonly used for advertising attribution, but their specific purpose (functional vs. advertising) is not clearly distinguished.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Users can opt out of receiving additional information about third-party products and services via account settings, but the process is not fully described and no explicit opt-out from data sharing with advertisers (as opposed to receiving communications) is stated.

r507.riskReason: NSC holds highly sensitive K-12 student PII (names, dates of birth, enrollment records) received institutionally under FERPA school-official exceptions, shares it with loan servicers and verifiers, uses cookies and web beacons on its site, and does not explicitly address COPPA compliance despite confirmed data collection on minors under 18.
r507.parentSummary: The National Student Clearinghouse is a nonprofit that receives student enrollment and degree records from schools and districts — including high schools — under FERPA's school-official exception, and uses that data primarily for enrollment reporting to the Department of Education, student loan deferment processing, and credential verification. The Clearinghouse explicitly states it does not sell student personal information, holds iKeepSafe FERPA and SOPIPA privacy badges, and requires strict contractual safeguards when data is shared with third parties. However, parents of K-12 students should be aware that their child's name, date of birth, and enrollment history may be shared with the Clearinghouse as directory information — and can opt out through their school — and the platform's COPPA compliance posture for direct online interactions is not explicitly addressed in its public policies.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The policy states material changes will be notified via website or email, but all changes are effective immediately upon posting with no advance notice period guaranteed before taking effect.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy policy provides a detailed enumeration of data types collected, including education records from institutions, directly submitted personal information, and automatically collected usage/technical data.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy specifically describes how data is collected — directly from users, from participating institutions under FERPA exceptions, automatically via cookies/web beacons/Flash cookies, and from third parties like lenders.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The Clearinghouse explicitly acknowledges that institutions own the data and it acts only as a school official disclosing data at the institution's direction, consistent with FERPA data ownership principles.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Students can request deletion through the Privacy Block Setting or by contacting the Clearinghouse, and the policy states data will be returned or deleted when a school ends its contract, but individual end-user deletion is not described as a self-service process.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy references retaining aggregate de-identified data for benchmarking and deleting PII when institutions end contracts, but does not state specific retention periods (e.g., number of days or years) for all data categories.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The Clearinghouse maintains SOC2 Type 2 and SOC3 certifications, partners with the Center for Internet Security (CIS), follows NIST cybersecurity frameworks, and conducts annual mandatory employee privacy and security training.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The iKeepSafe FERPA badge assessment requires evaluation of encryption practices, and the Clearinghouse passes this audit, but the public privacy policy and terms of use do not explicitly describe end-to-end or at-rest encryption in plain language.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The platform requires users to be at least 18 years old and uses institutional account relationships; direct consumer account security requirements are governed by the Myhub terms, though password strength enforcement specifics are not detailed in the public policy.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: The privacy and terms documents do not explicitly mention MFA availability; institutional access uses secure site credentials but no MFA or SSO requirement is stated in the public-facing documentation.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The privacy policy lists cookies, Flash cookies, web beacons, and analytics as tracking technologies used, but does not provide a full cookie inventory with individual purpose descriptions or a separate cookie consent mechanism.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The policy references broad categories of third parties (lenders, loan servicers, payment processors, contracted service providers) but does not name specific third-party companies by name beyond the payment processor category.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy groups data sharing by use case (enrollment reporting, verification, loan deferment) rather than specifying exactly which data fields are shared with each individual third-party category.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Individuals can opt out of directory information sharing through their institution (e.g., via school opt-out forms), and the Privacy Block Setting allows institutions to restrict certain uses, but a direct opt-out for end users on the Clearinghouse platform itself is limited.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The Clearinghouse explicitly states it requires strict contractual safeguards and prohibits unauthorized use or re-identification when data is shared with third parties performing services.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy states it is updated when new services or technologies are developed, but does not specifically commit to notifying users when third-party service providers change or are added.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The Clearinghouse is a nonprofit operating a B2B and institutional platform; no advertising is displayed to users, and the privacy policy contains no mention of ads being served.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: There is no evidence of targeted advertising in the platform; the Clearinghouse explicitly states it does not sell student personal information and does not reference any advertising targeting mechanisms.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: The platform does not engage in third-party ad tracking; web beacons and analytics mentioned in the policy are described as being used for site integrity, fraud detection, and usage analytics rather than for advertising.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The policy discloses the use of web beacons and Flash cookies for site statistics and system integrity, but does not fully clarify whether any third-party analytics tools (e.g., Google Analytics) are used and their tracking scope.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Because no advertising or data sharing with advertisers occurs, there is effectively a full opt-out by default; the Clearinghouse's explicit policy of not selling student data removes the need for an advertiser opt-out mechanism.

r508.parentSummary: NaturalReader collects minimal data from students — primarily an email address to create an account, and temporary access to uploaded documents only during the text-to-speech conversion process. The platform states it does not sell user data, does not show ads, and does not use student content to train AI models. The company claims compliance with FERPA, COPPA, and GDPR, and uses industry-standard encryption (SSL/TLS, AWS S3 AES encryption) to protect user data, though parents should note the formal privacy policy was last formally dated 2018 and a unified, up-to-date standalone document is not prominently linked from the main naturalreader.com domain.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The 2018 PDF privacy policy states users will be notified via email and a prominent notice prior to changes, but the policies page lacks a visible revision history or changelog, and it is unclear whether the policy has been updated since 2018.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The policies page and privacy FAQ list key data types (email, billing info, uploaded files, usage data), but a comprehensive, exhaustive list of all data collected is not presented in a single formal document.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The privacy FAQ describes how data is collected (account registration, file upload, Amazon Cognito for login), but this information is spread across multiple help articles rather than consolidated in one clear policy statement.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: NaturalReader explicitly states 'Your documents remain yours and your reading experience stays private' and does not claim ownership of user content, meeting the user-owns-data standard.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: The privacy FAQ explicitly states that users can delete their accounts and files, and uploaded files are automatically deleted one year after creation, satisfying full deletion rights.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The platform states files are deleted automatically one year after upload or creation, and text submitted for conversion is deleted immediately after processing, providing a clear retention statement.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: Specific security measures are listed across help articles and the data security FAQ, including SSL/TLS, AWS S3 AES encryption, Amazon Cognito authentication, API origin access control, and PCI-DSS compliant payment processing via Stripe.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The platform confirms SSL/TLS encryption for all data in transit and AES (AWS S3 default) encryption for data at rest, meeting the encryption standard.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: Registration documentation states passwords must be '6 or more characters,' which is a weak minimum and falls short of enforcing strong password complexity; SSO via Google or Apple ID is available as an alternative.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: The platform supports SSO via Google Account and Apple ID, which inherits those providers' MFA capabilities, but NaturalReader itself does not explicitly offer or enforce native MFA for email/password accounts.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The 2018 PDF privacy policy mentions session, preference, and security cookies by category, but there is no comprehensive cookie banner or detailed cookie list with specific names and purposes on the main naturalreader.com site.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The data security FAQ names specific third-party providers (Amazon AWS, Stripe, Google, IBM, Microsoft) used for backend services, but the main policies page does not enumerate them clearly.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The privacy FAQ specifies which data goes to which provider (e.g., login to Amazon Cognito, billing to Stripe, files to AWS S3), but this is presented informally in a help article rather than a formal policy table.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: NaturalReader states it does not sell or share customer data with third parties for marketing, and third-party use is limited to service delivery, effectively constituting a no-sharing-for-ads posture with no opt-out needed.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The 2018 privacy policy states third parties with access to personal data 'are obligated not to disclose or use it' outside their service tasks, but a formal Data Processing Agreement or vendor responsibility claim is not explicitly described.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The 2018 privacy policy states users will be notified of changes by email or prominent notice, but there is no explicit commitment to notify users specifically when third-party sub-processors change.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: NaturalReader explicitly states 'We do not show ads' on its webapp page, fully meeting this standard.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: The platform explicitly states it does not sell user data to third-party advertisers and shows no ads, meaning no targeted advertising occurs.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: NaturalReader confirms no sale or sharing of data with third-party advertisers, meaning no third-party ad tracking takes place.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: No advertising-related tracking or web beacons are disclosed or indicated; tracking is limited to functional cookies and service-delivery analytics.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Because NaturalReader does not engage in advertising data sharing, no opt-out mechanism is needed, and this standard is met by default.

r509.riskReason: Naviance/PowerSchool settled a $17.25 million class action lawsuit in 2026 over allegations that hidden third-party analytics code (Heap) secretly recorded student interactions and transmitted sensitive student data to third parties without consent, and a separate December 2024 data breach exposed sensitive records for tens of millions of students, reflecting serious historical and ongoing compliance and security failures.
r509.parentSummary: Naviance (owned by PowerSchool) collects extensive student data including names, contact details, academic records, demographic information, and behavioral/interaction data to support college and career planning. While PowerSchool states it does not sell student data and claims FERPA and COPPA compliance, a 2026 federal class action settlement revealed that hidden analytics tracking code was embedded in the platform, secretly sharing student data with third-party companies including Google, Microsoft, and Heap without disclosure or consent — affecting over 10 million students between 2021 and 2026. As a result of the settlement, PowerSchool is now banned from using these third-party tracking tools in Naviance for two years and must enhance its privacy disclosures, but parents should be aware of this platform's significant recent privacy history.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The privacy policy states it may be updated and users should check back, but there is no clearly documented advance notification process or publicly maintained revision history with dates beyond archived versions hosted on the PowerSchool domain.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy policy and archived versions enumerate specific categories of data collected, including name, ID, email, date of birth, demographic data, grades, test scores, survey responses, geolocation, usage/interaction data, and parent contact information.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy explains that data is collected directly from users, from educational institutions (Clients), and through cookies and third-party service providers such as Google Analytics.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: PowerSchool explicitly states that schools and districts (Customers) own their data, and Naviance holds data as a processor on the institution's behalf, which constitutes a clear acknowledgment of user/client data ownership.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Deletion is addressed but is mediated through the school or district — individual users must contact their institution to request deletion, and post-submission data sent to postsecondary institutions cannot be retracted, limiting full user-initiated deletion.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy references data retention in the context of client-controlled retention and de-identified aggregated data kept indefinitely, but does not state a specific retention period (e.g., 90 days or otherwise) for identifiable student data.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The privacy policy references firewalls, industry-standard prevention and detection technologies, secure cloud environments, reCAPTCHA, and annual employee privacy training, but stops short of listing specific technical safeguards comprehensively.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: Encryption is not explicitly mentioned in the publicly available privacy policy text, though cloud hosting with industry-standard security is referenced; the December 2024 breach and related lawsuits citing weak security (including lack of MFA) further undermine this rating.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The privacy FAQ explicitly states Naviance enforces complex passwords following NIST standards, and the platform requires unique credentials each login, satisfying strong password enforcement.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: PowerSchool's December 2024 data breach was attributed in part to a failure to use multi-factor authentication, and neither the privacy policy nor ToS describe MFA as available or required for student or staff accounts on Naviance.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The policy mentions cookies generally and identifies Google Analytics as a third-party cookie user, but does not provide a comprehensive cookie list with individual purposes, categories, or a cookie consent mechanism.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The policy broadly describes sharing with 'third-party service providers' and optional Marketplace partners, and names Google Analytics, but does not provide a complete named list of all third parties, and the Heap/Google/Microsoft/Hotjar/Gainsight disclosures only emerged through litigation.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy groups third-party data sharing into functional categories (feature delivery, analytics) rather than specifying which data elements are shared with each named third party, resulting in only a partial disclosure.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Schools/districts can disable optional third-party features, and students have consent-based opt-in for sharing with colleges, but there is no clear direct opt-out mechanism for individual students or parents regarding analytics or operational third-party data sharing.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The Terms of Service contractually require all third-party service providers to comply with applicable laws, use data only as necessary, delete data when no longer needed, and adhere to the privacy policy, which constitutes a formal vendor obligation.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy states third-party features may change at Naviance's discretion and that users should check back for updates, but does not commit to proactively notifying users when specific third-party data-sharing arrangements change.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: PowerSchool states Naviance does not use student data for targeted advertising and does not enable colleges to conduct targeted advertising with identifiable student PII, but historical reports and the class action lawsuit alleged that ad-tracking code was embedded and colleges used the platform to send disguised targeted ads.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: While PowerSchool's official policy denies targeted advertising using student PII, the settled class action lawsuit and prior investigative reporting alleged that colleges could target students through Naviance, including by demographic filters, indicating a gap between policy claims and actual practice during the class period.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: The class action lawsuit established that third-party tracking code (Heap, Google, Microsoft, Hotjar, Gainsight) was embedded without disclosure or user opt-out; while the settlement now bans these tools for two years, no opt-out was available to students during the class period and no clear opt-out mechanism is described in current policy.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The lawsuit alleged Heap used session replay and behavioral tracking (clicks, keystrokes, page views) inside Naviance, constituting undisclosed tracking for analytics/advertising purposes; the current policy does not provide a transparent accounting of all tracking technologies employed.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: There is no clear, user-facing opt-out process for data sharing with analytics or advertising-adjacent companies described in Naviance's privacy policy; opt-out is only available at the school/district level for optional features, not for individual users regarding embedded analytics tools.

r510.riskReason: NCCER's privacy policy explicitly permits third-party behavioral advertising using cookies and web beacons, does not address COPPA or minimum age requirements, retains training and credential records indefinitely, and shares PII publicly through its Online Verification portal — all significant concerns for K-12 student deployments.
r510.parentSummary: NCCER Connect collects sensitive personal information including name, date of birth, place of birth, email, phone number, and full training/assessment records, which are stored indefinitely and made publicly searchable via the NCCER Online Verification portal. complianceNotes.DCQ1: The FAQ page lists specific credential data collected (name, email, date of birth, place of birth, phone, alternate ID), and the policy mentions non-personal/browsing data, but a comprehensive, single enumerated list of all data types is not provided in one place within the policy.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy references cookies, tags, and web beacons as collection mechanisms and mentions data provided directly by users, but does not systematically explain how each category of data is collected.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The Terms & Conditions authorize NCCER and accredited organizations to store and use personal information and training records without clearly stating user ownership; NCCER effectively controls records indefinitely.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users may request deletion by contacting NCCER, and deletion is permitted if required by law, contract, or user request, but there is no self-service deletion option and NCCER retains training/credential records indefinitely by default.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy states training and certification records are maintained 'indefinitely' for credential verification, and non-personal company data is retained indefinitely post-termination, but no defined retention period for other personal data categories is given.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The policy states NCCER 'implements commercially reasonable security measures' but does not enumerate specific technical or organizational security controls such as encryption standards, access controls, or audit practices.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: No mention of encryption (in transit or at rest) is made in NCCER's privacy policy or terms; the policy acknowledges that internet transmissions cannot be guaranteed secure.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: Neither the Terms & Conditions nor the Privacy Policy mention password complexity requirements or enforcement of strong passwords for NCCER accounts.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No mention of multi-factor authentication (MFA) or SSO/LTI integration options is made in NCCER's publicly available privacy or terms documents.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The policy describes cookies, tags, and web beacons generally and their purposes (usability, advertising), but does not provide a complete enumerated cookie list with specific names, categories, and retention periods.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: Credlens is specifically named as a data trust partner; accredited organizations are mentioned as a category; but other third-party service providers and advertisers are described only in general terms without naming specific vendors.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: Credlens' permitted uses are described in detail, and the public credential verification portal sharing is described, but data shared with unnamed third-party advertisers and service providers is not itemized per recipient.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can opt out of online behavioral advertising via the Digital Advertising Alliance website, but this is an industry opt-out tool rather than a direct, platform-level opt-out, making it a limited mechanism.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy states partner organizations are 'bound by confidentiality obligations' and subject to discipline for violations, and Credlens' use is governed by a Data Contributor and Use Agreement, which partially meets this requirement.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy does not describe any process for notifying users when third-party sharing arrangements change; it only states that policy changes will be posted to the site.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The NCCER privacy policy explicitly states that third-party advertising companies and NCCER itself may use non-personal data to 'provide advertisements and targeted advertisements' to users browsing the site.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: The policy confirms that non-personal data is used for 'Online Behavioral Advertising' — targeted ads based on browsing behavior — by both NCCER and third-party advertising companies.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: An opt-out from Online Behavioral Advertising is available via the Digital Advertising Alliance, but it is an external industry opt-out rather than a platform-native control, providing only limited protection.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The policy explicitly confirms use of cookies, tags, and web beacons by both NCCER and third parties for behavioral tracking and advertising purposes, going beyond functional tracking.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: An opt-out link to the Digital Advertising Alliance is mentioned in the policy, but the process is externally managed and vague; no direct in-platform opt-out mechanism for data sharing with advertisers is described.

r511.parentSummary: NCH Express Accounts collects personal information including names, email addresses, IP addresses, device data, and behavioral/ad interaction data, and may share this with third-party advertising partners and NCH affiliates worldwide. The platform explicitly states it is intended for adults and teens 16 and older and does not knowingly collect data from children under 16, making it wholly unsuitable for K-12 student use. There are no FERPA, COPPA, or student data protection commitments anywhere in the available policies, and the platform uses demographic and preference data to enable targeted advertising.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The privacy statement notes it may be updated periodically with a 'Last Updated' date and a homepage notice for material changes, but there is no advance notification process or versioned revision history provided.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The policy lists several categories of data collected (name, address, email, IP address, device info, behavioral data, purchase data), but the disclosure is incomplete and does not exhaustively enumerate all data types collected by the software itself.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy makes a general statement that data is collected directly from users, through authorized third parties, publicly available sources including social media, and automatically via cookies and tracking technologies, but lacks specific detail for each collection method.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The policy does not address user data ownership; NCH reserves the right to transfer personal information within its global group of companies and to third-party service providers without clearly affirming user ownership of their data.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: GDPR-based data subjects may submit deletion requests via a formal Data Access Request Form, but this right is not broadly or clearly extended to all users, and there is no self-service deletion option described for general users.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy does not state a specific data retention period for personal data collected through the Express Accounts platform or its website, making this requirement unmet.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The policy references password protection, firewalls, and SSL encryption for purchase transactions as general security measures, but does not provide specific detail on the full scope of security controls applied to user data.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: SSL/TLS encryption is mentioned specifically for checkout transactions, but there is no statement confirming end-to-end encryption of all stored or transmitted user data across the platform.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The policy and EULA do not mention password strength requirements or enforcement of strong passwords for user accounts on the platform.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No mention of multi-factor authentication or SSO/LTI integration is made anywhere in the available terms or privacy documentation.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The policy acknowledges the use of cookies and references a separate Cookies Policy page, but does not fully enumerate all cookies by name and purpose as required for a 'Meets' rating in an educational context.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The policy references 'third-party service providers' and 'advertising partners' broadly but does not name specific third parties with whom data is shared.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy does not specify what data is shared with each individual third-party category; data sharing disclosures are grouped and generic rather than itemized per partner.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: An opt-out for offline communications is mentioned, and the NCH Software privacy page indicates opt-out requests will be honored, but the process is not clearly described or easily accessible for all forms of third-party data sharing.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The NCH Corporation Data Privacy Statement states that third-party data processors are bound by contract to manage data in accordance with the privacy statement, which partially meets this requirement, though specifics are vague.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy states it may be updated at any time and users should check periodically, but there is no commitment to specifically notify users of changes in third-party relationships.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The NCH privacy policy explicitly states it uses demographic and preference data to enable targeted advertising for NCH products and services, and third-party advertising partners may collect information automatically.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: The policy confirms that demographic and preference information may be used to allow targeted advertising, indicating active user targeting rather than generic or platform-only ads.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Third-party advertising partners are stated to collect information automatically from users, including ad interaction data, with no clear opt-out mechanism for this tracking described in the policy.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The policy confirms automatic collection of ad interaction data and use of cookie technology for advertising purposes, with no statement limiting this to functional tracking only.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: An opt-out for offline communications is mentioned, and general opt-out requests are referenced as being honored, but there is no clear, specific opt-out process described for sharing data with advertising partners.

r512.riskReason: Netflix is a general-audience consumer streaming platform that collects extensive personal and behavioral data, engages in targeted advertising and data sales, has no K-12 or COPPA-specific protections, and explicitly requires users to be 18 or have parental supervision — making it wholly unsuitable for direct K-12 school use.
r512.parentSummary: Netflix collects a broad range of personal information including name, email, payment details, viewing history, device identifiers, and behavioral data used for targeted advertising on and off the platform. Data is shared with Netflix affiliates, third-party service providers, and marketing companies, and Netflix's own policies indicate personal information may be sold to third parties. Netflix is not designed or marketed for K-12 educational use, has no FERPA or COPPA compliance framework, and requires account holders to be 18 or older, making it inappropriate for direct student use in a school setting.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: Netflix notifies users of material changes to Terms of Use at least one month in advance and maintains a prior-version history page, but policy change notifications are primarily by email and continued use implies consent, which is incomplete for K-12 contexts.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: Netflix's Privacy Statement provides detailed categories of personal data collected, including personal details, payment data, usage data, device identifiers, voice inputs, and behavioral data, meeting the standard for listing all data collected.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The Privacy Statement specifically describes multiple collection methods including account registration, automatic collection, cookies, pixel tags, web beacons, and third-party sources.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: Netflix does not assert user ownership of data; the policies are silent on user data ownership and the company retains broad rights to collect, use, share, and sell personal information, indicating company control over data.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users can request deletion of personal information under applicable US state privacy laws and GDPR, but deletion is subject to exceptions under applicable laws and may take up to 30 days to process, constituting limited rather than full deletion.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: Netflix states data is retained as required or permitted by applicable laws and as needed to fulfill stated purposes, but does not provide specific retention periods for each data category, making this only a general retention statement.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: Netflix states it takes reasonable administrative, logical, physical, and managerial measures to safeguard information, but does not list specific technical security measures such as encryption standards or audit practices.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: Netflix uses HTTPS and standard industry security practices, which implies encryption in transit, but the Privacy Statement does not explicitly confirm end-to-end encryption or encryption at rest for stored data.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: Netflix's Terms of Use and Privacy Statement do not mention password strength requirements or enforcement of strong passwords; there is no indication of minimum password complexity rules.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: Netflix does not offer multi-factor authentication as a standard or required feature, and there is no mention of SSO/LTI integration or MFA availability in the platform's policies.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: Netflix mentions cookies and provides a cookie preference tool and categorizes advertising cookies separately, but does not provide a fully itemized list of all cookies with individual purposes, constituting only a general cookie policy.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: Netflix identifies broad categories of third parties (service providers, marketing providers, Netflix affiliates, payment processors, game providers) but does not name specific companies in its main Privacy Statement, only generalizing by category.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: Netflix describes what types of data are shared with categories of third parties but does not map specific data elements to each named third-party provider, making this a grouped rather than granular disclosure.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can opt out of behavioral advertising and some third-party data sharing via Privacy and Data Settings, and California/GPC opt-out signals are honored, but opt-out is not comprehensive for all third-party sharing and varies by plan tier.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: Netflix states it does not authorize service providers to use data except in connection with providing their services, indicating some contractual limits exist, but this is described only in general terms without reference to specific binding agreements.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: Netflix's Privacy Statement does not include a specific commitment to notify users when third-party sharing relationships change or when new third-party partners are added, constituting no stated notification process for third-party changes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: Netflix's ad-supported tier displays targeted advertisements to users, including behavioral advertising based on viewing history and profile data, meaning targeted ads are confirmed on the platform.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Netflix confirms the use of behavioral advertising on its ad-supported tier, where data profiles are created and used for personalized advertisements, constituting confirmed user-level targeting.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Advertising companies collect information via cookies on the Netflix service for behavioral ad targeting, including third-party ad tracking, with only partial opt-out available through account settings or cookie tools.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Netflix uses cookies, pixel tags, and web beacons, including advertising cookies through which third-party advertising companies collect user data, confirming tracking for advertising purposes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Netflix provides opt-out controls for behavioral advertising in account Privacy and Data Settings, and honors GPC signals in California, but the opt-out process is not universally clear or available to all users across all plan tiers.

complianceNotes.DCQ1: The policy lists specific data types (first name, birthday, location, IP address, teacher email, school address, usage data), but the school/EDU version's full student data inputs by teachers are only partially enumerated.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy specifically describes how each data type is collected—either voluntarily during registration, automatically (IP address), or entered by teachers for school accounts.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The policy does not clearly assert user ownership of personal data; content ownership is explicitly claimed by Press4Kids, and user data ownership is neither affirmed nor denied.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Parents can request deletion of their child's data at any time via email (info@newsomatic.org), and the Terms of Use state all data is deleted within 60 days of service agreement termination.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The Terms of Use state data is deleted within 60 days of termination, but no active retention period during service use is specified, making ongoing retention duration vague.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The policy states data is stored on restricted database servers, but does not describe specific security measures such as encryption standards, access controls, or audit logging.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The privacy policy makes no mention of encryption in transit or at rest, leaving encryption practices entirely unaddressed.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: There is no mention of password strength requirements or enforcement; teachers create student usernames and passwords with no stated complexity policy.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No mention of multi-factor authentication or SSO/LTI integration is made anywhere in the Terms of Use or Privacy Policy.

complianceNotes.SHRQ2: No breakdown is provided of what specific data is shared with any particular third party; the disclosure is a single broad statement covering all third-party sharing.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can unsubscribe from email/newsletter services at any time via an unsubscribe link, but no broader opt-out from third-party data sharing for operational purposes is described.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy describes third parties as 'respected and secure' but does not reference any formal data processing agreements, contractual obligations, or vendor compliance requirements.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy states changes will be posted but does not specifically address notification of changes involving third-party relationships or new third-party data sharing arrangements.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The privacy policy and terms contain no mention of advertising, and the platform is subscription-based with no indication that ads are displayed to students or teachers.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: No targeted advertising is mentioned or implied anywhere in the policy; the platform does not reference behavioral or interest-based ad targeting.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: No third-party ad tracking is referenced; cookies are described as solely functional for subscriber status and preferences, with no advertising tracking purpose stated.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: No web beacons, tracking pixels, or ad-related tracking technologies are mentioned; cookies are described as functional-only for the platform.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Since no advertising or data sharing with advertisers is disclosed or conducted, no opt-out process is needed, and this is consistent with the policy's scope.

Key protections include SSL encryption and the ability to request data deletion via email, though the policy does not specify a minimum user age, a precise data retention timeline, or name all third-party vendors individually.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The policy states changes will be announced publicly on the NGPF website and emailed to members, and the policy shows a revision history date (last updated May 1, 2023), but does not guarantee advance notice before changes take effect.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy policy enumerates specific data types collected including name, email, school name, city/state, username, password, IP address, browser type, OS, ISP domain, referring/exit pages, date/time stamps, clickstream, cookies, and analytics demographics.

complianceNotes.SECQ2: The policy explicitly states that information transmission is encrypted using SSL (Secure Socket Layer) or similar technologies, satisfying the encryption disclosure requirement.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The privacy policy and terms of service make no mention of password strength requirements, password enforcement policies, or any single sign-on (SSO) mechanism.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No mention of multi-factor authentication (MFA), SSO, or LTI integration is made anywhere in the privacy policy or terms of service.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The policy describes cookie categories (authentication, features/services, analytics) and provides opt-out guidance via browser settings, but does not provide a comprehensive list of all specific cookies used by name or purpose.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The policy broadly references 'contractors, service providers, and other third parties' and specifically names Google Analytics, but does not provide a comprehensive named list of all third-party vendors.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy states that data shared with third-party service providers is limited to what is needed for business support, and that aggregate data (not individual data) is shared with partners/investors, but does not specify exactly what data each third party receives.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: NGPF explicitly states it does not knowingly share or sell personal information with third parties for direct marketing use, and users can opt out of marketing emails at any time via unsubscribe links.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy states that third-party service providers are 'bound by contractual obligations to keep personal information confidential,' which constitutes a general contractual commitment but does not detail specific vendor agreement terms.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy states that changes to the privacy policy will be posted on the website and emailed to members, which implicitly covers third-party changes, but there is no specific commitment to notify users of individual third-party vendor changes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The privacy policy and terms of service make no mention of advertising being displayed to users, and NGPF explicitly states it does not share data for direct marketing; the platform appears ad-free.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: NGPF explicitly states it does not share or sell personal information for third-party direct marketing use, indicating no targeted advertising is conducted using user data.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Google Analytics is used to collect demographics and interests data, which involves third-party tracking; users can opt out only via browser-level cookie settings, not via an in-platform control.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The policy acknowledges cookies and log files are used for analytics (Google Analytics) and session tracking, but it is unclear whether web beacons or pixel tracking are in use, and no explicit functional-only tracking statement is made.

r515.riskReason: Nintendo Switch Online is a consumer gaming platform not designed for K-12 educational use, lacks FERPA compliance, collects advertising identifiers and uses third-party targeted advertising for general accounts, and has no school or district data processing agreement framework.
r515.parentSummary: Nintendo Switch Online requires a Nintendo Account; for children under 13, a parent or guardian must provide verifiable parental consent (via a $0.50 credit card charge) to create a child account. Nintendo collects personal information such as name, email, date of birth, device identifiers, gameplay history, and purchase history, and shares this with third-party service providers for analytics and advertising purposes, though Nintendo states it does not sell user data to third parties. While Nintendo has COPPA-compliant child account controls and parental oversight tools, this platform is a consumer entertainment service with no FERPA compliance, no school data processing agreements, and is not designed for K-12 classroom use.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: Nintendo's privacy policy states it will notify users of material changes via email or posted notice and will revise the 'Last Updated' date, but does not provide a full revision history or advance timeline for non-material changes.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy policy provides a detailed list of data categories collected, including personal information provided at registration, device information, advertising identifiers, gameplay history, and persistent identifiers collected from children under 13.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The privacy policy clearly explains that data is collected when users register, use services, connect to third-party services, and through cookies and device-level telemetry.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: Nintendo's Terms of Use grant Nintendo a perpetual, royalty-free, irrevocable license to user-submitted content, and the platform data collected is owned and controlled by Nintendo — user data ownership is not clearly reserved to users.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users may request full deletion of their Nintendo Account and all associated data; account deletion takes 30 days to process with a 30-day recovery window, constituting a limited waiting period before permanent deletion.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The privacy policy states data is retained 'only for as long as reasonably necessary' but does not specify a concrete retention period in days or years for most categories of data, making this a vague rather than specific retention statement.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The privacy policy states Nintendo has implemented 'administrative, physical and technical security measures' but does not specify the actual measures (e.g., encryption standards, access controls), constituting only a general security statement.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: Nintendo uses HTTPS for its web services and the privacy policy references security measures, but does not explicitly state end-to-end encryption or specify encryption standards used for data at rest or in transit.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: Nintendo's account FAQ advises users to set 'a unique password that will be difficult for other people to guess' but does not enforce specific password complexity requirements as part of the account creation flow.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: Nintendo Account supports optional two-step verification (Google Authenticator), but it is not mandatory; MFA is available but not enforced, particularly for child accounts.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: Nintendo's privacy request page lists cookie categories (functional, performance, targeting) and offers a cookie preference manager, and names third-party cookie providers, but the cookie disclosure is not fully centralized and may not apply uniformly across all Nintendo digital properties.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The privacy policy references 'third-party service providers' for analytics and advertising but does not name all of them in the policy itself; a partial list is available via a linked page on the privacy request portal.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy groups data sharing by purpose (analytics, advertising, legal) but does not provide a granular breakdown of exactly which data fields are shared with each named third party.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can opt out of non-essential cookies and targeted advertising via cookie preference settings and Nintendo Account settings, but the opt-out process is not straightforward and may not apply across all Nintendo services.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The privacy policy states Nintendo shares data with third-party service providers 'for business purposes' but only generally references contractual restrictions; it does not explicitly state that all third parties are bound by data processing agreements equivalent to Nintendo's own standards.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The privacy policy says Nintendo may update the policy and will notify users of material changes, but does not specifically commit to notifying users when third-party sharing relationships are added or changed.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: Nintendo's privacy policy explicitly states third-party service providers may use cookies 'to provide you with targeted advertisements,' confirming that targeted ads can be displayed to users of Nintendo's online services.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Nintendo explicitly uses gameplay, purchase, and browsing data to provide 'tailored advertising,' and permits third-party providers to serve targeted ads based on cross-site online activity, confirming user-level targeting.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Third-party tracking for advertising is used, but Nintendo provides a cookie preference manager and opt-out tools via the privacy request page; however, the opt-out process is incomplete and may not cover all tracking across all Nintendo services.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Nintendo's privacy policy and cookie disclosures confirm the use of tracking cookies, web beacons, and advertising identifiers by both Nintendo and third-party providers for targeted advertising purposes, not just functional tracking.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Nintendo provides opt-out mechanisms for targeted advertising through account settings and cookie preferences, but the process is not clearly documented in one location and may not fully apply to all data sharing with advertising partners.
