r596.riskReason: RocketLit acknowledges FERPA and processes student education records for legitimate educational purposes, but the privacy policy hosted at rocketlit.com fails to render meaningful content, third-party sharing with marketing and analytics vendors is broadly defined without naming specific providers, no explicit COPPA compliance statement is made, data retention periods are not specified, California Student Data Privacy Agreement is not signed, and targeted advertising opt-out mechanisms are unclear.
r596.parentSummary: RocketLit (operated by RocketLit, Inc.) collects student names, email addresses, reading level data, quiz scores, usage activity, and device/cookie identifiers to deliver its adaptive science and history reading platform. The company acknowledges it processes student education records under FERPA and commits to using that data only for legitimate educational purposes, but it also shares personal information with broadly-defined third-party service providers including those supporting marketing, analytics, and website operations, and does not explicitly state it will not sell student data. Parents and guardians with concerns about student data should direct requests to the school or district, as RocketLit treats schools as the data controller for platform-related student information.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The privacy policy on innerorbit.com (shared with RocketLit) states supplemental notices may be provided but does not describe a formal advance-notification process or maintain a publicly visible revision history.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The policy lists several categories of data (contact data, communications data, usage/device data, marketing preferences) but the rocketlit.com privacy page does not render full content, making a complete inventory uncertain.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy notes data is collected through user-provided forms, automatic technical means, cookies, and third-party login services, but descriptions remain general rather than exhaustively specific.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The policy positions schools/districts as data controllers for student platform data and RocketLit as a processor, implying institutional ownership, but explicit user data ownership language is absent.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: The policy directs users to contact their school or district to exercise data rights including deletion, which creates an indirect path rather than a direct self-service deletion mechanism.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: No specific data retention period or deletion timeline is stated anywhere in the accessible policy text, which is a gap under both COPPA and general best practices.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The policy states RocketLit employs 'technical, organizational and physical safeguards' but does not enumerate specific security measures such as encryption standards, access controls, or audit practices.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: No explicit encryption statement is made in the accessible policy text; the platform uses HTTPS at the domain level, but in-transit and at-rest encryption are not confirmed in writing.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The platform supports Clever SSO and Google Login, which offload password strength enforcement to those providers, but RocketLit's own password policy is not described.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: RocketLit supports Clever SSO and Google Login/SSO for both teachers and students, which provides an SSO/MFA-equivalent authentication pathway satisfying this requirement.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The policy acknowledges use of session cookies, persistent cookies, first-party and third-party cookies, local storage (HTML5), and web beacons, but does not provide a detailed cookie inventory listing each cookie by name and purpose.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: Third-party sharing is described in broad functional categories (service providers, partners, linked services) without naming any specific vendor companies.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: Data shared with each category of third party is described at a general level without specifying which data elements go to which specific provider.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: No explicit opt-out mechanism for third-party sharing is described; users are instructed to contact their school for data rights, providing only an indirect path.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy states that service providers assist under RocketLit's direction but does not explicitly require third parties to sign data processing agreements or confirm they are bound by equivalent protections.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy does not include any commitment to notify users or schools when the list of third-party recipients changes materially.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: No ads are explicitly described as being shown to students within the platform, but the policy does not contain a clear no-advertising pledge, leaving this ambiguous.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: There is no explicit statement prohibiting the use of student data for targeted advertising, and the policy references sharing with marketing and analytics partners, which creates uncertainty.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Third-party cookies and web beacons are acknowledged, including from analytics and marketing partners, but no clear opt-out mechanism for tracking by these third parties is specified.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The policy discloses use of web beacons and third-party cookies but does not clearly distinguish between functional tracking and ad-related tracking, leaving the purpose ambiguous.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: No clear opt-out process for data sharing with advertisers is described; general browser-level cookie controls are implied but not formally offered as a platform-level opt-out.

dataSharedWith: Ad networks (for targeted digital advertising on third-party websites)
r597.riskReason: Rockwell Automation is an industrial automation company — not a K-12 EdTech platform — with no COPPA or FERPA compliance language, no minimum age restrictions, and an explicit practice of using ad networks to serve targeted advertisements to users based on their data, making it wholly unsuitable for K-12 student use.
r597.parentSummary: Rockwell Automation is an industrial automation company whose website and platform are designed for enterprise and industrial customers, not K-12 students. The platform collects personal data including name, email, IP address, and usage data, and explicitly uses ad networks to serve targeted advertisements on third-party websites. There are no COPPA or FERPA protections stated anywhere in the privacy policy, no minimum age requirement is specified, and the platform is not designed or marketed as a K-12 educational tool.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The Terms and Conditions state changes may be made 'at any time without notice,' with no advance notification or revision history commitment for users.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy policy lists several categories of personal data collected (name, email, IP, usage data, professional info), but the full enumeration is incomplete and grouped broadly rather than exhaustively listed.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy provides a general statement that data is collected via website interactions, account registration, and business interactions, but does not specifically detail all collection mechanisms (e.g., pixels, SDKs, form submissions).
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The Terms of Use state the user retains ownership of their data but simultaneously grant Rockwell Automation a broad royalty-free license to use that data to improve products and services, creating unclear effective ownership.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: The privacy policy states users may contact the Privacy Office to exercise rights including deletion, but the process is via email request only with no guaranteed deletion — only a 30-day response commitment — and deactivation is available for registered accounts.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The privacy policy does not state any specific data retention period or general retention schedule for user personal data.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The Data Handling Commitments document references alignment to industry-leading cybersecurity frameworks and minimum security standards, but the public-facing privacy policy only provides a general security commitment without listing specific measures.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The privacy policy does not explicitly state that data is encrypted in transit or at rest; no mention of encryption protocols is present in the publicly accessible policy.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: There is no mention of password strength requirements or enforcement in the public Terms of Service or Privacy Policy.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No mention of multi-factor authentication or SSO support is made in the public-facing privacy policy or terms of service.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The privacy policy is titled 'Privacy and Cookies Policy' and references the use of cookies, but specific cookies, their names, and individual purposes are not fully enumerated in the publicly accessible portions reviewed.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The privacy policy references sharing with 'ad networks,' 'business partners,' and 'third-party service providers,' but does not name specific third-party vendors or ad networks.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy does not specify what particular data elements are shared with each category of third party; data shared is described only in general terms.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: While a Communications Preference Center is mentioned for marketing opt-outs, there is no clear, easy opt-out process for third-party data sharing with ad networks or other partners.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The Data Processing Addendum references sub-processors being bound to contractual terms, but the public privacy policy only makes a general reference to third parties without explicitly requiring them to follow equivalent privacy standards.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The Terms and Conditions state changes may be made 'at any time without notice,' and no specific commitment to notify users of third-party changes is made in the privacy policy.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The privacy policy explicitly states Rockwell Automation utilizes ad networks to display targeted digital advertisements on third-party websites, confirming ads are served to users.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: The privacy policy confirms data is used to match and serve targeted advertisements about Rockwell's products and services on third-party sites, confirming user-level targeting.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: The policy acknowledges use of ad networks for targeted advertising on third-party websites with no clear opt-out from third-party tracking for ad purposes described.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The use of ad networks for targeted advertising on third-party websites strongly implies third-party tracking technologies such as web beacons or pixels, though these are not explicitly disclosed.

complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Saturn states it may infer interests and use that data to display ads, and may enable social media platforms to identify lookalike audiences, suggesting a degree of interest-based targeting.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Saturn shares hashed phone numbers with social media platforms for advertising purposes; while data is not sold to advertisers, this sharing enables third-party ad targeting with limited opt-out described.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The policy references cookies, device identifiers, and inferred interest data used partly for ad personalization, but does not fully detail tracking methods or clearly distinguish functional vs. advertising trackers.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Users can adjust privacy settings on Saturn, but a clear, dedicated opt-out from all data sharing with social media platforms for advertising purposes is not explicitly described in the policy.

r606.riskReason: Savvas explicitly pledges never to sell student data or perform targeted advertising, holds iKeepSafe FERPA/COPPA certifications, operates under ISO 27001 and NIST frameworks, and contractually binds all subprocessors to equivalent privacy protections.
r606.parentSummary: Savvas Interactive Science CC1.2 collects student roster data (name, email, grade), usage/activity data, and device/browser information solely to deliver the educational service. Savvas explicitly commits to never selling student data or using it for targeted advertising, and has been certified compliant with FERPA and COPPA by the Internet Keep Safe Coalition (iKeepSafe). Parents wishing to exercise access, correction, or deletion rights should contact their school or district, as educational institutions bear primary responsibility for fulfilling such requests under FERPA.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The Learning Services Privacy Policy states that advance notice of material changes will be attempted via email, postal mail, or posted website notice, but revisions become effective immediately upon posting, which falls short of a guaranteed pre-effective notification window or a maintained revision history.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy policy describes categories of data collected (roster PII, usage data, device/browser info) but does not provide a fully exhaustive enumerated list of every specific data element collected across all service configurations.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy specifically describes multiple collection methods: direct upload by customer institutions, data generated by student and educator use of the service, and data generated through service interactions.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: Savvas explicitly states it will 'NEVER claim ownership of your student data,' and the Trust Center page confirms customer data belongs to the customer, satisfying user data ownership.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Deletion is supported via protocols described in the privacy and security documentation, but students and parents must route deletion requests through their educational institution rather than directly to Savvas, creating an indirect and potentially delayed path.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy states that Savvas 'follows specific protocols for the deletion and retention of student data' and references an organizational data retention policy, but does not publicly disclose a specific retention period in days or months.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: Savvas describes specific security measures including ISO 27001 and NIST Cybersecurity Framework governance, Amazon Web Services infrastructure, logging and monitoring, vulnerability management, annual policy reviews, and a dedicated Data Privacy and Security team.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The policy explicitly states that industry-accepted encryption technology is used to protect customer data and communications, and the corporate privacy statement confirms SSL/TLS encryption for data in transit.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The policy requires user authentication to access Savvas platforms and references access controls based on least privilege principles, but there is no explicit public statement that strong password complexity rules are enforced for all user account types.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: Savvas Realize supports Single Sign-On (SSO) and LTI integrations with major K-12 LMS platforms, which satisfies the SSO/LTI criteria as a strong authentication mechanism in lieu of standalone MFA.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The corporate privacy statement mentions cookies, pixels, web beacons, and similar tracking technologies, and describes their general purposes, but does not provide a granular cookie inventory or explicit categorization (e.g., strictly necessary vs. analytics vs. advertising) for the educational product platform.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The policy references subprocessors and third-party vendors generally and notes that a current subprocessor list is available via the Trust Center, but specific named third-party vendors are not enumerated within the privacy policy text itself.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy states that third parties are subject to prohibitions on non-educational use of personal information but does not specify which data elements are shared with each individual subprocessor or vendor category.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Students and parents must direct data access, amendment, or deletion requests to their educational institution, which then liaises with Savvas; there is no direct user-facing opt-out mechanism for third-party subprocessor data sharing.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: Savvas explicitly states that all subprocessors and third-party vendors are subject to stringent contractual requirements equivalent to those in its own Privacy Policy, including prohibitions on non-educational use and maintenance of a comprehensive information security program.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The privacy policy states that in the event of a merger, acquisition, or asset sale, Savvas will condition any such transaction on continued adherence to the policy and will provide users with advance notice and information about any changes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The privacy policy and Trust Center explicitly state that Savvas will 'NEVER perform targeted advertising of your Student Users,' and there is no indication that any advertising is displayed within the educational platform.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Savvas provides an explicit and unconditional commitment that targeted advertising of student users will never be performed, and student data will never be used to build marketing profiles.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: The policy explicitly prohibits the use of student data for targeted advertising and states that third-party subprocessors are contractually barred from using student data for non-educational purposes, effectively prohibiting third-party ad tracking.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The corporate privacy statement acknowledges use of web beacons and pixel tracking technologies on the marketing website; while the educational platform policy prohibits their use for advertising, the tracking methods across all Savvas-operated web properties are not fully delineated.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Because Savvas commits categorically to never performing targeted advertising with student data and never sharing student data for advertising purposes, there is no need for a separate opt-out mechanism, which constitutes full compliance with this criterion.

Savvas explicitly commits to never selling student data to third parties, never performing targeted advertising, and never building marketing profiles of students, and has earned independent FERPA and COPPA certifications from iKeepSafe. Data deletion and access requests for students enrolled through a school must be routed through the school or district, and while Savvas states it follows specific protocols for data deletion and retention, exact retention timeframes are not spelled out in the publicly available policy.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The Learning Services Privacy Policy states Savvas will attempt to provide advance notice of material changes via email, postal mail, or website posting, but also reserves the right to make revisions effective immediately upon posting, which does not guarantee advance notification in all cases.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The policy identifies categories of data collected (personal info provided by the customer/institution, data generated by student and educator users, usage data) but does not provide a fully exhaustive enumerated list of every specific data field collected.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy specifically describes multiple collection methods including direct customer upload, data collected from student/educator platform use, and data generated through service usage, satisfying this requirement.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: Savvas explicitly states it will 'NEVER claim ownership of your student data,' clearly affirming that data ownership remains with the user/institution.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Deletion rights exist but are routed through the school or district for K-12 students rather than being directly accessible to students or parents, creating a dependency on institutional intermediaries.

complianceNotes.SECQ3: The platform supports SAML 2.0 SSO and integrates with identity providers including Google and Active Directory Federation Services, satisfying the SSO/strong authentication requirement.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: Savvas Realize supports SAML 2.0 SSO and LTI integrations, which function as federated identity management meeting the spirit of this requirement for school-managed access.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The privacy policy mentions cookies and their purposes (navigation, recognition, usage tracking) and notes use of analytics services, but does not provide a comprehensive enumerated cookie list with individual names and specific purposes for each.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The policy references use of sub-processors and third-party vendors but directs users to a separate sub-processor list rather than naming all parties directly within the policy document, providing only a generalized disclosure in the policy text.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy states sub-processors are subject to contractual requirements and data is shared only for educational purposes, but does not itemize exactly which data types are shared with each individual third party.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: There is no straightforward direct opt-out mechanism for K-12 students or parents from third-party sub-processor sharing; requests must be routed through the school district, limiting direct parental control.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy explicitly states all third parties with access to personal information are 'subject to stringent privacy and security contractual requirements,' and Savvas performs due diligence on all sub-processors, clearly meeting this requirement.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: While the policy describes general notification methods for policy changes, it does not include a specific, dedicated process for notifying users when sub-processors or third-party partners change.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: Savvas explicitly and prominently commits to never performing targeted advertising of student users and never building marketing profiles, confirming no ads are displayed to students.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: The policy and Trust Center both contain unambiguous statements that Savvas will 'NEVER perform targeted advertising of your Student Users,' meeting this requirement fully.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: The policy prohibits sub-processors from using student personal information for non-educational purposes, and no third-party ad tracking of students is disclosed or permitted under the stated terms.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The corporate-facing privacy statement does reference use of web beacons, pixels, and similar technologies for tracking on the marketing website (savvas.com), though the Learning Services policy for the educational platform is more restrictive; this dual-policy structure creates some ambiguity.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Since Savvas commits to no targeted advertising or data sharing with advertisers for student users, there is effectively nothing to opt out of, which satisfies the spirit of this requirement.

r608.riskReason: Scholastico's privacy policy (last updated April 2019) does not explicitly address COPPA or FERPA compliance, does not specify a minimum age, lacks detailed security disclosures, and relies on an outdated EU Privacy Shield framework, creating meaningful gaps for K-12 deployment.
r608.parentSummary: Scholastico collects minimal personally identifiable information — primarily staff and parent names and emails provided by the school — to operate parent-teacher conferences, surveys, elections, and activity signups. The platform states it does not sell personal data to advertisers and only shares data when legally required or with service providers like Google Analytics, Braintree (PayPal), and MailChimp. However, the privacy policy does not explicitly mention COPPA or FERPA compliance, does not specify a minimum user age, and has not been publicly updated since April 2019, which may concern school administrators seeking current, comprehensive compliance documentation.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The privacy policy states an effective date of April 4, 2019, but provides no explicit process for advance notification of policy changes or a publicly accessible revision history.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The policy states only minimal PII is collected and lists some categories (usage data, payment email, staff names), but does not exhaustively enumerate all data types collected across all product modules.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy generally describes data collection as occurring when customers sign up or use services, but does not specifically detail collection methods (e.g., forms, cookies, server logs) in a comprehensive way.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The policy states that HR/staff data 'is provided by the client school or organization and can be purged by them at any time,' indicating the school/user retains effective ownership and control.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: The policy explicitly states data is retained 'for no more than 30 days after you request deletion,' and client schools can purge their own data at any time, indicating full deletion is available.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy states personal info is retained for no more than 30 days after a deletion request, but does not specify the full active retention period prior to any deletion request being made.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The privacy policy does not describe any specific technical or organizational security measures (e.g., firewalls, access controls, audits, encryption standards) used to protect data.

complianceNotes.SECQ3: The privacy policy and terms do not mention password complexity requirements, strong password enforcement, or any equivalent authentication standard for user accounts.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: The platform's app login page (scholastico.net) supports SSO via Google and Microsoft, which provides MFA capability, but this is not explicitly documented in the privacy policy.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The privacy policy acknowledges cookie use and states browsers can refuse or disable cookies, but does not provide a full list of cookies used, their names, or their specific purposes.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The privacy policy specifically names Google Analytics, Braintree Payments (PayPal), and MailChimp as third-party service providers, meeting the requirement for named third parties.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy identifies which third parties are used but groups data sharing descriptions generally (e.g., 'payment information and email' go to Braintree/PayPal) without itemizing exactly which data fields are shared with each party.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: The policy provides an opt-out link for Google Analytics data collection, but does not describe a clear opt-out process for data shared with Braintree/PayPal or MailChimp beyond not using those features.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy does not contain an explicit statement requiring third-party vendors to adhere to Scholastico's privacy standards or a formal vendor agreement obligation, only noting data is subject to third parties' own policies.

complianceNotes.ADVQ3: The policy confirms no data is shared with advertisers and only named analytics tools (Google Analytics, with an available opt-out) are used, indicating no third-party ad tracking.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Google Analytics is used on public-facing websites for aggregate usage tracking; while an opt-out is available, the policy does not fully detail all tracking technologies or web beacons used.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: A clear opt-out mechanism for Google Analytics is provided via the Google Analytics Opt-out Browser Add-on, and the policy confirms no data sharing with advertisers, satisfying this requirement.

r609.riskReason: Schoolconomy collects sensitive PII from K-12 students including home address and birthday, allows businesses to purchase advertising space directly within the student-facing app, uses unnamed third-party services that may collect identifying data, and fails to explicitly claim COPPA or FERPA compliance or prohibit the sale of student data.
r609.parentSummary: Schoolconomy collects significant personal information from students including name, birthday, home address, phone number, school name, device data, and uploaded grade records. The platform shares data with unspecified third-party service providers and explicitly allows businesses to purchase advertising space within the app, raising serious concerns about commercial exploitation of student data. The privacy policy does not explicitly claim COPPA or FERPA compliance, does not state a data retention period, does not describe a clear data deletion process, and does not name specific third parties — making it difficult for parents to fully assess the privacy risks for their children.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The privacy policy contains no mention of advance notification of policy changes, version history, or a revision date — users are not informed of how or when they will be notified of updates.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The policy lists several specific data types (Name, Birthday, School Name, Home Address, Phone Number, IP address, device data) but uses 'including but not limited to' language, leaving the full scope of collection undefined.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy states data is collected when users provide it and via log data automatically, but does not clearly explain all collection mechanisms such as what specific third-party SDKs or trackers are embedded in the app.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The policy does not address data ownership; it states data is retained by the company and used as described, implying company control with no user ownership rights articulated.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: There is no mention of a user data deletion process; the only reference to data action for minors under 13 is to contact the company, with no guarantee or timeline for deletion.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The privacy policy does not state any data retention period or general retention policy — it only says data will be retained and used as described, with no timeframe specified.

complianceNotes.SECQ2: The platform uses HTTPS for its web APIs, which implies transport-layer encryption, but the policy does not explicitly state encryption of data at rest or specify encryption standards.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The policy and terms make no mention of password strength requirements or enforcement of strong passwords for student or parent accounts.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No mention of multi-factor authentication (MFA), SSO, or LTI integration is made anywhere in the privacy policy or terms of service.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The policy states the service does not use cookies explicitly but acknowledges third-party code and libraries may use cookies; specific third-party cookies and their purposes are not listed.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The policy acknowledges use of third-party services that may collect identifying information but does not name any specific third parties.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: No breakdown of what specific data is shared with which third parties is provided — only a general statement that third parties have access to personal information to perform assigned tasks.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: No opt-out mechanism for third-party data sharing is described; users are not given a process to limit or refuse sharing beyond potentially refusing cookies.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy states third parties are 'obligated not to disclose or use the information for any other purpose,' which is a general contractual claim but lacks specifics about formal data processing agreements or vendor accountability frameworks.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy does not mention any process for notifying users when third-party relationships change or new data processors are added.

Data is shared with cloud hosting providers, analytics services, and YouTube/Google for certain features, but SchoolStatus states it does not use student data for targeted advertising or sell it. The platform has achieved iKeepSafe COPPA Safe Harbor certification and claims FERPA compliance, with school consent serving as the mechanism for under-13 access.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The privacy policy states material changes will receive advance notice and consent, and maintains a revision history with effective dates published at the top of the policy.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy policy and DPA enumerate collected data types including name, email, student ID, school affiliation, age, grade, parent identities, contact info, IP address, device data, and usage/log data.

complianceNotes.DCQ3: The service-specific supplemental terms grant SchoolStatus a 'perpetual, exclusive, royalty-free license' to aggregate district data for service improvement, creating ambiguity around full user ownership of data.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Account deletion is available for SchoolStatus Connect users via account settings or email request, but for Attend and Boost products users must contact the school district (Customer), and residual data may be retained for business or legal reasons.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy states data is retained for the duration of services or as required by law and contractual terms, but does not specify a concrete retention period in days or years, making this only a general retention statement.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The policy makes a general commitment to security and references commercially available cloud storage, but does not enumerate specific technical security measures such as encryption standards, access controls, or audit logging.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The DPA acknowledges data may be transmitted over the public internet and stored in cloud systems, and while the blog references encryption for sensitive messages, the privacy policy itself does not explicitly confirm end-to-end or at-rest encryption.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: Authorized users receive unique login credentials per the supplemental terms, but the policy does not explicitly state that strong password complexity is enforced platform-wide.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: The platform provides unique username/password credentials to authorized users but does not explicitly document MFA or SSO options in the publicly available policy documents reviewed.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The privacy policy mentions cookies and web beacons are used and lists general categories of information collected via them, but does not provide a comprehensive list of each specific cookie, its name, and its individual purpose.

complianceNotes.SHRQ2: Third-party data sharing is described by category rather than specifying which precise data fields are shared with each individual service provider.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: For YouTube API services, users can delete stored data via Google security settings; general opt-out of other third-party sharing is not explicitly described as a straightforward user-facing process.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy states contracts are in place with service providers addressing their protection of information, and the DPA imposes binding data use restrictions on SchoolStatus itself when acting as a data processor.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy commits to advance notice for material changes to data practices, and the revision history (e.g., the 2.5.2025 update adding YouTube API disclosure) demonstrates active maintenance and user notification of third-party changes.

complianceNotes.ADVQ2: SchoolStatus explicitly prohibits use of student/pupil records for targeted advertising purposes in its service-specific supplemental terms, and analytics providers are generally prohibited from using data for their own purposes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: No third-party ad tracking of students is described or permitted; analytics providers are restricted from using student/educator/parent data for their own purposes per the privacy policy.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The privacy policy acknowledges the use of cookies and web beacons for logging and tracking user interactions, but does not clearly distinguish between functional-only tracking and any potential analytics tracking methods.

r611.riskReason: Scratch is a nonprofit with a child-focused privacy approach and no advertising, but the January 2026 ToS update grants a perpetual, irrevocable license to use user-posted content (including content from minors) for AI model training, which raises meaningful concerns for K-12 deployment without updated parental consent flows.
r611.parentSummary: Scratch collects minimal personal information such as a username, email, country, and usage activity to operate the platform and improve learning experiences; it explicitly states it does not sell student data and does not collect FERPA-covered education records. However, the January 2026 Terms of Service update grants Scratch a perpetual, royalty-free license to use content posted on the platform—including projects by minors—to train AI models, which is a notable new concern schools should evaluate. Third-party analytics providers such as Google Analytics also collect usage data through cookies, though Scratch provides opt-out mechanisms and a separate cookie policy.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The privacy policy states an effective date (last updated May 25, 2023, with ToS revised January 2026) and users are notified via the discussion forum, but there is no clearly documented advance notification process or versioned revision history maintained in the policy document itself.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy policy enumerates specific categories of personal information collected including account data, usage/activity data, inferred location via IP, device identifiers, cookies, and user-generated content.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy specifically describes how data is collected—directly by users during account creation, automatically via cookies and server logs, and through third-party analytics providers such as Google Analytics.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: Users are stated to own their output content, but the January 2026 ToS grants Scratch a perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free license to use posted content including for AI training, creating an unclear effective ownership situation.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Account deletion is available via account settings, but the privacy policy (via Scratch Wiki summary) indicates that deleting an account hides information from public view but does not immediately remove it from Scratch's servers without contacting support.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy states data is deleted or anonymized when no longer necessary and lists criteria for determining retention periods, but does not specify a concrete retention timeframe (e.g., 90 days or 1 year), making this only a general/vague statement.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The privacy policy references administrative, physical, and technical procedures to protect data, but does not enumerate specific security measures such as named encryption standards, penetration testing, or security certifications.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: Scratch uses HTTPS (TLS) for data in transit based on site infrastructure, but the privacy policy does not explicitly state encryption at rest or detail the encryption protocols used.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The privacy policy and terms do not mention password strength enforcement requirements; there is no stated policy for enforcing strong passwords on accounts.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: Scratch does not support SSO/LTI integration or multi-factor authentication (MFA) for standard user accounts, and neither the ToS nor Privacy Policy mentions MFA availability.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: Scratch maintains a separate, dedicated Cookie Policy that lists cookie categories (essential, functional, analytical/performance) with named providers such as Google Analytics and describes opt-out options.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The privacy policy references categories of third parties (hosting, analytics, research institutions) but names only Google Analytics specifically; a comprehensive list of named third-party vendors is not provided.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: Data shared with third parties is described at a category level (e.g., de-identified data with researchers, analytics data with Google Analytics) but specific data fields shared with each named third party are not itemized.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can opt out of Google Analytics via a browser add-on and manage cookies via browser settings, but there is no in-platform opt-out mechanism for all third-party sharing, particularly for research data sharing.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The privacy policy states data is shared with service providers but, per Common Sense evaluation findings, contractual limits on third-party data use are not explicitly claimed in the public-facing policy.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy does not specify a process for notifying users when third-party service providers change; general policy update notices are announced via the Scratch discussion forum but without a guaranteed advance notice period.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: Scratch is a nonprofit platform and does not display advertisements to users; the privacy policy makes no mention of ad serving.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: No targeted advertising is conducted on the Scratch platform; the policy confirms data is used for platform improvement and research, not for advertising targeting.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Google Analytics is used and collects user behavior data; while Scratch provides a link to Google's opt-out add-on, third-party tracking by Google for its own purposes is not fully restricted within the platform.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Cookies, beacons, invisible tags, and unique IDs are used per the cookie policy primarily for functional and analytical purposes, not for advertising; however the policy acknowledges third-party analytics providers collect data for their own use.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: An opt-out for Google Analytics is provided via external browser add-on link, and browser-level cookie management is described, but there is no clear, centralized in-platform opt-out process for all data sharing with third-party service providers.

r612.parentSummary: Scratch Golf Academy collects personal data including IP addresses, email addresses, browser information, and behavioral/usage data via cookies, and allows advertising partners to deploy targeted ad cookies on its platform. The platform is designed for adult consumers and requires users to be at least the age of majority, with no COPPA, FERPA, or student data protections in place. User data is explicitly identified as a business asset that may be transferred to third parties in a merger or acquisition, posing significant privacy risks if used in a K-12 school context.

complianceNotes.DCQ1: The policy lists some data types (browser info, IP addresses, email for registered users) but does not comprehensively enumerate all categories collected, such as payment data, swing video submissions, or app-level behavioral data.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy generally describes data collection occurring through website visits and account registration but lacks specificity about all collection mechanisms, including app-based tracking, form submissions, and third-party cookie collection.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The privacy policy explicitly states user information is 'one of the assets' transferred in a sale or bankruptcy, indicating the company treats data as company-owned property with no stated user data ownership rights.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: No data deletion process is described in the privacy policy; account cancellation instructions exist (via support ticket) but no right to data deletion or erasure is mentioned.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The privacy policy contains no statement about how long user data is retained, either specifically or generally, leaving data retention practices entirely undisclosed.

complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Advertising partners are confirmed to set tracking cookies that recognize users across visits and compile browsing profiles, with no opt-out mechanism described in the privacy policy.

complianceNotes.ADVQ5: The privacy policy explicitly disclaims coverage of advertiser cookie practices and provides no opt-out process for data sharing with advertising networks, leaving users with no stated recourse.

r613.riskReason: ScratchJr is a locally stored, offline-capable app with no account required, no ads, no data sold or shared for marketing, and explicitly states it does not collect personal information from children under 13.
r613.parentSummary: ScratchJr is a free, primarily offline coding app for children ages 5–7 that stores all projects locally on the device and does not require an account or collect personal information from children. The app displays no ads, does not sell or rent user data to third parties, and does not use children's information for marketing or targeted advertising. The Scratch Foundation, a nonprofit, operates the app and states it has no actual knowledge of collecting personal information from children under 13, making it one of the lowest-risk EdTech tools available for K-12 classrooms.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The Scratch Foundation posts privacy policy update dates (e.g., last updated March 27, 2026) and notifies users of material changes, but ScratchJr's own policy page content was not fully retrievable to confirm a complete revision history is maintained.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The policy and Common Sense evaluation state the service does not collect personal information from children under 13, and all project data is stored locally on the device, providing clear disclosure that minimal to no data is collected.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy generally states data is stored locally on device and that aggregated/anonymized usage data may be collected, but does not provide a specific, detailed breakdown of every data collection method (e.g., analytics SDKs, device identifiers).
complianceNotes.DCQ3: Project data belongs to and remains on the user's device; the policy and third-party evaluations confirm the platform does not claim ownership of children's content or personal data.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Since projects are stored locally, users can delete them directly from the device, but the policy does not explicitly describe a formal data deletion request process for any server-side data that may exist.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy does not specify a precise data retention period for any server-side aggregated data; it only generally implies local storage with no cloud retention for project content.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The Scratch Foundation references a commitment to protecting user data and the app is offline-capable, but specific technical security measures (e.g., encryption standards, penetration testing) are not enumerated in publicly available policy documents.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The scratchjr.org website uses HTTPS, indicating transport-layer encryption, but the privacy policy does not explicitly state that data is encrypted at rest or in transit beyond standard app store and OS protections.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: No account is required to use ScratchJr, which eliminates password-related risks entirely and fully satisfies the intent of this requirement.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No account creation is required for core functionality, meaning MFA concerns are not applicable and the risk is effectively mitigated by the accountless design.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The scratchjr.org website likely uses functional cookies as part of the broader Scratch ecosystem (which has a cookie policy), but ScratchJr's own privacy page does not provide a detailed cookie listing specific to the ScratchJr app or site.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The policy references that service providers such as those involved in website hosting and analytics may receive data, but does not name specific third-party vendors used by ScratchJr.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: Specific data shared with each named third party is not itemized; the policy gives only a general statement that service providers may receive data necessary to perform their functions.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: The policy and Common Sense evaluation confirm that no data is shared with third parties for advertising or marketing purposes, effectively making opt-out from harmful sharing a non-issue.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy includes a general statement that third-party service providers receive data only for the purpose of operating the service, but does not cite a formal vendor agreement or data processing agreement framework.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The Scratch Foundation states it will notify users of material policy changes, but does not specifically commit to notifying users whenever a third-party service provider relationship changes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: ScratchJr displays no advertisements of any kind; the app is free and ad-free as confirmed by multiple independent sources and the policy itself.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: No targeted advertising is used; the policy explicitly states children's information will not be used for marketing, online advertising, or third-party tracking that would identify a child.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: No third-party ad tracking is employed; the Common Sense evaluation confirms that user information is not used to track and target advertisements on other third-party websites or services.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: No web beacons or ad-tracking mechanisms are described or confirmed; all project data remains local and the app operates offline, making ad-tracking technically infeasible in normal use.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Because no advertising or data sharing with advertisers occurs, there is nothing to opt out of, and this requirement is fully satisfied by the platform's design.

r615.riskReason: Scribbr is a paid proofreading and editing platform primarily designed for college and graduate students, not K-12; it lacks explicit COPPA or FERPA compliance statements, uses interest-based advertising cookies and third-party ad networks, does not prohibit targeted advertising, and offers no K-12 school-specific data governance or institutional controls.
r615.parentSummary: Scribbr collects personal information including name, email, payment data, and uploaded documents, which are stored on secure servers and shared with affiliated Learneo companies, third-party vendors (including Turnitin), and advertising partners. The platform uses advertising and tracking cookies for interest-based advertising and does not have explicit COPPA or FERPA compliance protections, making it unsuitable for use by students under 13 and a significant privacy risk for K-12 school deployments. Parents should be aware that documents uploaded to the platform are retained for up to 12 months and that users can delete their accounts, but the platform is not designed with K-12 student data protections in mind.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The Learneo master privacy policy states it will alert users to material changes via website notice or email, but no formal revision history is publicly maintained.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy policy references data collection (name, email, documents, usage data, payment info) but defers to Learneo's master policy and Part Two sections rather than providing a single comprehensive list in Scribbr's own policy page.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy generally states data is collected via account registration, document uploads, and cookies/tracking technologies, but specifics are spread across multiple Learneo policy documents rather than consolidated.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The Terms of Use grant Scribbr a broad, perpetual, irrevocable license to use submitted content, which creates ambiguity about user data ownership despite a statement that user ownership rights are not otherwise limited.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users can delete individual orders and uploaded documents from their dashboard, and can delete their account via 'Manage Account,' constituting full deletion capability.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: Specific retention periods are stated: proofreading documents retained up to 12 months, citation checker documents up to 90 days, citation generator uploads up to 30 days, and general account data retained while account is open.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The policy states commitment to protecting personal information and that employees follow confidentiality guidelines, but specific technical security measures (e.g., encryption standards, access controls) are not enumerated in the Scribbr-specific policy.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The site uses HTTPS (standard transport encryption), and documents are stored on a 'secure server,' but end-to-end or at-rest encryption is not explicitly detailed in the privacy policy.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: No mention of password strength requirements or enforcement in the Terms of Use or Privacy Policy.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No mention of multi-factor authentication, SSO, or LTI integration in any Scribbr policy document.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: A detailed Cookie Policy exists at scribbr.com/legal/cookie-policy/ listing cookie types (essential, analytics, advertising), purposes, storage periods, and named third-party partners (e.g., Google Analytics, OneTrust), with an opt-out mechanism available.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The Cookie Policy names some third parties (Google Analytics, Google AdSense, OneTrust, ad networks), but the main privacy policy refers to broad categories of 'third-party service providers' and 'Learneo affiliates' without a comprehensive named list specific to Scribbr.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The Cookie Policy groups cookies by type and purpose but does not specify which exact data fields are shared with each individual third party; the Learneo master policy defers detailed sharing to 'Part Two' sections not prominently surfaced on Scribbr's own policy page.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can opt out of non-essential and advertising cookies via the cookie consent manager and the 'Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Info' footer link, but opt-out is not available for all third-party sharing categories.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The Learneo master policy states that third-party recipients of personal data agree to safeguard it, and experts are contractually obligated to delete documents after review, but a formal vendor data processing agreement is not explicitly referenced for all third parties.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The cookie policy states it may be updated and encourages users to check frequently, but there is no commitment to proactively notify users specifically when third-party sharing partners change.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: Scribbr/Learneo explicitly uses advertising cookies and Google AdSense for interest-based and contextual advertising, meaning ads are served to users of the platform.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: The Cookie Policy confirms that advertising cookies collect data about online activity to identify interests for targeted/interest-based advertising, including retargeting cookies, constituting confirmed user targeting.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: An opt-out for interest-based advertising is available via the cookie consent manager and the 'Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Info' link, but third-party tracking (e.g., Google AdSense pixel tags, web beacons) remains active unless users actively opt out, limiting the effectiveness.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The Cookie Policy explicitly confirms the use of pixel tags, web beacons, clear GIFs, and JavaScript by Learneo and third-party advertising providers for tracking and ad performance purposes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: A 'Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Info' opt-out link is present in the site footer and leads to a preferences center, but the process is not prominently communicated and does not cover all forms of data sharing with advertisers.

r616.riskReason: SCUTA collects identifiable student counseling records and activity logs in a K-12 context, but its publicly accessible privacy policy and terms of use pages return virtually no substantive policy text, leaving COPPA compliance, FERPA commitments, data retention, third-party sharing, security measures, and advertising practices entirely undisclosed.
r616.parentSummary: SCUTA is a school counseling management tool used by counselors to log student interactions, case notes, and time-use data aligned to the ASCA National Model, meaning sensitive student counseling records are stored on its platform. However, the platform's Privacy Policy and Terms of Use pages (myscuta.com/privacy and myscuta.com/terms-of-use) return no substantive policy content publicly, making it impossible to verify what data protections, deletion rights, or third-party sharing restrictions are in place. Parents and school administrators should request a Data Processing Agreement directly from SCUTA before allowing the platform to handle any student data.

r617.riskReason: SentenceBuilders is GDPR-aligned and explicitly prohibits third-party ads, but it lacks explicit COPPA/FERPA compliance statements, makes no mention of encryption standards or MFA, relies on implicit consent, and its privacy policy has not been updated since May 2021, leaving US K-12 schools with material compliance gaps.
r617.parentSummary: SentenceBuilders collects teacher account information (name, email, password) and limited student data including activity scores and assignment completion; student names may be pseudonymous. There is no third-party advertising, and Google Analytics is the only named third party, used for aggregated usage statistics only. Parents or users can request full data deletion by emailing the platform's Data Protection Officer, but the policy does not explicitly address COPPA or FERPA compliance, and the policy has not been updated since 2021.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The privacy policy states it is kept under regular review and updates are posted on the same page, but the Terms and Conditions explicitly state they may be updated without notice to users, making this only partially compliant.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: Teacher account data is specifically listed (name, email, password, optional school name), and student data is described at a high level (scores, assignment completion, name data), but behavioral or device-level data collected via Google Analytics is not clearly enumerated for all user types.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy states data is collected when registering or sending personal data to SentenceBuilders, and Google Analytics collects usage data via cookies, but the precise collection mechanism for student data entered by teachers is not fully described.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The policy frames data use as necessary for service provision and references GDPR rights, but does not explicitly state that users own their data; ownership is ambiguous and no explicit data ownership clause is present.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users can request full deletion of all personal data by emailing the Data Protection Officer, and teachers can self-delete much of their own data (resources, class lists) directly within the platform.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: No specific data retention period is stated in the privacy policy; the policy does not address how long student or teacher data is retained after account deletion or subscription cancellation.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The policy states that 'appropriate measures' have been taken to protect personal information, but no specific security measures (e.g., encryption standards, access controls, audits) are enumerated.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The Terms and Conditions confirm that passwords are stored in encrypted form, but no broader encryption standard (e.g., TLS in transit, AES at rest) is mentioned for other personal or student data.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The policy notes that passwords are stored encrypted and places responsibility for password confidentiality on the user, but does not state that strong passwords are enforced at the platform level.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No mention of multi-factor authentication or SSO/LTI integration is made anywhere in the privacy policy or terms and conditions.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: Three cookie categories are named (non-essential notification cookies, Google Analytics cookies, and essential site cookies), but specific cookie names, durations, and detailed purposes are not listed.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: Google Analytics is the only named third party; no other third-party vendors or service providers are identified.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The data shared with Google Analytics is described in general terms (usage data, regional IP information), but precise data fields transmitted are not specified per third party.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: No third-party advertising is present, and users can withdraw consent and request deletion at any time by contacting the Data Protection Officer, effectively providing an opt-out of data retention.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy does not reference any data processing agreements, supplier contracts, or statements that third parties like Google Analytics are contractually bound to the platform's data protection standards.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy does not describe any process for notifying users if third-party relationships change; the Terms and Conditions state updates may occur without notice.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The privacy policy explicitly states there is no third-party advertising on SentenceBuilders.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: No targeted advertising of any kind is mentioned or implied; the platform states explicitly that no third-party advertising exists.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Google Analytics is used for aggregate usage tracking only, with no advertising tracking; no third-party ad tracking is present.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Google Analytics cookies are used and categorized, but specific tracking methods beyond cookies (e.g., web beacons, pixels) are not addressed, leaving this partially unclear.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Since there are no advertisers or advertising data-sharing relationships, no opt-out mechanism is needed, and the deletion-by-email process effectively covers all data sharing opt-out scenarios.

r618.riskReason: Seterra (operated by GeoGuessr AB) uses third-party marketing cookies, creates targeted advertising profiles using browsing history, shares personal data with advertisers, and sets a minimum account age of 16 — yet the platform is widely used by K-12 students with no explicit COPPA compliance mechanism or school-consent framework disclosed.

With marketing consent, the platform creates personalized advertising profiles using data from Google and other third parties, and uses third-party cookies for targeted ads. There is no explicit COPPA compliance statement, no FERPA acknowledgment, and no dedicated school or student data protection agreement publicly disclosed.

complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy does not include a specific commitment to notify users when third-party sharing arrangements change; users are expected to review the policy periodically.

r619.parentSummary: Setgame.com collects IP addresses, demographic data, and browsing behavior via Google Analytics, which is also used for remarketing and advertising — a significant concern for a site accessible to children. While the site acknowledges children under 13 in its privacy policy and states it adheres to applicable laws, it does not describe a verifiable parental consent mechanism and does not clearly limit data collection for minors. Parents should be aware that Google Analytics Demographics and Interest Reporting is enabled, meaning behavioral and demographic profiling may occur even for child visitors.

complianceNotes.DCQ1: The policy lists some data types (IP address, age, gender, interests, browsing behavior, login info, purchase info) but does not provide a comprehensive enumerated list of all data collected, particularly regarding cookies and form submissions.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy generally describes data collection via Google Analytics, cookies, and user-submitted forms, but does not specifically describe all collection methods (e.g., Mollom form submissions are mentioned but not explained).
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The policy does not clearly state who owns user data; it describes internal use and limited sharing but makes no explicit ownership statement in favor of users.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Registered users can review, update, and delete their contact information by editing their profile on the website, satisfying the deletion requirement.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The privacy policy does not state any specific or general data retention period for any category of data collected.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The policy states that 'appropriate physical, electronic, and managerial procedures' are in place, but does not specify any particular security measures or standards.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: No mention of encryption for data in transit or at rest is made anywhere in the privacy policy or terms of service.

complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy states personal information is shared only with entities that use it 'solely to provide support for internal operations,' implying a contractual limitation, but no explicit data processing agreement or supplier accountability language is stated.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy states changes will be posted on the page but does not specifically commit to notifying users when third-party vendor relationships change.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: Google Analytics is used for remarketing and advertising purposes, meaning behavioral data collected from site visitors including potentially children is used for ad targeting.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Google Analytics Demographics and Interest Reporting is explicitly enabled, indicating that user demographic and interest profiles are built and may be used for targeted advertising.

r620.riskReason: Shapegrams has no publicly discoverable Privacy Policy or Terms of Service pages, despite being actively used with K-12 students as young as 2nd grade, leaving data collection, sharing, security, and compliance practices entirely undisclosed.
r620.parentSummary: Shapegrams is a Google Slides/Drawings-based digital art platform used in K-12 classrooms, requiring a teacher membership account and restricting membership to users over age 13. However, no standalone Privacy Policy or Terms of Service pages could be located on shapegrams.com, meaning parents have no way to know what data is collected about teachers or students, how it is protected, or whether it is shared with third parties. Until the platform publishes clear and accessible legal policies, schools should exercise significant caution before deploying it in classrooms.

complianceNotes.DCQ5: No Privacy Policy was found; data retention periods are never mentioned anywhere on the platform's publicly accessible pages.

complianceNotes.SECQ2: The shapegrams.com website itself serves over HTTPS (standard TLS), providing basic transport encryption, but no policy documents confirm broader encryption practices for stored data.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: No account security requirements (strong passwords, complexity rules) are described anywhere on the public-facing site or in any discoverable policy document.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No mention of multi-factor authentication or SSO integration is made in any discoverable policy or help documentation on the platform.

r621.riskReason: Showbie explicitly prohibits selling student data, serves no ads to students, names its sub-processors, requires school/teacher consent before collecting minor data, and stores data on AWS with encryption at rest and in transit.
r621.parentSummary: Showbie collects minimal personal data from students — primarily name, optional email, and usage/device metadata — only after a teacher or school has agreed to Showbie's terms on the student's behalf. The platform does not sell student data, does not display advertisements to students, and shares student information only with the student's teacher(s), parent(s), and a small list of named sub-processors (AWS, Peaberry, Intercom) bound by data protection agreements. Student information is encrypted at rest and in transit, and parents or schools can request data deletion at any time.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: Showbie states it will notify users of ownership/use changes via email or prominent site notice, but no explicit advance-notification period or publicly accessible policy revision history is documented on the main policy pages.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy policy and COPPA compliance page enumerate specific categories of data collected from students and teachers, including name, email, usage data, device info, class/assignment metadata, and IP address.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: Showbie clearly explains that data is collected directly from users filling out forms, automatically through service usage, and via third-party SSO providers such as Google and Microsoft.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: Showbie explicitly states it does not claim ownership of user content and acts as a Data Processor on behalf of schools/teachers who are the Data Controllers, preserving user data ownership.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: A deletion request form is available and Pro school data is retained until the Data Controller (teacher/school/district) requests deletion, with stale Basic accounts deleted after 2 years of inactivity following a 30-day deactivation notice.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: Showbie provides a data retention policy that outlines Pro data is kept until deletion is requested and Basic/stale accounts are deleted after 2 years of inactivity, but does not specify a precise maximum retention period in days for all data types.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: Showbie references a Security Statement and states data is stored in secure AWS data centres, but the main privacy policy provides only a general security commitment rather than listing specific technical controls such as access controls, audits, or certifications.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: Showbie explicitly states that student personal information entered into the iOS or web app is encrypted across its service, including at rest, satisfying encryption requirements.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: Showbie supports login via Google and Microsoft SSO (which enforce strong authentication on their end), and teacher account setup requires institutional email credentials, meeting this standard through SSO delegation.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: Showbie supports SSO via Google and Microsoft, both of which offer MFA at the identity-provider level, satisfying the SSO/MFA availability requirement for teacher and school administrator accounts.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: Showbie acknowledges use of session-based and persistent cookies and references a separate Cookie Policy, and uses third-party analytics tools, but the main privacy policy does not enumerate all individual cookies and their specific purposes inline.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: Showbie's sub-processor disclosure page specifically names Amazon Web Services, Peaberry Software Inc., and Intercom Inc. as third parties with access to personal data, along with their roles.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The sub-processor page details what each named third party can access — for example, AWS processes file URLs, Peaberry accesses student posts for email notifications, and Intercom may access student PII only through direct support contacts.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Showbie states student personal data is shared only with the student's teacher(s) and parent(s) and named sub-processors; no third-party sharing for marketing occurs, and schools can request deletion, effectively providing opt-out control.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: Showbie explicitly states it performs due diligence on sub-processors before engagement and requires them not to use personal information beyond the services requested, satisfying the vendor agreement requirement.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: Showbie states it will notify users of changes in ownership or data use practices via email or prominent notice, but does not explicitly commit to advance notification before sub-processor list changes take effect.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: Showbie's COPPA compliance page explicitly states it will not disclose personal information collected from children to any third party for direct marketing purposes, and no ads are displayed within the student-facing platform.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Showbie states it does not engage in personal predictive profiling and does not use student data for targeted advertising, meeting this criterion fully.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Showbie confirms it does not use student data for advertising tracking; analytics data collected automatically is not linked to a child's personal information and is used only for internal service improvement.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Showbie uses only functional/session and persistent cookies for service navigation and analytics, with no confirmed use of web beacons or tracking technologies for advertising purposes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Because Showbie does not share student data with advertisers and explicitly prohibits marketing disclosures of children's data, there is no advertising data-sharing opt-out needed, which satisfies this criterion.

r622.riskReason: The developer (24x7digital LLC) previously settled a New Jersey COPPA lawsuit for collecting and transmitting children's personal data without parental consent, the app has not disclosed privacy nutrition labels to Apple, no Terms of Service page was found, and the privacy policy lacks specificity around data retention, advertising, third-party names, and student data protections required for K-12 use.
r622.parentSummary: SightWords Pro is developed by 24x7digital LLC, which states it does not routinely collect personal data from children under 13 and claims COPPA compliance; however, the company previously settled a COPPA lawsuit for collecting children's data without parental consent. No Terms of Service page was found, no privacy nutrition labels have been submitted to Apple, and there is no mention of FERPA compliance, making this platform a higher-risk choice for classroom use without further vetting.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: No Terms of Service page was found at sightwordspro.com, and the 24x7digital privacy policy states changes take effect upon posting with no advance notification process described.

complianceNotes.DCQ5: The privacy policy does not state any specific data retention period or general retention timeframe for any category of data collected.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The policy states only that 'reasonable efforts' and 'security measures' are taken to protect data, without listing any specific technical or administrative safeguards.

complianceNotes.SECQ4: No mention of multi-factor authentication, SSO, or LTI integration is found; core functionality appears to require no account, but this is not explicitly confirmed for all features.

complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy states that parties receiving data are required to process it in compliance with the privacy policy, representing a general contractual commitment but without detail.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy does not mention any process for notifying users when third-party sharing relationships change or new third parties are added.

r623.riskReason: SignUpGenius displays targeted/interest-based ads using third-party tracking cookies and web beacons on a platform widely used in K-12 school contexts, lacks explicit FERPA compliance language, and does not prohibit commercial data use in educational settings — posing significant risk under COPPA and SOPIPA for student users.
r623.parentSummary: SignUpGenius collects names, email addresses, IP addresses, usage/behavioral data, and cookie data from users, including participants who do not need an account. The platform serves targeted advertising through third-party ad networks like Google DoubleClick that track user behavior across the web using cookies and web beacons, and while it states it does not sell membership information directly, it does share behavioral and interest data with advertising partners. The platform states it does not knowingly collect data from children under 13 without parental consent, but it lacks explicit FERPA compliance commitments or a dedicated student/school data protection addendum.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The privacy policy is dated (February 2026 version visible) but the policy does not clearly describe an advance notification process or maintain a public revision history for users.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy policy lists several categories of data collected (IP, cookies, usage, demographic, interest, name, email) but does not provide a comprehensive exhaustive list in one place, and participant data fields vary by organizer configuration.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy specifically describes how data is collected — through account registration, sign-up participation, log files, cookies, web beacons, and third-party analytics — meeting this requirement.

complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy mentions archived sign-ups are retained for 4 years and notes data may be retained for legal/security/business purposes, but does not provide a clear, specific retention schedule for all data categories.

complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Opt-out mechanisms are provided for Google Analytics and DART/DoubleClick advertising cookies, but opt-out from all third-party ad tracking is not centralized or straightforward.

complianceNotes.SHRQ4: No statement requiring third-party vendors to contractually comply with the platform's privacy standards or be bound by data processor agreements is disclosed in the accessible policies.

r626.riskReason: Simpleshow uses Facebook pixel remarketing, Google Ads, LinkedIn tracking, and multiple third-party AI processors without any minimum age requirement, COPPA disclosure, or FERPA protections — making it unsuitable for K-12 use without a specific Data Processing Agreement.

The platform does not mention COPPA or FERPA compliance, does not set a minimum user age, and actively uses interest-based advertising technologies (Facebook Custom Audiences, Google Ads remarketing) that are inappropriate for student use. complianceNotes.SHRQ2: While third parties are named, the specific data shared with each is described at varying levels of detail — some are well-documented (e.g., YouTube tokens, payment data to BS PAYONE) while others are described only broadly.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: The policy offers some opt-out mechanisms (e.g., deactivating Facebook plugin, logging out of Vimeo/YouTube before visiting, cookie consent settings) but there is no single, centralized opt-out process for all third-party data sharing.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy references GDPR data processing agreements with some vendors (e.g., standard contractual clauses with Google) but does not universally state that all third-party vendors are contractually bound to equivalent data protection standards.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy does not explicitly commit to notifying users when third-party sub-processors are added or changed, though GDPR obligations implicitly require this for material changes.
