complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Google Ads remarketing and Facebook Custom Audiences are both confirmed as in use, meaning user behavioral data is leveraged for targeted advertising across the web — wholly inappropriate for a K-12 context.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Facebook pixel and Google Ads tracking are active on the website with no confirmed opt-out mechanism within the platform itself for these specific trackers, beyond general cookie consent banners.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The privacy policy confirms use of Facebook pixel, Google Ads cookies, Google Tag Manager, and LinkedIn Insight Tag — all of which are tracking technologies used for advertising purposes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Some opt-out guidance is provided (e.g., deactivating Facebook plugin, browser-level cookie controls) but there is no clear, prominent, user-friendly opt-out process specifically for advertiser data sharing.

r627.riskReason: Sketchbook's privacy policy explicitly permits third-party advertisers to deliver targeted ads directly to users, allows IP-based targeting by third parties, does not respond to Do Not Track signals, sets the minimum age at 16 (not COPPA's required 13 with parental consent), lacks explicit COPPA or FERPA compliance statements, and does not name specific third parties or detail per-party data sharing—all of which create significant risk for K-12 deployment.
r627.parentSummary: Sketchbook collects personal information such as your child's email address, name, IP address, country, and app usage data when they use the app or contact support. This data may be shared with a broad range of unnamed third-party service providers including analytics, marketing, and advertising companies, and the policy explicitly notes that third-party advertisers may deliver ads directly to users and use IP addresses for targeting. While users can request deletion of their data by email and Sketchbook states it implements general security measures, the platform lacks explicit COPPA compliance, does not name specific third parties, does not respond to Do Not Track signals, and has no stated FERPA or SOPIPA commitments—making it a higher-risk tool for classroom use with minors.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The privacy policy is dated (April 19, 2026 update visible) but does not explicitly state an advance notification process or maintain a public revision history for users.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The policy lists several categories of data collected (email, name, IP, country, usage, feedback) but does not provide an exhaustive enumeration of all data types, particularly around device identifiers and third-party cookie data.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy specifically describes how data is collected: through app use, contact forms, mailing list subscriptions, user surveys, cookies, web beacons, and mobile device permissions.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The policy does not clearly assert user ownership of personal data; it implies Sketchbook retains and controls data for business purposes, leaving data ownership ambiguous.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users can request deletion by emailing Sketchbook, but deletion is not self-service and may take up to 30 days to complete, representing a limited and delayed deletion process.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy states data is kept only as long as necessary for the stated purposes or as required by law, but does not provide a specific retention period in days or months.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The policy states 'appropriate technical and organizational security measures' are implemented but does not specify what those measures are (e.g., encryption standards, access controls, audits).
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The privacy policy makes no mention of encryption in transit or at rest for user data, and no encryption standard is referenced anywhere in the policy.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The policy contains no mention of password strength requirements, enforcement of strong passwords, or SSO options for users.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: There is no mention of multi-factor authentication, SSO/LTI integration, or any equivalent access security mechanism in the policy or legal documents.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The policy discusses functional, preference, and third-party advertiser cookies in general terms and offers a cookie preference management link, but does not provide a full enumerated list of all cookies with their specific purposes.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The policy references broad categories of third parties (analytics, marketing, social media, security vendors) but does not name any specific third-party companies.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy groups data sharing disclosures broadly by purpose category and does not specify which data types are shared with each individual third party.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can manage some cookie preferences via a provided link, but there is no clear opt-out mechanism for all third-party data sharing, particularly for advertising-related disclosures.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy states all third parties with access to user information must comply with the privacy policy and 'appropriate confidentiality and security measures,' representing a general contractual claim without specifics.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy does not include any commitment to notify users when third-party service providers or data sharing arrangements change.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The policy explicitly states the app may contain 'advertisements that are delivered directly to you from third party advertisers,' confirming that targeted ads are displayed to users.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Third-party advertisers are permitted to use user IP addresses to target rewards or promotions and use technologies to personalize and measure ad effectiveness, confirming user-level ad targeting.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: The policy acknowledges that third-party advertiser cookies and tracking technologies are used but explicitly states these are not covered by Sketchbook's privacy policy and that Sketchbook does not control third-party practices, with no opt-out provided.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Marketing emails contain web beacons, and third-party advertisers may use tracking technologies; the policy does not limit tracking to functional purposes only and does not clearly enumerate all tracking methods.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: The policy offers an unsubscribe option for marketing email web beacons but provides no clear, comprehensive opt-out process for sharing user data with third-party advertisers or for ad-targeting based on user data.

dataSharedWith: Google for Education / Microsoft for Education (Schools version only)
r628.riskReason: The provided URL (sketchuppro2020.com) does not appear to be an official Trimble/SketchUp domain and could not be verified; the official SketchUp Pro product is an adult-oriented general audience application not designed for K-12 use, uses cookie data for ad targeting on third-party sites, and while a separate SketchUp for Schools product has COPPA-specific protections, SketchUp Pro 2020 itself lacks explicit FERPA/COPPA commitments appropriate for direct K-12 student deployment.
r628.parentSummary: SketchUp Pro 2020, made by Trimble, is primarily a professional 3D modeling tool designed for adults and collects account information (name, email), usage data, IP addresses, and cookie data, some of which is used to serve targeted ads on third-party websites and social networks. The official SketchUp for Schools product has stronger child privacy protections including a children's privacy notice and a statement that no children's personal information is stored or shared with third parties, but SketchUp Pro is not that product. Parents and schools should note that the URL provided (sketchuppro2020.com) is not an official Trimble/SketchUp domain, raising additional authenticity and safety concerns.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The Trimble/SketchUp Terms state they may update terms at their discretion and continued use constitutes acceptance, but advance notification to users before changes take effect is not clearly guaranteed.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy notice lists several categories of data (name, email, usage data, IP, cookies, crash data, license info) but the listing is spread across product-specific sections and is not presented as a single comprehensive data inventory.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The privacy policy specifically describes how data is collected: directly from users at account creation, automatically via cookies and log files, and via third-party integrations such as Google/Microsoft for Schools.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The Terms of Service grant Trimble broad rights to use customer data 'in perpetuity' for product development and machine learning, creating ambiguity about effective user ownership of data despite nominal user retention of rights.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: SketchUp provides a dedicated account/data deletion form at privacy.sketchup.com, and for the Schools product, deletion requests are routed through Google or Microsoft Education as applicable.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The privacy policy does not state a specific data retention period in days; it references retention tied to account activity and legal obligations without specifying a concrete timeframe.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The privacy notice states only that 'reasonable administrative, technical, and physical security controls' are used to protect user data, without enumerating specific security measures.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: No explicit encryption-in-transit or at-rest commitment is stated in the publicly available SketchUp/Trimble privacy documentation; the Trimble Offering Terms reference industry-standard security measures generally.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: Trimble requires passwords with specific complexity rules during Trimble ID account creation, meeting the standard for enforced password requirements.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: Trimble requires all SketchUp users to use at least one form of MFA, including OTP, authenticator apps, passkeys, or SSO via Google/Apple/Microsoft, fully meeting this criterion.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The privacy notice mentions use of cookies and links to cookie preference management via OneTrust, and notes targeting cookies can be turned off, but does not provide a comprehensive list of all individual cookies and their purposes.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The privacy notice names some third parties (Chaos Group, Google for Education, Microsoft for Education, ARCore/Google) but does not provide a complete named list of all third-party service providers used.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: Some information about what is shared with specific parties is provided (e.g., PII shared with Chaos Group for V-Ray users, CPI routed via Google/Microsoft for Schools), but a full data-per-third-party breakdown is not available.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can opt out of targeting cookies via cookie preferences on SketchUp.com, and marketing emails include unsubscribe links; a data deletion form is also available.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The Trimble Developer Terms require third-party developers to handle customer data per legally adequate privacy policies and applicable law, but the standard vendor DPA obligations for all third-party processors are not explicitly described in the public privacy notice.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The privacy notice and terms do not include a commitment to notify users specifically when third-party data sharing arrangements change; users are expected to periodically review the updated terms.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: Cookie data collected on SketchUp.com is explicitly used to serve ads on other websites and social networks, meaning targeted ads are displayed beyond the platform itself.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: The privacy notice confirms that cookie information is used to serve users 'ads relevant to SketchUp on other websites and social networks,' constituting confirmed third-party targeted advertising.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Users can opt out of targeting cookies via cookie preferences on SketchUp.com, providing a limited opt-out, but third-party ad network tracking may persist through other means.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The privacy notice confirms use of cookies for ad retargeting on external sites and social networks, indicating tracking methods beyond functional use are deployed.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: An opt-out for targeting cookies is available through cookie preferences on the SketchUp.com site, but the process is not prominently featured and may not cover all advertising data sharing channels.

r629.riskReason: IBM SkillsBuild (skillsbuild.org) has a dedicated student privacy policy with strong institutional controls, but shares student PII with multiple named and unnamed third parties globally, uses third-party analytics/tracking cookies, and does not explicitly claim COPPA or FERPA compliance by name.
r629.parentSummary: IBM SkillsBuild collects student names, email addresses, school names, and learning activity data to provide its free tech education platform for high school students ages 13 and older. Data is shared with school administrators, and with named third-party processors like Credly (for digital badges) and Chronus (for mentoring), with IBM requiring these processors to protect student data under contractual obligations. IBM does not sell student data, provides deletion rights, and uses encryption in transit, though parents should be aware that data may be transferred to IBM subsidiaries globally and that third-party analytics partners may also access usage data.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The Terms of Use states IBM will notify users of changes and the date is visible at the top of the page, but there is no formal revision history or advance notification window specified.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The student Data Privacy Policy provides a detailed list of collected data including registration info, usage/learning data, survey responses, submissions, and optional fields like grades and parent email.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy clearly describes how data is collected — through account registration forms, automatic platform interaction logging, surveys, and institution-provided registration by teachers.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: Data ownership is ambiguous; IBM acts as data controller and the policy does not explicitly state that users own their data, though institutions control registration data and users can request deletion.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users and institutions can request access, correction, or deletion of personal information, and account closure is available, satisfying full deletion allowance.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy states data is retained for administrative purposes and as long as needed for the relationship, but does not specify a concrete retention period in days or years beyond the 90-day re-registration lockout after account deletion.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: IBM states it implements 'reasonable physical, electronic, administrative, managerial and technical safeguards' and references GDPR and ISO/IEC 27001 compliance, but does not enumerate specific technical security measures in the student policy.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The policy mentions that 'certain personal information' is encrypted during transmission over the Internet, but does not confirm end-to-end or at-rest encryption comprehensively.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: Account registration requires users to create a username and password, and the platform supports SSO via institutional access, meeting this criterion through standard account security practices.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: The platform supports institutional SSO/LTI-style access through school-registered accounts and Chronus SSO integration, satisfying the MFA/SSO requirement for school users.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The student privacy policy references third-party cookies and analytics partners that may use cookies, but does not provide a detailed cookie list with individual purposes or a dedicated cookie policy page.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: Some specific third parties are named (Credly, Chronus, Tribe, a third-party survey platform), but the policy also references unnamed 'analytics partners' and 'IBM subsidiaries globally' without full enumeration.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: Data shared with Credly (name, email, badge earned) and Chronus (name, ID, email, school) is specified, but data shared with analytics partners and IBM subsidiaries is described only in general terms.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can request data deletion and opt out of optional data sharing, but there is no clearly described easy opt-out mechanism specifically for third-party data processor sharing without closing the account.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy states that those with access to student data 'are under a contractual obligation' to protect it and not further disseminate it, and IBM requires suppliers to protect data from unauthorized access.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The Terms of Use states IBM may change terms at any time and will notify users, but there is no specific commitment to notify users when new third-party processors are added to the ecosystem.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The platform is a free educational tool with no advertising; the policy and platform documentation contain no mention of ads being displayed to students.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: There is no mention of targeted advertising in the student privacy policy; learning recommendations are made using internal platform data only, not for commercial advertising.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Third-party analytics partners are mentioned as potentially using cookies to track usage, but no opt-out mechanism for this analytics tracking is described in the student policy.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The archive policy references third-party cookies and data collection technologies used by analytics partners, but purposes and tracking methods are not fully enumerated or distinguished.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: The policy allows users to request data access and deletion but does not describe a clear, specific opt-out process for data sharing with analytics or other third-party data processors short of account deletion.

dataCollected: School name and State/Territory or Country
Audio recordings (for spelling, word pronunciation, narrating books)
dataSharedWith: MailChimp (email delivery to parents and teachers)
Other students (first name, school, game result via multiplayer)
r630.riskReason: Skoolbo collects audio recordings from children and shares child first names and school details in multiplayer games, while its policies lack specific encryption disclosures, detailed cookie purpose listings, MFA, and strong password enforcement, and its reserved right to sell aggregated data raises concerns despite stated anonymization.
r630.parentSummary: Skoolbo collects minimal student information including first name, surname initial, birth month, school name, game scores, and audio recordings for educational features, and stores it on cloud platforms including Microsoft Azure and Amazon Web Services. The platform does not sell personally identifiable information, claims COPPA compliance, and requires parental consent for teacher-created student accounts, but does share a child's first name and school with other players in multiplayer games and uses web beacons for tracking. Parents should be aware that audio recordings are processed by third-party services (Google Cloud API and Soapbox Labs), and the policy lacks specific detail on encryption practices or a comprehensive cookie inventory.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The privacy policy states teachers and parents will be notified of any updates and the most current version will be found at the policy URL, satisfying advance notification requirements.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The policy lists some data collected (first name, surname initial, birth month, device ID, IP, audio) but does not provide a complete enumerated list in one place, and the distinction between what is and is not collected is split across sections.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy states data is collected automatically during use and via account registration, but does not fully specify collection mechanisms for all data types (e.g., how audio consent is obtained or how multiplayer data is triggered).
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The policy does not explicitly state that users own their data; the Terms and Conditions grant Skoolbo broad rights to use non-personally-identifiable material sent to the platform, leaving data ownership ambiguous.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: The privacy policy states that removal of personal information occurs within 72 hours upon request, and inactive accounts are deleted after 12 months, providing a clear deletion pathway.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy specifies that inactive accounts are deleted after 12 months and that deletion requests are processed within 72 hours, providing a concrete retention and deletion timeline.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The policy mentions physical, electronic, and managerial safeguards and use of major cloud providers, but does not enumerate specific technical security measures such as access controls or audit logging.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The privacy policy makes no mention of encryption (in transit or at rest) for user data, representing a significant gap for a platform serving children under 13.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: There is no mention of strong password requirements or enforcement in either the Terms of Service or the Privacy Policy; teacher guides reference default passwords set to the color 'black', indicating weak password practices.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No mention of multi-factor authentication or SSO/LTI integration is found in the policy documents; standard username/password login appears to be the only access method.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The policy mentions cookies and web beacons generally and explains their purpose for web traffic analysis, but does not provide a categorized list of all cookies used or distinguish functional from tracking cookies.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The privacy policy specifically names third-party providers including Microsoft Azure, Amazon Web Services, Alibaba Cloud, MailChimp, Webengage, Google Cloud API, and Soapbox Labs.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: While third parties are named, the policy does not clearly specify which specific data elements are shared with each individual third party (e.g., what data goes to Webengage vs. MailChimp vs. Soapbox Labs).
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can contact Skoolbo to request data removal which would apply to third parties per the policy, but there is no explicit opt-out mechanism described for third-party data sharing short of full account deletion.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy references use of reputable cloud providers with 'robust security systems' but does not explicitly state that third-party vendors are contractually bound to a data processing agreement or privacy standards.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy states teachers and parents will be notified of policy updates, which would cover third-party changes, but does not specifically commit to notifying users when third-party vendor relationships change.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The privacy policy and terms make no mention of advertising being displayed to users within the platform, and the platform appears to be a paid subscription service with no ad-supported tier.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: There is no indication in the policy documents that user data is used for targeted advertising; data use is described as limited to educational and service improvement purposes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Web beacons are mentioned as being used to count visits and track email opens, which could involve third-party tracking, but no explicit opt-out mechanism for this tracking is provided.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The policy confirms use of web beacons and traffic log cookies without providing clarity on whether these serve only functional purposes or also enable third-party ad tracking, leaving this unresolved.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: No opt-out process for data sharing with advertisers is described; while Skoolbo states it does not sell personal data, no formal opt-out mechanism for any form of data sharing is documented.

r631.riskReason: SkyView Lite has received a 'Warning' rating from Common Sense Media due to personal information being shared for third-party marketing, unclear data sale practices, unclear targeted advertising, and an absence of FERPA compliance language or K-12 educational use protections.
r631.parentSummary: SkyView Lite (by Terminal Eleven LLC) claims not to directly collect personal data, but acknowledges disclosing data to unnamed 'trusted partners,' including for third-party marketing purposes. The app uses location services and device identifiers that may be shared with third-party advertising networks. No dedicated K-12 or FERPA safeguards are mentioned, no minimum age is stated, and the privacy policy lacks a Terms of Service, a data retention policy, and clear opt-out mechanisms for data sharing.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: No Terms of Service page exists and the privacy policy provides no stated process for advance notification of changes or a revision history/changelog.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The policy claims no personal data is collected but simultaneously acknowledges disclosing personal data to third-party partners, making the full data inventory incomplete and contradictory.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy provides only a vague general statement that data is disclosed to trusted partners without specifying how data is collected (e.g., via SDK, sensors, or cookies).
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The policy is silent on user data ownership, and the acknowledgment of third-party data disclosure without clear user control implies the company or its partners control the data.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: The policy explicitly states no means for data deletion exists because the company claims it does not collect personal data, leaving no deletion path when data is in fact shared with third parties.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: No data retention period is stated anywhere in the privacy policy, and Common Sense Media confirmed this was not assessed or addressed.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: No specific security measures (e.g., encryption standards, access controls, audits) are described in the privacy policy.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The privacy policy makes no mention of encryption for data in transit or at rest.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: No account creation is required to use the app, satisfying the no-account-required criterion for this standard.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No account or login is required to use SkyView Lite, satisfying the no-account-required criterion for MFA.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The privacy policy contains no cookie policy, no list of cookies used, and no disclosure of tracking technologies employed.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The policy references 'trusted partners' without naming any specific third parties, providing no actionable transparency.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: No breakdown of what specific data is shared with each third party is provided; Common Sense Media flagged this as unclear.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: No opt-out process for third-party data sharing is described anywhere in the policy.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy makes no mention of requiring third-party partners to adhere to equivalent privacy protections or a vendor agreement.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy does not indicate that users will be notified if third-party partners change or if new data-sharing arrangements are established.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: Common Sense Media confirmed personal information is shared for third-party marketing, and user reviews note ads are present in the free version.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Common Sense Media rated targeted/personalized advertising as 'unclear,' meaning the policy does not rule out user-level ad targeting.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: The policy does not address third-party tracking for advertising purposes, and Apple's App Store listing indicates data may be used to track users across apps and websites.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The policy does not disclose the use of web beacons, pixels, or SDK-based tracking methods, despite Apple confirming cross-app tracking data use.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: No opt-out process for data sharing with advertisers is described, and Common Sense Media confirmed this was not assessed or available.

r632.riskReason: Slack is a workplace productivity tool not designed for K-12 students — it sets a minimum age of 16, lacks a dedicated COPPA framework, places full FERPA compliance responsibility on the school, uses third-party advertising cookies, and collects broad data including usage analytics and location that may not be appropriate for minors in an educational context.
r632.parentSummary: Slack collects significant personal data including names, email addresses, message content, device details, location approximations, and usage behavior to operate its workplace communication platform. The platform is not designed for K-12 students — it requires users to be at least 16 years old and places the burden of FERPA compliance and parental consent on the school, not on Slack. Slack does not sell student data, provides encryption in transit and at rest, and offers a subprocessor list, but it uses third-party advertising cookies and its policies offer limited specific protections for minors, making it a high-risk choice for K-12 deployment without careful administrative controls and a formal Data Processing Agreement.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: Slack states it will provide reasonable notice of material changes to its terms, but continued use of the service after changes constitutes acceptance, and a full revision history is archived publicly — however, individual user notification is not guaranteed, only workspace-level customer notification.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: Slack's Privacy Policy lists specific categories of data collected including account information, message content, usage data, log data, device data, location, cookie data, and audio/video metadata.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The Privacy Policy clearly explains that data is collected through direct user input, automated means (logs, cookies, device signals), third-party integrations, and employer/customer submissions.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: Slack explicitly states that the Customer (school/organization) owns and controls all content submitted to the workspace, and Slack processes data on behalf of the Customer.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users can deactivate accounts and request profile deletion, but full deletion requires action by a Workspace Owner, and Slack may retain 'Other Information' (usage/log data) for legitimate business interests even after account deactivation.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: Slack specifies that on free plans messages can be retained for 90 days or 1 year, on paid plans data is kept as long as the workspace exists, and deleted Customer Data is permanently removed from backups within 14 days — a clear retention framework is stated.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: Slack details specific security measures including encryption at rest and in transit, regular vulnerability scans, application-level penetration tests, SOC 2 audits, ISO 27001/27017/27018 certifications, and Enterprise Key Management options.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: Slack explicitly states that customer data is encrypted at rest and in transit by default, using the latest recommended secure cipher suites and protocols.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: Slack's policies do not explicitly enforce specific password strength requirements on end users, though enterprise SSO/SAML options are available for organizations that configure them.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: Slack supports SSO/SAML integrations and MFA options, particularly at the Enterprise Grid plan level, satisfying this requirement for institutions that configure these features.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: Slack maintains a dedicated Cookie Policy listing cookie types (session, persistent) and similar technologies like web beacons, with opt-out controls referenced, though not all individual third-party cookies are named by vendor.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: Slack references a publicly available subprocessor list with identities and locations, but within the Privacy Policy itself, third-party service providers are described in broad categories rather than named individually.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The Privacy Policy groups data shared with third parties by purpose category (e.g., infrastructure, analytics, AI) rather than specifying exactly which data fields are shared with each named subprocessor.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can opt out of certain data sharing (e.g., CCPA rights, AI model opt-out) by contacting Slack, but the process is not self-service and requires submitting requests, making opt-out limited rather than fully easy.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: Slack explicitly states it performs due diligence on subprocessors and executes agreements requiring them to meet privacy, security, and confidentiality obligations before engagement.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: Slack provides a subscription mechanism to receive subprocessor change notifications, but does not guarantee advance notice to end users — only to workspace-level customers, and notification of third-party app changes is not clearly stated.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: Slack does not serve behavioral ads within its core platform to workspace users, but does use third-party advertising cookies on its marketing websites (slack.com), creating a partial concern for users who visit the site.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Slack states it does not sell personal data and does not target workspace users with behavioral ads inside the app, but third-party cookies on its website may be used for interest-based targeting by advertising partners.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Slack's Cookie Policy acknowledges use of third-party advertising cookies and references the Digital Advertising Alliance opt-out, but states that 'do not track' signals are not honored, limiting user control.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Slack's Cookie Policy explicitly confirms use of single-pixel gifs and web beacons in addition to cookies, and these tracking technologies are used for advertising purposes on its websites, not solely for functional purposes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Slack references the Digital Advertising Alliance opt-out tool and CCPA opt-out rights for California residents, but the opt-out process is external and indirect rather than a clear in-product control for all users.

r633.riskReason: Slice the Price Card is a commercial fundraising platform, not an EdTech platform — it has no FERPA compliance, no SOPIPA acknowledgment, no school data agreements, and explicitly prohibits use by children under 13, making it wholly unsuitable for K-12 student use.
r633.parentSummary: Slice the Price Card is a Domino's pizza discount fundraising platform operated by Platinum Fundraising LLC; it collects personal and payment information from users who register or purchase cards online. The site states it does not sell personal data to third parties and does not engage in targeted advertising or behavioral tracking directed at children. However, this is a commercial fundraising tool with no EdTech-specific student data protections, no FERPA compliance, and a minimum age requirement of 13, making it inappropriate for direct use by K-12 students.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The privacy policy does not describe any advance notification process for policy changes, nor is a revision history or versioning system mentioned.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The policy references collecting PII such as name, contact, and order information when ordering or registering, but the exact enumerated list of data types is obscured with an ellipsis in available text and is not fully disclosed.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy gives a general statement that data is collected when 'ordering, registering, or otherwise interacting with our site,' but does not specifically enumerate all collection methods (e.g., cookies, forms, purchase flows).
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The policy does not explicitly state that users own their data; data ownership terms are silent, leaving ownership ambiguous or implicitly retained by the company.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users may change personal information by contacting the company via email or phone, but there is no explicit full deletion right described — only modification is mentioned.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: No specific data retention period is stated anywhere in the accessible privacy policy text; retention duration is not addressed.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The policy references Squarespace's attack monitoring, regular security testing, access controls, and safeguards against unauthorized access, but these are general platform-level statements rather than specific named security measures.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The site is hosted on Squarespace (which uses HTTPS/TLS by default), but the privacy policy does not explicitly mention or guarantee encryption of data at rest or in transit.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: No mention of password strength requirements or enforcement policies is found anywhere in the terms or privacy policy.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No mention of multi-factor authentication or SSO/LTI integration is present; accounts appear to rely on standard username/password access only.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The policy mentions cookies and allows users to disable them via browser settings, but does not enumerate specific cookies by name, category, or purpose.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: Only Squarespace is implicitly identified as a platform/infrastructure provider; no other third parties are specifically named despite Squarespace's own use of third-party security providers.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy does not specify what data, if any, is shared with Squarespace or any other party; data sharing details per third party are not disclosed.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can disable cookies via browser settings, and the platform states it does not sell PII, which constitutes a limited opt-out, but no formal opt-out mechanism for third-party sharing is provided.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: No vendor data processing agreement, contractual data protection obligations for third parties, or supplier accountability language is mentioned in the policy.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: There is no mention of notifying users if third-party data sharing relationships change; users would not be informed of such changes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The policy states Google AdSense has not been enabled but may be in the future, creating uncertainty about whether ads could appear; currently no ads are shown.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: The policy explicitly states the platform does not engage in targeted advertising or behavioral tracking directed at children, and currently has no ad targeting active.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: The policy states third-party behavioral tracking is not allowed and that Do Not Track signals are honored, indicating no third-party ad tracking is in use.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The policy does not enumerate specific tracking technologies (e.g., pixels, web beacons) in use; tracking methods beyond cookies are not clearly disclosed.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: No explicit opt-out mechanism for data sharing with advertisers is provided; while the platform states it does not currently sell data, no formal opt-out process is documented.
