r790.riskReason: Writable explicitly prohibits selling student data, bars advertising to students, restricts minor access to teacher/school-authorized accounts only, and contractually obligates service providers to protect student information consistent with its privacy policy.
r790.parentSummary: Writable collects minimal student data — including name, username, email, school, grade level, and writing submissions — solely to operate its writing instruction service for grades 3–12. The platform does not sell student data, does not serve ads to students, and restricts minor access to teacher- or school-authorized accounts only. Parents, schools, or districts can request to review, correct, or delete student data by contacting privacy@writable.com, and Writable notifies account holders via email when material policy changes occur.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The privacy policy states that material changes trigger email notification to account holders (which may include the student's teacher or school), and users are informed before data is used in a manner inconsistent with original terms.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy policy enumerates specific data types collected including name, username, email, profile picture, school, grade level, class access code, writing submissions, log data, device info, and third-party account data.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy explicitly describes data collected via registration, third-party SSO (Google, Microsoft, Schoology, Canvas, HMH Ed), automatic collection from service usage, and cookies/web beacons.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The Terms of Service explicitly state that all intellectual property rights in Student Data remain the exclusive property of the school, student, or student's parent or legal guardian.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Deletion is available but requires submitting a written request to privacy@writable.com rather than a self-service in-platform deletion tool, making it partially accessible rather than fully immediate.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy states data is deleted or anonymized within 'a reasonable period' after an account is terminated or becomes inactive, but does not specify a precise retention period in days or months.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The Terms of Service reference 'appropriate administrative, physical and technical safeguards' and periodic risk assessments, but specific technical security measures (e.g., encryption protocols, SOC certification) are not enumerated in the public policy.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The policy does not explicitly state that data is encrypted in transit or at rest; HTTPS is implied by standard web practice but not confirmed in the policy text.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: Writable supports SSO via Google, Microsoft, Schoology, and Canvas, which satisfies strong authentication requirements without requiring standalone password management.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: SSO/LTI integrations with Google, Microsoft, Schoology, and Canvas effectively provide federated authentication and MFA capabilities managed by those identity providers.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The policy acknowledges use of cookies, web beacons, tags, and scripts and notes users can configure browsers to refuse cookies, but does not provide a detailed list of each cookie by name, type, and specific purpose.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The policy references third-party service providers for maintenance, database management, web analytics, and DRM management, and SSO partners by name (Google, Microsoft, Schoology, Canvas, HMH Ed), but does not list all specific vendor names.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy groups data shared with service providers broadly rather than specifying precisely which data elements are shared with each individual third party.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can configure browsers to block cookies and may contact Writable to delete data, but there is no explicit self-service opt-out mechanism for third-party service-provider data sharing specifically.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy explicitly states that service providers are contractually required to protect Personal Information and Minor Student Personal Information consistent with the privacy policy and are forbidden from selling it.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy states changes will be communicated via email for material updates but does not specifically address whether changes to the list of third-party service providers will be proactively announced.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The Terms of Service explicitly state Writable will not use Student Data to advertise or market to students or their parents/guardians, and no advertising is displayed within the student platform.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: The policy and Terms of Service confirm no targeted advertising is directed at students; Writable explicitly states it does not track users across third-party websites for targeted advertising.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: The policy explicitly states Writable does not track users over time and across third-party websites to provide targeted advertising and does not respond to Do Not Track signals in an ad-targeting context.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The policy acknowledges use of cookies, clear GIFs (web beacons), tags, and scripts for service functionality, but does not fully enumerate each tracking technology and its specific purpose, leaving some ambiguity.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Writable explicitly commits to no advertising to students and no cross-site tracking for ads, effectively eliminating the need for an opt-out by not engaging in such practices at all.

dataSharedWith: Third-party linked websites (no data transfer disclosed)
r791.riskReason: Houston Zoo is not an EdTech platform and has no school data agreements, FERPA compliance, SOPIPA compliance, or student-specific data protections, making it unsuitable for K-12 school use.
r791.parentSummary: The Houston Zoo website collects names, email addresses, and usage data via Google Analytics and cookies, and processes e-commerce data through a third-party vendor called Galaxy. While the site states it will not sell or share user information and prohibits use by children under 13, it is a general public zoo website — not an educational technology platform — and lacks the contractual, FERPA, or SOPIPA protections required for K-12 school deployment. Parents and educators should be aware this site is not designed or certified for student use.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The policy states it reserves the right to update at any time and will post changes on the website, but provides no advance notification to users and no revision history or version dating.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The policy names some collected data (name, email, form data, analytics) but does not provide a comprehensive or exhaustive list of all data types collected across all site interactions.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy describes some collection methods (forms, cookies via Google Analytics, newsletter sign-up) in general terms but lacks a systematic breakdown of how each data type is collected.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The policy does not explicitly address data ownership; it states data will not be sold or shared but makes no affirmative declaration that users own their data.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: The privacy policy provides no mechanism for users to request deletion of their personal data; only an opt-out from the newsletter email list is mentioned.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: No data retention period is stated anywhere in the policy for any category of data collected.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The policy states it takes 'every precaution' and restricts access to staff, but does not enumerate specific technical security measures such as firewalls, encryption standards, or access controls.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The policy references a 'secure e-commerce site' managed by Galaxy but does not explicitly confirm encryption (e.g., TLS/SSL) is used throughout the main website.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: No account registration is required for general browsing, but no password policies are stated for any account features that may exist.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No mention of multi-factor authentication or SSO is made anywhere in the policy or terms.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: Google Analytics cookies are mentioned by name with a general description of their function, but no full cookie inventory, cookie categories, or opt-out mechanism for cookies is provided.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: Galaxy (e-commerce) and Emma (email) are named as third-party vendors, and Google Analytics is mentioned, but no other third parties are disclosed and the list appears incomplete.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy indicates Emma receives name and email for newsletters and Galaxy handles e-commerce, but does not specify precisely what data fields are shared with Google Analytics or other parties.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: An opt-out link is provided within newsletter emails to unsubscribe from Emma, but no opt-out mechanism for Google Analytics tracking or other third-party data sharing is described.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy does not state that third-party vendors (Galaxy, Emma, Google Analytics) are contractually bound to any data protection or privacy standards.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy does not address whether users will be notified if third-party service providers change or if new third parties are added.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The policy does not address advertising at all; the website's general public nature and use of Google Analytics suggests potential ad-related tracking may occur without disclosure.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: No statement is made prohibiting targeted advertising; Google Analytics use combined with personal data profiling language raises targeting concerns without explicit prohibition.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Google Analytics is disclosed as a tracking tool but no opt-out mechanism (such as Google Analytics opt-out browser add-on) is mentioned, and third-party tracking for advertising purposes is not addressed.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Google Analytics HTTP cookies are disclosed generally, but no comprehensive tracking method inventory (web beacons, pixels, fingerprinting) is provided or addressed.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: No opt-out process for data sharing with advertisers or marketing partners is described anywhere in the privacy policy.

dataSharedWith: Trusted service providers (hosting, email, data storage)
Post-Secondary Schools (Higher Ed Platform, if enabled by school)
r792.riskReason: Xello explicitly prohibits selling student data, does not serve ads to students, explicitly acknowledges COPPA and FERPA obligations, holds SOC2 Type 2 certification, and provides strong deletion and data ownership protections to schools.
r792.parentSummary: Xello collects student personal and academic information (such as name, grade, career interests, and course plans) provided by schools to help students explore college and career pathways. Student data is never sold or used for advertising, and no third-party ads are shown to students within the platform. Schools retain ownership of student data and can request full deletion at any time, and Xello commits to COPPA, FERPA, and GDPR compliance with annual third-party security audits.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The Privacy Policy provides at least 30 days' advance email notice to schools for material changes, and the Terms of Service requires 14 days' notice with customer consent before material changes take effect.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The Privacy Policy provides a detailed enumeration of data collected from schools, students, educators, and visitors, including Student ID, name, gender, DOB, grade, email, interests, test scores, course plans, IP address, device data, and reCAPTCHA behavioral data.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy specifically describes data collection methods including direct school/district provisioning, student self-entry, automated collection via cookies and analytics, and Google reCAPTCHA on login.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The Terms of Service explicitly state that all Student Personal Information 'is and will continue to be the property of and under the control of the Customer,' clearly assigning ownership to the school.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Schools can request deletion of all Student Personal Information at any time and Xello commits to fulfilling the request within 30 days; students can also edit or delete their own User Content through the platform.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The Privacy Policy states a specific 90-day retention period following account termination before deletion, with school-directed earlier deletion honored within 30 days of request.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: Specific security measures are listed including SSL encryption, hashed passwords, encrypted backups, physical security, employee data access restrictions, 24/7 network intrusion detection, and annual SOC2 Type 2 and CyberEssentials audits.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The policy explicitly states all traffic is encrypted via SSL, all backups are securely encrypted, and passwords are hashed using industry-standard mechanisms.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The policy references password hashing and session timeouts but does not explicitly state requirements for password complexity or strength enforcement; SSO is supported but not universally mandated.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: Xello supports SSO/LTI integration for districts, which serves as a federated authentication mechanism, but MFA is not explicitly described as available or enforced for all account types.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The policy mentions cookies and distinguishes between functional/service cookies and third-party advertising cookies (used only on business websites, not the student platform), but does not provide a fully enumerated cookie list with per-cookie purpose descriptions.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The policy references categories of third parties (service providers, analytics partners, Google reCAPTCHA, post-secondary schools) but does not publish a comprehensive named list of all subprocessors.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy groups data sharing by category of third party rather than specifying exactly which data elements are shared with each named third party, though it does state student data is not shared except as described.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Student Personal Information is explicitly not sold or shared for advertising; schools control all data sharing; users can opt out of analytics cookies on business websites via a cookie preference tool.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The Terms require subcontractors to follow the same deletion and privacy standards, and in merger/acquisition scenarios Xello states it will only disclose to a company agreeing to 'data privacy standards no less stringent than our own.'
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: Schools receive 30 days' advance written notice of material Privacy Policy changes, and the Terms require customer consent before material Terms changes take effect, covering changes that would affect third-party arrangements.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The Privacy Policy explicitly states 'we do not serve third-party advertisements to you while using our Services,' and advertising cookies are restricted to the business marketing website only.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: No targeted advertising is directed at students or within the educational platform; third-party advertising partners only interact with the business information website for marketing Xello services to potential customers.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Third-party tracking and advertising cookies are explicitly excluded from the student-facing services and limited to the business marketing website, and an opt-out tool is provided for the marketing site.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The policy mentions use of analytics tools and reCAPTCHA (which collects behavioral data like mouse movements) on the student platform for security purposes; while not for advertising, web beacon/tracking technology use within the service is not fully enumerated.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: A cookie preference manager is provided for the business website to disable targeted advertising cookies, and Google Analytics opt-out is explicitly documented; student platform is stated to have no advertising data sharing.

dataCollected: Social login profile data (Apple, Google, Facebook, Shopify)
dataSharedWith: Payment processors (Shop Pay, Stripe, Affirm, Afterpay, PayPal, Google Pay)
r793.riskReason: xTool is a consumer hardware/e-commerce platform actively marketed to K-12 schools but with no COPPA or FERPA compliance statements, no minimum age requirement, no parental consent mechanism, and confirmed use of third-party advertising tracking (Google Analytics, interest-based ads) that is inappropriate for student users.
r793.parentSummary: xTool collects personal data including name, email, phone, address, device identifiers, usage data, and cookies for account management, order fulfillment, analytics, and marketing — including interest-based advertising via Google Analytics and third-party ad networks. While xTool states it does not sell data of users it knows to be under 16, the platform has no minimum age requirement, no parental consent process, and makes no COPPA or FERPA compliance claims, posing significant privacy risks when used by K-12 students. Schools considering xTool should be aware that the platform's data practices are designed for adult consumers and have not been adapted for the student-user context required by federal education privacy law.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The Terms of Use states material changes will be notified 30 days in advance, but the privacy policy indicates updates may be made via policy page posting without a guaranteed advance notice period, making notification incomplete.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy policy lists several data categories (name, email, device IDs, usage data, cookies, geolocation, payment info) but uses open-ended language like 'may include' and 'other information,' making the list non-exhaustive.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The privacy policy specifically describes how data is collected: directly from users at account creation, automatically via cookies/web beacons/server logs, and from third-party sign-on and analytics partners.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The privacy policy designates xTool as the 'Controller' of personal data, but does not clearly affirm that users own their own data; ownership language is absent and control rests primarily with xTool.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users may delete their account to remove personal data, and the privacy policy references self-service deletion tools, but residual copies may be retained on backup systems after deletion, limiting full data removal.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The privacy policy states data is kept only as long as necessary and is retained until account deletion, but does not specify concrete retention periods (e.g., number of days or years) for different data types.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The privacy policy details specific security measures including SSL/TLS encryption in transit, password hashing, access controls, pseudonymization, role-based access, and incident response procedures.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: The policy explicitly states SSL/TLS encryption is used for data in transit and encryption safeguards are applied to data at rest, meeting the encryption standard.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The privacy policy advises users to use strong passwords but states this is the user's own responsibility rather than enforcing strong password requirements at the platform level.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No mention of multi-factor authentication (MFA) or SSO/LTI integration for school use is found in the Terms of Service or Privacy Policy; social login options are available but MFA is not offered or described.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The privacy policy mentions cookies, web beacons, pixels, and SDKs used for core functions, analytics, and advertising, and references a Cookie Settings tool, but does not provide a comprehensive named list of all cookies and their individual purposes.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: Some third parties are named (Shopify, Google Analytics, Zendesk, xTool Squad Hosts, payment processors), but the list is not comprehensive and advertising network partners are not individually identified.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: Data shared with Shopify and Zendesk is described at a category level (e.g., contact and booking details for Hosts, support history for Zendesk), but data shared with advertising networks and analytics partners is not broken down per third party.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can opt out of Google Analytics via a browser add-on and manage cookie-based advertising via Cookie Settings, but there is no simple, centralized opt-out from all third-party data sharing.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy states Trusted Third Parties must agree to confidentiality and security commitments, and Squad Hosts are under written agreements, but this general statement does not specifically enumerate binding vendor data protection requirements for all partners.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The privacy policy states that third-party changes may be communicated by updating the policy page itself, meaning users are not proactively notified of third-party changes but rather must re-check the policy periodically.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The privacy policy confirms that third-party advertising providers including Google Analytics deliver interest-based ads on xTool's behalf, meaning targeted ads are present and not limited to platform-based promotions.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: The privacy policy confirms interest-based and behavioral advertising via third-party ad providers, and the passport policy explicitly states Google Analytics is used for 'delivery of interest-based ads,' confirming user-targeted advertising.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Third-party tracking for advertising is confirmed (Google Analytics, web beacons, pixels), and opt-out options exist (Google opt-out add-on, Cookie Settings), but these are not prominently surfaced or easy to use for a school user.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The privacy policy explicitly lists web beacons, pixels, SDKs, and server logs used in combination with third-party ad networks for behavioral tracking and advertising measurement, confirming tracking for ad purposes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Cookie Settings and Google Ads opt-out options are mentioned, but there is no single, clear opt-out mechanism that covers all advertising-related data sharing, and the process is fragmented across multiple external tools.

r794.riskReason: xTool Creative Space is a consumer laser-design tool with no K-12-specific privacy protections, no COPPA or FERPA compliance statements, conflicting minimum age requirements (13 vs. 18), third-party ad network data sharing including behavioral tracking via cookies and pixels, no data use agreement for schools, and no prohibition on using student data for commercial or advertising purposes.
r794.parentSummary: xTool Creative Space (XCS) collects account information (name, email, password), device identifiers, usage logs, and design content, and shares data with affiliated companies worldwide, payment processors, cloud providers, and advertising/analytics partners including Google and social media platforms. The platform does not have a dedicated K-12 or student privacy policy, does not claim COPPA or FERPA compliance, and uses behavioral tracking technologies (cookies, web beacons, pixels, SDKs) that may support targeted advertising. Parents should be aware that this platform was designed for adult hobbyists and laser machine operators, not for school-age students, and lacks the contractual and technical safeguards typically required for K-12 use.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The Terms of Service states 30 days' advance notice for material adverse changes, but no revision history or policy changelog is provided on the policy page itself.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy policy enumerates multiple specific data categories including Identity Data, Contact Data, Financial Data, Services Data, Profile Data, Content Data, Usage Data, Technical Identifiers, Device Data, and Marketing/Communications Data.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The privacy policy specifically describes three collection methods: direct interactions (account creation, support), automated technologies (cookies, server logs, web beacons, pixels, SDKs), and third-party sources.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The policy states xTool acts as the 'Controller' of personal data and content submitted by users is treated as non-confidential, with no explicit statement that users own their data; ownership is ambiguous.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users may request account deletion by contacting xTool, but deletion requires contacting support rather than a self-service option, and residual copies may remain in backups without being linked to personal information.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy states data is retained until the user requests deletion or for as long as necessary for legitimate business purposes, but no specific time periods (e.g., in days or months) are given for most data categories.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The privacy policy mentions 'reasonable safeguards' and one version references TLS encrypted transmission and hierarchical access control, but the primary xtool.com policy only offers a general security statement without listing specific measures.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: One Xtool policy variant references TLS encrypted transmission, but the main xtool.com privacy policy does not explicitly confirm encryption in transit or at rest, making this only partially addressed.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The policy and terms of service make no mention of password strength requirements or enforcement of strong passwords; sign-up requires email and a user-set password with no stated complexity rules.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: No mention of multi-factor authentication (MFA), SSO, or LTI integration is found in any of the xTool policies or support documentation for XCS accounts.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The privacy policy mentions cookies and similar technologies (web beacons, pixels, SDKs) and references a 'Cookie Settings' link, but does not provide a full cookie list with individual names, types, and purposes as required for full compliance.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The policy names broad categories of third parties (Shopify, payment processors, cloud providers, ad networks) and some specific companies (Amazon, Microsoft, YouTube, Facebook), but does not provide a comprehensive named list of all third-party processors.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy groups data shared with third parties by category (e.g., Identity Data, Contact Data shared with processors) rather than specifying exactly what data each named third party receives.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can opt out of marketing-related tracking via the Cookie Settings link, browser Do Not Track signals, or email unsubscribe, but no clear opt-out from all third-party data sharing (particularly ad networks) is offered.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The policy states that Trusted Third Parties must commit to keeping personal data confidential, but this is a general claim with no reference to formal data processing agreements or equivalent contractual obligations for all vendors.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The policy states that changes to third-party relationships may be communicated by updating the privacy policy itself, but does not commit to direct user notification when third-party data sharing partners change.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The privacy policy and passport policy confirm that third-party ad networks and advertising partners receive user data, and behavioral tracking via cookies/pixels is used for advertising purposes, indicating targeted ads may be served.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: The policy explicitly lists 'ad networks and advertising partners' as data recipients and describes behavioral tracking via cookies, web beacons, and pixels for advertising, indicating user-level targeting is confirmed.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Third-party ad networks (including Facebook and YouTube integrations) place cookies and pixels that track user behavior, and while some opt-out mechanisms are mentioned (e.g., platform ad settings), no comprehensive opt-out from all third-party tracking is available.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The policy explicitly states the platform uses 'web beacons, pixels, server logs, SDKs, and similar technologies' for behavioral tracking, and third-party social widgets may collect traffic data even when not actively used.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Users can opt out of marketing tracking via Cookie Settings, Do Not Track browser settings, or email unsubscribe links, but the process is not straightforward and does not clearly cover all advertising data-sharing scenarios.

r796.riskReason: YouScience claims COPPA and FERPA compliance and has a detailed Data Privacy Addendum, but the Terms of Use grant YouScience a perpetual, irrevocable license over 'Operational Data,' third-party cookies are used without a granular cookie policy, specific subprocessors are not named publicly, and policy change notifications are not clearly defined as advance notice.
r796.parentSummary: YouScience collects student names, school IDs, aptitude and interest assessment results, career data, certification scores, and usage/device data to provide its college and career readiness platform. For students under 13, the platform relies on schools to provide COPPA consent on behalf of parents, and states that student-generated content is owned by parents or guardians of minor students. Notably, YouScience grants itself a perpetual, irrevocable license over aggregated/de-identified 'Operational Data' and uses third-party cookies, though it states it will not share personally identifiable user data without express consent outside of service provision.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The Privacy Policy states it 'may change at any time' and users are advised to 'review it regularly,' but no advance notification process or revision history is explicitly promised.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The Privacy Policy enumerates multiple categories of data collected including name, school ID, grade, assessment results, device info, usage data, and data from third-party sources.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The policy clearly states data is collected directly from users upon account creation and assessments, automatically via device/usage tracking, and from third-party subprocessors and sponsors.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The Data Privacy Addendum states parents/guardians own minor student-generated content and schools retain Sponsor Data, but YouScience claims full ownership of all 'Operational Data' (de-identified/aggregated data), and the Terms of Use grant YouScience a perpetual irrevocable license over Operational Data.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users may request account cancellation by emailing support, but deletion of data within Sponsor Data requires sponsor approval and is not guaranteed, making full self-service deletion unavailable.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The Privacy Policy states data is retained only as long as there is a 'legitimate business purpose' and lists factors considered, but no specific retention periods in days or months are stated, making this vague.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The compliance page references NIST framework adherence, and the DPA references 'Data Security' obligations, but specific technical security measures (e.g., encryption standards, access controls) are not enumerated in the public-facing privacy policy.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: No explicit mention of encryption protocols (e.g., TLS, AES) is made in the Privacy Policy or Terms of Use; the site itself uses HTTPS but this is not documented in policy.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: The Terms of Use require users to maintain password confidentiality but do not specify enforcement of password strength requirements; SSO is available as an option.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: SSO/single sign-on is supported as an option for school sponsors, which satisfies MFA-equivalent requirements for institutional users, but MFA is not mentioned for individual account logins.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: The Privacy Policy acknowledges use of both first-party and third-party cookies but does not provide a specific list of cookies, their names, or individual purposes as required for a full cookie policy.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The Privacy Policy references categories of third parties (subprocessors, analytics providers, payment providers, sponsors, certification providers) but does not name specific companies.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: Third-party categories and general data shared are described, but specific data elements shared with each individual third party are not itemized.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can opt out of marketing emails and optional employer/post-secondary sharing features, but there is no clear opt-out mechanism for subprocessor data sharing.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The Data Privacy Addendum explicitly states that YouScience imposes data protection terms on all subprocessors providing the same level of protection as the DPA, and remains responsible for subprocessor acts and omissions.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The Privacy Policy does not include any provision notifying users when third-party subprocessors are added or changed; only general policy update language is present.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: The Privacy Policy and Terms of Use contain no mention of advertising being displayed to users on the platform; the platform appears to be ad-free for students.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: There is no indication that student data is used for targeted advertising; the platform's stated data uses are limited to service delivery, improvement, and educational purposes.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Third-party cookies are acknowledged as placed by 'other parties we work with to collect information about your use,' which could include analytics tracking, but no opt-out mechanism for these third-party cookies is described.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: The use of third-party cookies is disclosed generally, but specific tracking technologies (e.g., web beacons, pixel tags) and their purposes are not enumerated, leaving the scope of tracking unclear.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Users can opt out of marketing emails and optional employer-sharing features, but no explicit opt-out for data sharing with third-party analytics or subprocessors in the context of advertising or tracking is described.

r797.riskReason: YouTube is a general consumer advertising platform that collects extensive behavioral and device data for targeted advertising, has a documented history of COPPA violations resulting in a $170 million FTC settlement, and is not designed or contracted as an educational tool with FERPA protections, making it unsuitable as a primary K-12 instructional platform without strict controls.
r797.parentSummary: YouTube, operated by Google, collects a wide range of personal data including watch history, search history, device identifiers, location, and IP address, and uses this data in part to serve personalized advertisements to users. While Google states it does not sell personal information and offers data deletion tools, YouTube was fined $170 million in 2019 for illegally collecting data on children under 13 without parental consent, and although post-settlement changes limit data collection on 'Made for Kids' content, the platform remains a general consumer advertising service not built for K-12 compliance. Parents should be aware that students using YouTube outside of designated child-safe channels may be subject to broad behavioral tracking and targeted advertising.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The Google Privacy Policy states changes are indicated with a published date, archived versions are available for review, and significant changes include advance notice or email notification; the YouTube ToS similarly commits to reasonable advance notice for material changes.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The Google Privacy Policy comprehensively lists data collected including account info, device identifiers, location, usage activity, content uploaded, and interaction data, providing a thorough enumeration of data types.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The Privacy Policy specifically describes how data is collected — through account creation, device sensors, cookies, service interactions, and third-party site/app integrations — meeting the standard for specific collection method disclosure.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: Google states it does not claim ownership over user-generated content, and users retain rights to their content, but the broad content license granted to Google and the extensive use of behavioral data for commercial purposes creates unclear effective ownership of derived data.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users can delete their Google Account (closing their YouTube channel and removing data), delete individual videos, clear watch/search history, and use Google Takeout to export data; however, aggregate analytics derived from deleted content may persist.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: Google publishes a detailed data retention policy explaining that some data is kept until deleted by the user, some is automatically deleted, and advertising data (e.g., anonymized server logs) is retained for defined periods such as 9–18 months before further anonymization.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: The Privacy Policy references security measures generally and mentions processes for safe deletion, but does not enumerate specific technical security controls (e.g., encryption standards, access controls, penetration testing) in the public-facing policy.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: YouTube uses HTTPS for data transmission, providing encryption in transit, but the Privacy Policy does not explicitly detail encryption at rest or specify encryption standards applied to stored user data.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: A Google Account is required for full YouTube functionality and Google enforces minimum password standards during account creation, but the policy does not explicitly state strong password enforcement requirements in user-facing documentation.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: Google offers optional two-factor authentication (2FA) for Google Accounts, which covers YouTube; however, MFA is not mandatory and YouTube does not natively support SSO/LTI integrations required for institutional K-12 deployments.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: Google's cookie policy pages describe categories of cookies used (functional, analytics, advertising) and their purposes, but the disclosure is spread across multiple pages rather than a single consolidated cookie list, making it partially meeting the standard.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The Privacy Policy broadly references sharing with 'affiliates,' 'service providers,' and 'advertising partners' but does not provide a specific named list of all third-party companies receiving user data, falling short of full disclosure.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The Privacy Policy groups data sharing by purpose category (e.g., service providers, legal compliance, advertisers) rather than specifying exactly which data types are shared with each named third party, providing only partial transparency.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can adjust ad personalization settings and opt out of targeted advertising via Google Ad Settings, but opting out of all third-party data sharing is not straightforward, and some sharing (e.g., with service providers) cannot be opted out of while using the service.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The Privacy Policy states that third-party service providers must process data 'based on our instructions and in compliance with our Privacy Policy and any other appropriate confidentiality and security measures,' indicating a general contractual obligation but without specific vendor agreement details.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The Privacy Policy notes that changes will be communicated when significant, but does not specifically commit to notifying users when new third-party data-sharing relationships are established or when existing third-party partners change.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: YouTube displays targeted advertisements to general (non-child-directed) content viewers, including personalized ads based on watch history and cross-service behavioral data, which is incompatible with K-12 use standards.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Google's Privacy Policy explicitly describes using activity data across services to serve personalized ads, including using YouTube watch history to target ads on other sites, confirming user-level behavioral targeting for non-child-directed content.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: YouTube and Google use persistent identifiers, cookies, and cross-site tracking technologies for advertising purposes on non-child-directed content, with only partial opt-out available through Ad Settings; complete opt-out of all tracking is not possible while using the service.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Google uses cookies, pixel tracking, and persistent identifiers for advertising across YouTube and third-party sites that embed YouTube content, with these tracking methods confirmed for advertising purposes in non-child-directed contexts.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Google provides an Ad Settings page where users can view and adjust ad personalization preferences and turn off personalized ads, but the opt-out process is spread across multiple settings menus and does not prevent all forms of data collection for advertising purposes.

r798.riskReason: YouTube Kids has implemented meaningful COPPA protections including no personalized ads for children and parental controls, but third-party advertising cookies are still set on child-directed content, the platform has a prior $170M FTC COPPA settlement, ongoing litigation over data retention, and no formal FERPA school-official agreement exists making it unsuitable as a school-deployed EdTech tool without district-level review.
r798.parentSummary: YouTube Kids collects device information, IP address, and usage data such as your child's watch and search history to recommend content and display contextual (non-personalized) ads; if you sign in with a Google Account, additional data including voice search recordings may be stored with your child's Google profile. Google states it does not sell children's personal information and does not serve personalized ads to children, but third-party partners may still place advertising-related cookies on the device for measurement and fraud-prevention purposes. Parents have meaningful controls including the ability to pause or clear watch/search history, block content, and unlink Google Accounts, though the platform is primarily designed for home use and lacks a formal school-data-processing agreement required for FERPA-compliant school deployment.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The Terms of Service state that material changes will be communicated with reasonable advance notice and opportunity to review, but urgent situations and new feature launches may take effect immediately without prior notice, making the process incomplete.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The YouTube Kids Privacy Notice explicitly enumerates categories of data collected including device info, IP address, log data, unique identifiers, and usage data such as watch/search history, and additionally lists account data collected when a parent signs in.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The Privacy Notice specifically explains that data is collected through the child's use of the app (e.g., watching videos), through device/app interaction with Google servers, and through parent-provided information during profile or account setup.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: The policy does not clearly assert that users own their data; Google claims broad rights to use collected data to provide, improve, and customize services, leaving ownership ambiguous rather than explicitly confirming it rests with the user or parent.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Parents can pause and clear watch/search history and unlink Google Accounts via parental settings, and Family Link provides tools to access and remove a child's data, but full account deletion requires going through Google's broader account deletion process and is not a simple in-app action.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy references general data retention practices tied to account or profile existence and the ability to clear history, but does not specify concrete retention periods in days or months for any category of collected data.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: Google's privacy terms reference employing advanced security infrastructure and built-in security technologies to detect and protect against threats, but the YouTube Kids-specific Privacy Notice does not list concrete technical security measures such as encryption standards or access controls.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: Google generally employs industry-standard encryption across its services and the site uses HTTPS, but the YouTube Kids Privacy Notice does not explicitly state that child data is encrypted at rest or in transit, making this only partially verifiable from the policy text.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: YouTube Kids can be used without any account or sign-in at all, and when a Google Account is used it leverages Google's account security infrastructure; the no-account-required option satisfies this criterion for the primary child-facing use case.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: Google Accounts support 2-step verification and the platform supports Google Family Link supervised account management, but MFA is not enforced or required for the parent account managing YouTube Kids, making this only an optional rather than mandatory control.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: Google's broader privacy policy and a research report confirm that advertising-purpose cookies (NID, IDE, VISITOR_INFO1_LIVE) are set during YouTube Kids sessions, but the YouTube Kids-specific Privacy Notice does not provide a comprehensive list of cookies used with their individual purposes.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: The Privacy Notice states data is shared with affiliates and 'trusted businesses or persons' who process data on Google's behalf, and mentions third-party advertising partners may use cookies, but does not name specific third-party vendors or partners by name.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policy describes categories of sharing (aggregated trends to partners, individual data to service providers, account info within family groups) but does not enumerate which specific data elements are shared with each distinct third-party category.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Parents can pause and clear watch/search history and unlink accounts to limit some data use, but there is no straightforward opt-out mechanism specifically for third-party advertising cookie placement, which requires browser-level controls outside the app.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: The Privacy Notice states that third-party service providers process data 'based on our instructions and in compliance with our Privacy Policy and any other appropriate confidentiality and security measures,' indicating a general contractual obligation but not citing specific vendor agreements or audits.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: The Terms of Service indicate users will receive reasonable advance notice of material changes but do not specifically commit to notifying users when third-party service provider relationships change, and changes for legal or urgent reasons may occur without prior notice.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: YouTube Kids displays contextual ads based on the video being watched (not the child's profile), and paid product placements and traditional advertisements from creators are prohibited in the app, but non-personalized contextual ads are still shown to children.

r801.riskReason: Zoho Show is a general-purpose business productivity tool not designed for K-12 use; it lacks explicit COPPA/FERPA compliance statements, has no K-12-specific data handling commitments, and while it pledges no advertising or data selling, its minimum age of 13 and general-audience TOS create compliance gaps for schools deploying it with students under 13.
r801.parentSummary: Zoho Show collects personal information such as names, email addresses, device details, and usage data when users create accounts and use the platform. Zoho explicitly commits to never selling user data or showing ads, uses strong encryption (TLS 1.2/1.3 in transit and AES-256 at rest), and states that users own their own data. However, Zoho Show is a general business tool with no specific COPPA or FERPA compliance statements, and its Terms of Service require users to be of legal age to contract, making it unsuitable without school-level oversight and a Data Processing Addendum for use with students, especially those under 13.

complianceNotes.DCQ3: Zoho explicitly states 'You own the content created or stored by you' and 'You own your service data,' satisfying the user data ownership requirement.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users may request export or deletion of service data, and account termination triggers data deletion; some profile/post data may persist unless specifically requested for removal.

complianceNotes.SECQ3: Zoho's Terms of Service place responsibility for password confidentiality on the user and do not describe server-side enforcement of strong password rules.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: MFA (two-factor authentication via SMS) is available as an optional setting for Zoho accounts but is not mandatory, so it does not fully meet the requirement.

complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Because Zoho does not share data with advertisers and runs no advertising, there is nothing to opt out of; this commitment is stated as a permanent policy.

r826.riskReason: Flex Curriculum (AOEU) explicitly does not collect student data — only licensed teachers hold accounts — and expressly states that PII is owned by the customer, is not sold to third parties, and is stored on encrypted servers, presenting minimal risk for K-12 student data exposure.
r826.parentSummary: Flex Curriculum is a teacher-facing K-12 art curriculum platform operated by The Art of Education University (AOEU); students do not have accounts and AOEU explicitly states it does not collect student information. Teacher account data (name, email, phone, usage analytics) is collected, stored on encrypted servers, and not sold to third parties, with contractors bound by data protection agreements. Parents should be aware that curriculum content is delivered through the school's own LMS, so the privacy practices of that LMS also apply to student interactions with the material.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The policy states registered users will be notified of changes via email and each update will include a revision date, but the Terms and Conditions reserve the right to make changes without advance notice in some circumstances.

complianceNotes.SECQ2: The policy explicitly states user information is stored on encrypted servers, meeting the encryption standard for data at rest; transit encryption (HTTPS) is implied but not explicitly stated.

complianceNotes.SECQ4: No mention of multi-factor authentication (MFA), SSO, or LTI integration is made in the publicly available privacy policy or terms and conditions.

r827.riskReason: Flippity's privacy policy explicitly states it does not collect or have access to user personal information, operates without user accounts, and stores activity content in Google Sheets owned and controlled by the teacher — minimizing virtually all K-12 data privacy risks.
r827.parentSummary: Flippity is a free, account-free tool that converts Google Sheets into classroom activities like flashcards and quizzes. According to its privacy policy, Flippity does not collect or access any personal information from users, as all content lives in the teacher's own Google Sheets. Because no student data is collected or stored by Flippity itself, the privacy risk to students is very low, though Google's own data practices apply separately when students interact with published Google Sheets.

r828.parentSummary: The Florida Center for Reading Research (FCRR), operated by Florida State University, does not appear to publish a standalone Privacy Policy or Terms of Service on its website (fcrr.org), making it impossible to determine what data is collected from student or educator users, how it is used, or what protections are in place. The FSU parent institution does maintain general privacy and FERPA policies, but these are not surfaced or linked from the FCRR platform itself. Until a dedicated, K-12-specific privacy policy is published, schools and parents cannot make an informed assessment of data risks for minors using this platform.

Any optional features like usage statistics or face gestures store data exclusively on the user's device and are never transmitted. The only data that touches forScore's servers is anonymized Apple receipt data used solely for transaction verification, which is not stored.

r830.riskReason: Gibbs-Smith's privacy policy explicitly enables targeted advertising using personal data, shares data with advertising partners and Google Analytics, does not respond to Do Not Track signals, has no COPPA or FERPA compliance statements, and sets no minimum age requirement for the platform, making it unsuitable for K-12 deployment without significant additional safeguards.
r830.parentSummary: Gibbs-Smith collects personal information including names, addresses, payment details, email, phone numbers, and detailed browsing behavior; this data is shared with Shopify, Google Analytics, advertising partners, and business affiliates to fulfill orders and deliver targeted advertisements. The platform does not specify a minimum user age, makes no COPPA or FERPA compliance claims, and explicitly states it does not honor Do Not Track browser signals. Parents should be aware that the site uses advertising and social media cookies and shares browsing data with third-party advertisers, which poses significant risks for student users.

r831.riskReason: Goodnotes sets a minimum age of 16 (not 13), does not sell personal data, and uses encryption, but it engages in targeted advertising and shares customer data with Google for ad-matching purposes, and does not explicitly claim COPPA or FERPA compliance, creating notable risks for K-12 deployment especially with students under 16.
r831.parentSummary: Goodnotes collects basic account information (name, email, country), usage data, and optionally diagnostic or AI feature data, primarily to deliver and improve the app. The platform does not sell personal data and employs encryption (AES-256 at rest, TLS 1.2+ in transit), but it does use cookies and shares customer data with Google for targeted advertising purposes. Parents should be aware that Goodnotes requires users to be at least 16 years old to self-register, meaning parental or guardian account creation is required for younger students, and the platform does not explicitly claim COPPA or FERPA compliance.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: The TOS states Goodnotes will 'do our best to notify you before any changes take effect' and paid users receive 30-day advance notice, but notification is not guaranteed for all users and no formal revision history is published.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The privacy policy and its California supplement enumerate specific categories of data collected including identifiers, contact info, usage data, commercial/transaction data, and device/IP data.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: The privacy policy clearly explains data is collected via account registration, automatic collection (cookies, device data), third-party social logins, Google Workspace APIs, and customer support interactions.

complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users can request erasure of personal data via the Goodnotes app or by contacting support, and deletion rights are acknowledged under GDPR, CCPA, and VCDPA frameworks.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: The policy states data is retained as long as necessary for service purposes or legal requirements, and inactive cloud data is deleted after two years with advance notice, but no single specific retention period is stated for all data categories.

complianceNotes.SECQ2: Goodnotes explicitly states data is encrypted at rest using AES-256 and in transit using TLS 1.2 or greater, representing full encryption coverage.

complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Users can opt out of targeted advertising cookies through the cookie consent mechanism, but the policy also relies on 'legitimate interests' for some profiling activities, making the opt-out process only partially effective.

r832.riskReason: Google AI Studio explicitly requires users to be 18 or older, is not designed for K-12 use, and on the free tier actively uses all submitted content—including prompts and uploaded files—to train AI models with possible human review, making it fundamentally unsuitable and potentially unlawful for use with K-12 students without a paid enterprise agreement.
r832.parentSummary: Google AI Studio is a developer-focused AI platform that requires users to be at least 18 years old and is not intended for K-12 students. On the free tier, all data submitted—including every prompt, uploaded file, and generated response—may be used by Google to improve its AI models and may be reviewed by human annotators, with no opt-out available. This platform lacks COPPA or FERPA compliance documentation for K-12 contexts and should not be used with students unless accessed through a paid enterprise Google Workspace for Education agreement, which carries different data protections.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: Google's Privacy Policy indicates a version/effective date and users are notified of material changes, but changes on continued use may take effect immediately, making advance notice incomplete for a K-12 context.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: The Gemini API Additional Terms of Service and Google Privacy Policy together provide a detailed enumeration of data collected including prompts, responses, uploaded files, usage metrics, device identifiers, IP addresses, cookies, and account information.
complianceNotes.DCQ2: Google's policies specifically describe how data is collected via direct user input, cookies, pixel tags, local storage, server logs, and automated systems, clearly addressing collection mechanisms.
complianceNotes.DCQ3: On the free (unpaid) tier, Google claims a broad license to use all submitted content and responses to improve its products and ML models, effectively asserting significant rights over user-submitted data with no clear statement of user data ownership.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Users can delete data via Google Account controls and My Activity, but reviewed/annotated training data from the free tier may be retained in anonymized form and deletion from backup systems may take up to two months, limiting full deletion.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: Google provides general retention statements (e.g., reviewed chats retained up to three years, advertising data auto-deleted, account data kept until deletion) but does not provide a single clear retention schedule specific to AI Studio inputs and outputs.
complianceNotes.SECQ1: Google explicitly lists specific security measures including encryption in transit and at rest, Safe Browsing, Security Checkup, 2-Step Verification, physical security reviews, and restricted employee access.
complianceNotes.SECQ2: Google states it uses encryption to keep data private while in transit and encrypts data at rest in its data centers, satisfying this requirement.
complianceNotes.SECQ3: Google AI Studio requires sign-in via an existing Google Account, which enforces Google's own strong password and account security policies, effectively meeting this standard.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: Google accounts support 2-Step Verification and Google SSO is used for authentication into AI Studio, meeting the MFA/SSO requirement.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: Google publishes a detailed cookie policy at policies.google.com/technologies/cookies listing specific cookies (e.g., SID, HSID, _ga, AEC) with their names, purposes, and durations.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: Google's policies reference sharing with 'trusted partners,' 'service providers,' and 'human reviewers' but do not provide a specific named list of all third-party vendors used for AI Studio processing.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The policies group data sharing with third parties broadly (e.g., for processing, security, legal reasons) without specifying exactly which data types are shared with each distinct third party.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: On the free tier, there is no opt-out from data use for model training and human review; the only option is to upgrade to a paid tier, which is a significant barrier and not a straightforward opt-out.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: Google states that third-party processors must comply with its Privacy Policy and confidentiality obligations, but this is described in general terms rather than with specific contractual accountability language for each sub-processor.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: Google's Privacy Policy states users will be notified of material changes, but the policy may be updated at any time and does not specifically commit to notifying users before new third-party processors are added to AI Studio.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: Google states it does not use content from Drive, Gmail, or AI Studio for advertising, and AI Studio itself does not display traditional ads; however, Google's broader advertising ecosystem relies on user data, creating partial concern.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Google states it does not use sensitive information or AI Studio inputs to personalize ads, and does not share personally identifiable info with advertisers, but aggregate behavioral data across Google's ecosystem may inform ad targeting.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Google uses cookies and similar technologies for ad measurement and tracking across its ecosystem; while AI Studio itself is not ad-supported, Google's broader infrastructure includes third-party ad tracking technologies.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Google uses multiple tracking technologies (cookies, pixel tags, local storage, server logs, advertising IDs) across its platform; the full scope of tracking within AI Studio sessions is not separately delineated from Google's broader tracking infrastructure.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Google provides opt-out mechanisms for ad personalization via My Ad Center and account settings, but these controls apply to Google's broader ad ecosystem and are not specific to AI Studio data; the process is functional but not straightforward for K-12 administrators.

r833.riskReason: Google Maps is a general-audience consumer product not designed for K-12 use; it collects precise location data, uses advertising tracking technologies (cookies, pixel tags), and shares data broadly with advertising partners, presenting significant risks when used by students without the protections of Google Workspace for Education.
r833.parentSummary: Google Maps collects detailed location data, search history, device identifiers, and usage activity, and may use this information for personalized advertising unless the child's account is managed through Google Family Link or Google Workspace for Education. When used as a standalone consumer app outside of Google Workspace for Education, Maps does not carry the student-specific privacy protections required for K-12 compliance, meaning advertising trackers and third-party data sharing may apply. Parents and schools should be aware that Google Maps is classified as an 'Additional Service' within Google Workspace for Education, is off by default for K-12, and requires parental consent before use, indicating it is not considered a safe default tool for students.

complianceNotes.GENQ1: Google's Privacy Policy states it will provide prominent notice (including email) for significant changes, but does not maintain a clearly accessible, versioned revision history for Maps-specific terms.
complianceNotes.DCQ1: Google's Privacy Policy comprehensively lists data types collected including location, device info, IP address, cookies, usage activity, and user-contributed content.

r834.riskReason: Google Translate (consumer version) is not listed as a Google Workspace for Education Core Service, does not have a dedicated K-12 data privacy agreement, collects and processes submitted text and usage data for Google's broad advertising and AI ecosystem, and has been identified as potentially COPPA non-compliant for K-12 student use without additional school-level controls.
r834.parentSummary: Google Translate collects the text students enter for translation, along with device identifiers, IP address, usage data, and cookies, which are processed under Google's broad consumer privacy policy that permits use of data for advertising and service improvement across Google's ecosystem. Unlike Google Workspace for Education, the consumer Google Translate service does not carry specific FERPA or COPPA protections or a Data Processing Agreement tailored for schools, meaning student data entered into the tool may be subject to Google's general advertising and analytics data practices. Parents and schools should be aware that pasting sensitive or personally identifiable student information into Google Translate may not meet FERPA obligations, and a dedicated K-12-compliant translation tool is recommended instead.

complianceNotes.DCQ1: Google's Privacy Policy lists broad categories of data collected (content, device info, usage, location, cookies) but does not enumerate every specific data type collected by Google Translate individually.

complianceNotes.DCQ3: Google's ToS states users retain intellectual property rights in their content, but also grants Google a broad worldwide license to use, host, store, reproduce, and modify submitted content, making effective data ownership unclear for K-12 purposes.
complianceNotes.DCQ4: Google provides account-level deletion tools (My Activity, Dashboard) that allow users to delete translation history, but server-side logs, analytics, and already-processed data may persist beyond visible deletion.
complianceNotes.DCQ5: Google's Privacy Policy acknowledges different retention periods for different data types but does not specify a concrete retention period for Google Translate content or usage logs, making this vague.

complianceNotes.SECQ3: Google Translate can be used without an account; when an account is used, Google enforces password standards and supports strong authentication, satisfying this criterion.
complianceNotes.SECQ4: Google accounts support 2-Step Verification and the Advanced Protection Program, and the service can be used without an account, satisfying MFA/SSO availability requirements.
complianceNotes.SECQ5: Google's Privacy Policy mentions cookies and links to a separate cookie policy with categories, but does not list all cookies used specifically by Google Translate with their individual purposes.
complianceNotes.SHRQ1: Google's Privacy Policy references broad categories of third parties (service providers, advertising partners, other businesses) but does not name specific third-party companies that receive data from Google Translate usage.
complianceNotes.SHRQ2: The Privacy Policy groups data sharing by purpose rather than specifying exactly what data is shared with each named third party, leaving per-third-party data disclosure incomplete.
complianceNotes.SHRQ3: Users can adjust ad personalization settings and opt out of some data uses via Google Account settings, but opt-out is partial and complex, particularly for non-account users or minors.
complianceNotes.SHRQ4: Google states that contractors and service providers must follow agreements consistent with its Privacy Policy, but does not provide detailed contractual obligations specific to Google Translate data handling.
complianceNotes.SHRQ5: Google's Privacy Policy states users will be notified of significant changes, but does not specifically commit to notifying users when new third parties are added to Google Translate's data sharing arrangements.
complianceNotes.ADVQ1: Google's Privacy Policy explicitly states that user data, including activity across services, is used to deliver personalized advertisements, and Google Translate usage data may inform cross-service ad targeting.
complianceNotes.ADVQ2: Google confirms that activity data from its services, potentially including Translate usage, may be used for personalized and targeted advertising based on user behavior and interests.
complianceNotes.ADVQ3: Google Translate uses cookies and device identifiers that feed into Google's advertising ecosystem, and while opt-outs exist they are limited; third-party tracking via Google's ad network is confirmed.
complianceNotes.ADVQ4: Google uses cookies, device identifiers, and usage logs across services including Translate for advertising measurement and targeting, which constitutes tracking for ad purposes beyond functional necessity.
complianceNotes.ADVQ5: Google provides Ad Settings and opt-out controls for personalized ads, but the process is not straightforward for K-12 contexts and does not fully prevent data use for advertising infrastructure.

r835.riskReason: GPB KIDS does not require student logins, explicitly prohibits selling student data or using it for targeted advertising, includes a dedicated Student Privacy Notice referencing FERPA, and limits third-party tracking pixels to non-educational general audience pages only.
r835.parentSummary: GPB KIDS does not require students to create accounts or submit personal information for educational use; only anonymous browser/usage data and cookies are collected automatically. The platform explicitly states it will not sell student data or use it for targeted advertising, and parents, teachers, or guardians can request deletion of any personally identifiable student data by contacting digital@gpb.org. Third-party tracking pixels (including Facebook) are used only on general audience pages and are stated to be excluded from children's or educational content areas.

r838.riskReason: I'm a Puzzle actively shares user data including hashed emails and IP addresses with numerous third-party advertising networks for interest-based targeting, displays ads, and explicitly states it does not knowingly collect data from users under 18—not under 13—making it wholly unsuitable for K-12 deployment without significant safeguards.
r838.parentSummary: I'm a Puzzle (im-a-puzzle.com), operated by Unwind Media, collects data such as IP addresses, email addresses (in hashed form), browser and device information, and usage data, which is shared with multiple advertising partners including Amazon, Google, LiveRamp, and others for interest-based advertising purposes. The platform explicitly states it does not solicit data from users under 18 years of age and will deactivate accounts if such data is discovered, but it provides no COPPA-specific parental consent mechanism or K-12 school compliance provisions. No account is required to play puzzles, but the site displays ads and uses tracking cookies and web beacons, posing meaningful privacy risks for minors.

The platform is restricted to users 13 and older (with limited supervised use of custom puzzles for younger children), but there is no explicit COPPA or FERPA compliance statement, no parental consent mechanism, and no clear process for users to request deletion of their data. Schools should exercise caution and consider limiting student use to ad-free custom puzzle links only.
